messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] When does the data dominates the posterior distribution?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] When does the data dominates the posterior distribution?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Bob, thank you for your time!

I get why this is not very useful in general, however in this particular case (epidemic data) it is important because I want to determine the earliest date at which we can produce reliable estimates (and whether using informative priors allow to produce estimates at an earlier date, which is always good when epidemics are ongoing). Informative priors are rarely used in my field, and we're doing a sort of simulation study to highlitght the advantages.

So using a conjugate example won't help much here, as I already have a model that I'm interested in. I already plotted the posterior and prior distributions and it works as intended, but I would like a measure of divergence to systematically compare my (numerous) models. I take from your point that I could include the computation of the KL divergence directly in Stan (maybe in the generated quantities)?

Best regards,
Julien

On Tuesday, February 28, 2017 at 8:52:49 PM UTC+1, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> This is good to think about for understanding, but in practice, isn't very useful.  We just want to put in a prior based on what we know.  It's just as much a part of the model as the likelihood, and we don't want to be thinking in terms of how we code it so it gets washed out.
>
> You might be able to get a decent feel for what's going on with a simple conjugate example (let's say normal with fixed variance or a beta distribution).  You can see that where the prior starts and how much it's concentrated matters.  Michael Betancourt's about to roll out a nice case study where you can see how much the fatness of the prior's tails (Cauchy vs. normal, say) and the consistency of the prior (is the posterior concentrating in the trunk or the tails) make a big difference.
>
> No idea about FNN.  KL-divergence requires computing an integral, which you
> can compute in one direction with MCMC if you have draws from the posterior and
> an analytic prior.   But you're probably better served by plotting out the
> priors and posteriors and seeing how the latter concentrate as a function of
> the prior and amount of data (and the variance in the data itself).
>
> - Bob
>
> > On Feb 28, 2017, at 5:54 AM, Julien Riou <julien...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Hi everyone,
> >
> > I have a probably naive question but I did not find a proper answer anywhere, so I apologize in advance.
> >
> > I have a time series on which I estimate a parameter (beta), and I want to know at which point in time does the data dominates the posterior distribution of my parameters (or in other words, at which point does the prior distribution not matter anymore). So my idea was to fit the model n times using data available until each date, and to measure the KL divergence between the prior and the posterior distribution computed at each point. I expect the KL divergence to be small at first when little data is provided, and to increase up to a plateau, at which point the posterior distribution depends mainly on the data.
> >
> > 1/ Is that a proper way to answer my question?
> >
> > 2/ I feel that my way of computing the KL-divergence is kind of rustic (using the nearest neighbor algorithm of package FNN), could someone confirm that this is correct (in particular considering the parameter k)?
> >
> > library(FNN)
> > beta_P <- rexp(length(R0_Q),rate=0.5) # my weakly informative prior distribution (exponential with rate 1/2), I follow a similar method with informative priors in another approach
> > beta_Q <- extract(S_D1_NIP,pars="beta")[[1]] # extract the posterior distribution
> >
> > mean(KL.divergence(beta_P ,beta_Q ,k=10)
> >
> > I hope that I was clear enough.
> >
> > Thanks in advance!
> > Julien
> >

messages.subject: Proposal to speed up grid-based GPs
messages.subject_clean: Proposal to speed up grid-based GPs
messages.body_plain:
Hi folks,

I came up with an idea to speed up sampling on Gaussian Processes when X is sampled on a grid, in which case the pairwise distance matrix has high redundancy (nX unique distances repeated over (nX^2-nX)/2 cells of the matrix for the 1D X case). By pre-computing the unique pairwise distances and their indices in the full pairwise distance matrix, you can compute unique values for the subsequent covariance matrix then fill the full covariance matrix using the aforementioned indices.

This ends up being about 2x faster than a standard GP (also faster than a GP where the pairwise distances are pre-computed, but uniqueness isn't considered) when the covariance matrix is computed by hand.

Now, I will note that computing on the unique distances then filling the covariance matrix by hand *isn't* much faster than using the in-built cov_exp_quad() function. Well, I have observed a 30% speedup over cov_exp_quad() in some situations, but that's not much to rave about. But where I have no idea what magic is happening in cov_exp_quad() to make it so fast, I wonder if there might be room to achieve further speedups (in, say, a new cov_exp_quad_grid() function that takes in the unique distances & indices thereof) by combining my ideas with whatever sourcery cov_exp_quad() is doing internally.

Thoughts?

Oh, and here's gist demonstrating the unique-distances approach with comparison to cov_exp_quad() and the non-unique-but-pre-computed-differences approaches:

https://gist.github.com/mike-lawrence/b56ac2d9450233837d426dd17fe20557

Mike

--
Mike Lawrence
Graduate Student
Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
Dalhousie University

~ Certainty is (possibly) folly ~

messages.body_plain:

and the posterior using posterior samples.  In general KL divergences
are incredibly difficult to estimate at all and hence they are of extremely
limited empirical use.  Ultimately there is little to be learned from trying
to quantify the qualitative results that you already have.

The following numerical problems occured the indicated number of times on chain 3
                                                                                                     count

I don't know why it'd be slow with fixed Sigma.

With variable Sigma, you should be using Cholesky factors,
or ideally, Cholesky factors of correlation matrices
with LKJ priors.

The rounding errors may be running off to -0.5 or + 0.5, forcing
the unconstrained parameters try to run off to + or - infinity.

I understand that you are assuming that the measurmeent is accurate
to +/- 0.5, but maybe loosening this assumption can help.

Too bad we don't have enough distributed functions to remove
the need for that loop.

I thought we'd squashed that symmetry bug.  But then this
model has problems that may make the symmetry a side-effect.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
I was able to get a one-dimensional PPCA working pretty well in some other constrained circumstances that would be applicable to some of my problems, but never was able to get it work (in the sense of having large N_eff for all variables and lp__) in a more general case that would work with any PPCA. Often, I would get a version working, then multiply the distribution by -1, re-run it, and get gibberish results.

One of my takeaways is the connection of PPCA to finite mixtures: any {w, z} will be equivalent to {-w, -z}. This will cause the mean of z to have a bimodal symmetric distribution a lot of the time. Sometimes also with the mean of w, depending on the assumptions. It can get pretty tricky.

I tend to think of it like: 50% of the time, the mean of w will be greater than or equal to zero, and w ~ N(mu(w+), sd_w), then the mean of z might be positive or negative depending on w, and z ~ N(mu(z(w+)), sd_z). And exactly the opposite the other 50% of the time.

I calculate a lambda score using a formula in Gelman's book and it is near zero after fitting the model (I noticed that non-centered parameterization helps most when lambda is above 0.5, indicating lots of pooling).
> > >>
> > >> On unit_normal and standardizing: the issue with the way you present them is that the x_raw's don't get identified. As a result, the N_eff's will be near zero for those, which is not a big deal, but it is a big deal for lp__. I really like being able to use lp__ as a diagnostic. I don't typically print all the variables to the screen, just the hyperparamters and lp__. If lp__ is near zero, then at that point I would inspect what's going on with the other variables, If not, then I assume they are fine. When I was using those x_raws, I would get into a habit of ignoring the lp__, so other things could be going wrong in the model and I wouldn't realize it until much later. The only thing I could think of is if the calculation of N_eff for lp__ understands to ignore transformed variables that are not part of the final model.
> > >>

> > >> unit_vector<lower=0>[N] w;

> > >> What I did in the model was enforce an approximate unit vector that was always positive (I don't think I can get it exact with this approach because I get imaginary numbers). The reason I included it is that the sign of z and the sign of w weren't identified in any way. Sometimes the model would output w>0 and some z[i] > 0 and sometimes it would output w<0 with that z[i] <0. Forcing w > 0 helped keep it identified in a way that putting priors on the mean of z could not. I got much better results when I included this constraint vs. doing the analysis with just the unit_vector. Indeed, the problem of nailing down the sign seems similar to the issue discussed in the Stan manual under "Inference under Label Switching" in the "Finite Mixtures" section. Unlike finite mixtures, you may not have the information necessary to put a prior that enforces the constraint in a more general PPCA model.
> > >>
> > >> A more general approach would probably to be something like below. This ensures that the largest square value is always positive. I haven't tried it yet and I don't know how well Stan would handle it, but I think it would be more useful than the positive_unit_vector above since it would allow sign identification in all these PPCA models, not just my specific case where I know all the w's are positive.

> > >>      unit_vector[N] raw_w;

> > >> transformed parameters {

> > >>
> > >>      w = raw_w;

> > >> > I have finally got to something that fits my data with reasonable N_eff using NUTS (300 of 1000 for lp__, 1000 of 1000 for all hyperparameters, rhats between 1 and 1.01) and thought I would share (below). ADVI also fits it reasonably well. Of the hyperparameters, sd_z was higher than NUTS and the standard deviations of mu_z and sd_z were bigger than NUTS. But overall, it looks like it fits it well.
> > >> >
> > >> > As many folks have noted, identification is very important for these PPCA-like models. What I really needed was a way to constrain w to be a positive unit normal vector. This isn't in Stan. However, I was able to make a close enough approximation by noting that var(w) should equal 1/N - mean(w)^2 for all unit vectors. The approach I took below uses this formula to constrain the mean. Since I didn't mind that w>0, it worked out pretty well. I also put a reasonably strong prior on the standard deviation of w, combined with constraints so mean(w) didn't have any imaginary variables in it.
> > >> >
> > >> > Another thing I tried was to constrain z to have mean of 0 AND standard deviation of 1. The approach usually fit the data well, but it can be hard to diagnose problems when you're not printing all the variables). > > >> > }

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

What you have in Stan is an array (N, C) dimensions whose elements are matrices of (K, D)  dimensions.
In R you need to shape the array in a way that you end with four dimensions (N, C, K, D) that you can supply to Stan. Even if arrays in R are column-major, and in Stan are in row-major, the program does the pertinent transformations.

You could use the print statement to check if the elements of the array that you pass ends in the right positions.

> On Mar 1, 2017, at 7:18 AM, Mike Lawrence <mike....@gmail.com> wrote:
>

> Hi folks,
>
> I came up with an idea to speed up sampling on Gaussian Processes when X is sampled on a grid, in which case the pairwise distance matrix has high redundancy (nX unique distances repeated over (nX^2-nX)/2 cells of the matrix for the 1D X case). By pre-computing the unique pairwise distances and their indices in the full pairwise distance matrix, you can compute unique values for the subsequent covariance matrix then fill the full covariance matrix using the aforementioned indices.
>
> This ends up being about 2x faster than a standard GP (also faster than a GP where the pairwise distances are pre-computed, but uniqueness isn't considered) when the covariance matrix is computed by hand.
>
> Now, I will note that computing on the unique distances then filling the covariance matrix by hand *isn't* much faster than using the in-built cov_exp_quad() function. Well, I have observed a 30% speedup over cov_exp_quad() in some situations, but that's not much to rave about. But where I have no idea what magic is happening in cov_exp_quad() to make it so fast, I wonder if there might be room to achieve further speedups (in, say, a new cov_exp_quad_grid() function that takes in the unique distances & indices thereof) by combining my ideas with whatever sourcery cov_exp_quad() is doing internally.
>
> Thoughts?
>
> Oh, and here's gist demonstrating the unique-distances approach with comparison to cov_exp_quad() and the non-unique-but-pre-computed-differences approaches:
>
> https://gist.github.com/mike-lawrence/b56ac2d9450233837d426dd17fe20557
>
> Mike

messages.body_plain:
Regarding speed-ups, one thing I've been thinking about lately is the way that lme4 speeds up computation by pre-computing X^tX.
In each step of the outer iteration, lme4 needs to compute X_*^tX_*, where X_* is an augmented version of X.  But in typical problems, most of this computation comes from the part of this that is X^tX.

The thing that's bugging me, though, is that X^tX is part of the (analytic) solution of the conditional MLE but it's _not_ part of the likelihood computation.  So it's not quite clear how Stan could make use of this pre-computation.  And maybe it's not possible to do this at all.  But I'd like to think it is.

A

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] When does the data dominates the posterior distribution?
messages.body_plain:
What do you mean by "a reliable estimate"?

Everything we're talking about here is model internal.  May I suggest
not putting so much trust in your model and rather going out and
trying to measure your models predictive calibration with real data?
Then you can start measuring the things you really care about.

- Bob

P.S.  I now see the problem with computing KL---we can't get the
normalizing term for the posterior density, which we need in the
expectation term.

Informative priors are rarely used in my field, and we're doing a sort of simulation study to highlitght the advantages.
>
> So using a conjugate example won't help much here, as I already have a model that I'm interested in. I already plotted the posterior and prior distributions and it works as intended, but I would like a measure of divergence to systematically compare my (numerous) models. I take from your point that I could include the computation of the KL divergence directly in Stan (maybe in the generated quantities)?
>
> Best regards,
> Julien
>
>
>
>
> On Tuesday, February 28, 2017 at 8:52:49 PM UTC+1, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> This is good to think about for understanding, but in practice, isn't very useful.  We just want to put in a prior based on what we know.  It's just as much a part of the model as the likelihood, and we don't want to be thinking in terms of how we code it so it gets washed out.
>
> You might be able to get a decent feel for what's going on with a simple conjugate example (let's say normal with fixed variance or a beta distribution).  You can see that where the prior starts and how much it's concentrated matters.  Michael Betancourt's about to roll out a nice case study where you can see how much the fatness of the prior's tails (Cauchy vs. normal, say) and the consistency of the prior (is the posterior concentrating in the trunk or the tails) make a big difference.
>
> No idea about FNN.  KL-divergence requires computing an integral, which you
> can compute in one direction with MCMC if you have draws from the posterior and

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Whassup with this simple bivariate normal model that's so damn slow and also throws weird exceptions?
messages.body_plain:
1000 data points but also 2 parameters per data point for 2000 total parameters.
Try fitting that many parameters in BUGS in three minutes!

Using the fixed hyperparameters I ran 4 chains and 3 ran really quickly but one
stalled and took about ten times as long as the rest.  The adaptation wasn’t off
for that chain, so it looks like it ended up getting stuck in an awkward region of
parameter space.

Looking at the energy diagnostic it looks like the posterior is might be heavy-tailed.
This is consistent with the performance variation — one chain could get stuck in
the tails and require very, very long trajectories to get back.  That motivates looking
at the treedepth/n_leapfrog…and indeed the slow chain did have _much_ longer
trajectories!  In three fast chains averaged around 15 leapfrog steps per transition
while the slow chain was saturating at the default threshold of 1023.

I didn’t see any obvious heavy-tailed behavior in the sample histograms, but I also
didn’t split anything up by chain.

The data clearly aren't informing the rounding error parameters at all (all of their
marginal histograms are uniform from -0.5 to 0.5) and this means that the posterior
density on the unconstrained scale is just the lower/upper bound Jacobian. If that
Jacobian looks heavy-tailed then we’d have the source of our problem.

Looks like those diagnostics really are useful...

Thanks again, Jonah.
I really appreciate your interest here. I have appended an RDS file I generated depicting data that looks like the data I am using (although I have vastly more data than this, it seemed sufficient for demonstration purposes). I have modified the variable names to match the example I provided in my original post. Participant is nested within experiment. As a refresher:

experiment_id: Unique ID for specific experiments
participant_id: Unique ID for specific participants
condition: conditions within the experiment (you could think of these as treatment groups, coded as 0 or 1)
design: whether condition is manipulated between- or within-subjects (coded within or between)
decision: Binary outcome variable

Using these data, I am fitting:

dat = readRDS("sample_dat.rds")

glmer_model = stan_glmer(decision ~ condition * design + (condition | participant_id) + (condition | experiment_id), data = dat, family = binomial)

I would like to be able to determine whether the difference between the two conditions is larger for within-subject designs than between-subject designs (so the interaction).

messages.body_plain:
Hey Mike, are you talking about a regular grid? Sounds to me like what
you have in mind is Toeplitz / circulant structure (e.g.
https://web.stanford.edu/~shenoy/GroupPublications/CunninghamShenoySahaniICML2008.pdf)

this structure. But the problem, as Bob discusses, is that getting any
of this implemented in Stan has proved to be quite the project in
terms of the plethora of specialized functions it all requires. And in
this case, I don't think Eigen has circulant / Toeplitz built in (but
maybe I just missed it while searching), so that's another factor to
consider.

Seth

messages.subject: Re: Proposal to speed up grid-based GPs
messages.subject_clean: Proposal to speed up grid-based GPs
messages.body_plain:
>  But where I have no idea what magic is happening in cov_exp_quad() to make it so fast,

In the current version most of the speedup comes from making the gradient computation faster by using analytic gradients for the end result of the computation instead of autodiffing through the small parts of the computation.
Similar speed-up can be obtained in also in other cases where such compound function can reduce the size of the autodiff expression tree considerably.

> I came up with an idea to speed up sampling on Gaussian Processes when X is sampled on a grid, in which case the pairwise distance matrix has high redundancy (nX unique distances repeated over (nX^2-nX)/2 cells of the matrix for the 1D X case). By pre-computing the unique pairwise distances and their indices in the full pairwise distance matrix, you can compute unique values for the subsequent covariance matrix then fill the full covariance matrix using the aforementioned indices.

This is called Toeplitz matrix https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toeplitz_matrix
In addition to speeding up the construction of Toeplitz matrix, you can do more.
For SPD Toeplitz matrix you need to store only n elements instead of usual n^2
You can solve matrix equation and make a matrix decomposition in O(n^2) instead of usual O(n^3)
And if you embed the Toeplitz in circular matrix, you can compute matrix-vector product with FFT in O(n log(n))

Thus even if you don't go to FFT, you could still get significant speedup from reduced autodiff tree not using O(n^3) Cholesky, even if not writing a compound function.

Mike, if you are interested in looking more to this then google "cholesky decomposition of toeplitz matrix" and you can find simple algorithms for computing the Cholesky in O(n^2)

Aki

>

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] When does the data dominates the posterior distribution?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] When does the data dominates the posterior distribution?
messages.body_plain:
It's trivial to show you get better inference with priors.  Just
set the prior to the posterior you'd get after seeing a lot of data.

To do this more realistically, what you care about is calibration of
your predictive intervals (so that when you say something is 50% likely
to fall in an interval, it falls in that interval 50% of the time [plus
or minus sampling error --- you expect binomial(N, 0.5) for N
50% interval tests]).  Once you're calibrated, you care about sharpness.
How narrow are the intervals?    Or if you're thinking of doing probabilistic
predictions of event probabilities, how close are those estimates to 0 or
1?

I really like this Gneiting et al. paper on these topics and wonder
why things are presented this way more often in Bayesin stats:

 Probabilistic forecasts, calibration and sharpness.
 https://www.stat.washington.edu/raftery/Research/PDF/Gneiting2007jrssb.pdf

- Bob

> On Mar 2, 2017, at 1:28 AM, Julien Riou <julien...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Sorry I was not clear enough. I'm already doing just what you say, and measure the predictive capabilities of the models at each point in time with real data (and that's indeed how I know when I obtain a "reliable estimate"). But you see, as I want to show that using informative priors allows to obtain better estimate at earlier dates (which is kind of obvious for many here but is unusual in my field), I'd like to have a concrete measure of how my priors and data interact, and whether data contradicts the prior distribution in some cases.
>
>
> On Thursday, March 2, 2017 at 3:37:21 AM UTC+1, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> What do you mean by "a reliable estimate"?
>
> Everything we're talking about here is model internal.  May I suggest
> not putting so much trust in your model and rather going out and
> trying to measure your models predictive calibration with real data?
> Then you can start measuring the things you really care about.
>
> - Bob
>
> P.S.  I now see the problem with computing KL---we can't get the
> normalizing term for the posterior density, which we need in the
> expectation term.
>
>
> > On Mar 1, 2017, at 2:59 AM, Julien Riou <julien...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Hi Bob, thank you for your time!
> >
> > I get why this is not very useful in general, however in this particular case (epidemic data) it is important because I want to determine the earliest date at which we can produce reliable estimates (and whether using informative priors allow to produce estimates at an earlier date, which is always good when epidemics are ongoing). Informative priors are rarely used in my field, and we're doing a sort of simulation study to highlitght the advantages.
> >
> > So using a conjugate example won't help much here, as I already have a model that I'm interested in. I already plotted the posterior and prior distributions and it works as intended, but I would like a measure of divergence to systematically compare my (numerous) models. I take from your point that I could include the computation of the KL divergence directly in Stan (maybe in the generated quantities)?
> >
> > Best regards,
> > Julien
> >
> >
> >
> >
> > On Tuesday, February 28, 2017 at 8:52:49 PM UTC+1, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > This is good to think about for understanding, but in practice, isn't very useful.  We just want to put in a prior based on what we know.  It's just as much a part of the model as the likelihood, and we don't want to be thinking in terms of how we code it so it gets washed out.
> >
> > You might be able to get a decent feel for what's going on with a simple conjugate example (let's say normal with fixed variance or a beta distribution).  You can see that where the prior starts and how much it's concentrated matters.  Michael Betancourt's about to roll out a nice case study where you can see how much the fatness of the prior's tails (Cauchy vs. normal, say) and the consistency of the prior (is the posterior concentrating in the trunk or the tails) make a big difference.
> >
> > No idea about FNN.  KL-divergence requires computing an integral, which you
> > can compute in one direction with MCMC if you have draws from the posterior and
> > an analytic prior.   But you're probably better served by plotting out the
> > priors and posteriors and seeing how the latter concentrate as a function of
> > the prior and amount of data (and the variance in the data itself).
> >
> > - Bob
> >
> > > On Feb 28, 2017, at 5:54 AM, Julien Riou <julien...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > Hi everyone,
> > >
> > > I have a probably naive question but I did not find a proper answer anywhere, so I apologize in advance.
> > >
> > > I have a time series on which I estimate a parameter (beta), and I want to know at which point in time does the data dominates the posterior distribution of my parameters (or in other words, at which point does the prior distribution not matter anymore). So my idea was to fit the model n times using data available until each date, and to measure the KL divergence between the prior and the posterior distribution computed at each point. I expect the KL divergence to be small at first when little data is provided, and to increase up to a plateau, at which point the posterior distribution depends mainly on the data.
> > >
> > > 1/ Is that a proper way to answer my question?
> > >
> > > 2/ I feel that my way of computing the KL-divergence is kind of rustic (using the nearest neighbor algorithm of package FNN), could someone confirm that this is correct (in particular considering the parameter k)?
> > >
> > > library(FNN)
> > > beta_P <- rexp(length(R0_Q),rate=0.5) # my weakly informative prior distribution (exponential with rate 1/2), I follow a similar method with informative priors in another approach
> > > beta_Q <- extract(S_D1_NIP,pars="beta")[[1]] # extract the posterior distribution
> > >
> > > mean(KL.divergence(beta_P ,beta_Q ,k=10)
> > >
> > > I hope that I was clear enough.
> > >
> > > Thanks in advance!
> > > Julien

messages.body_plain:
But it has a mode at zero.  If you really need to keep values away
from zero, you need something like a lognormal that drives the density
to zero as the parameter approaches zero.

Or you need to reparameterize the model.

Initialization is random in (-2, 2) by default *on the unconstrained
scale*.  For

real<lower=a, upper=b> x;

the inverse of the unconstraining transform is

  a + (b - a) * inv_logit(y)

So when you initialize y to zero, that (b - a) / 2, so you initialize
around the middle of that interval.

The definite bounds like that on intervals can also bias estimates
relative to the unbounded approach as mass bunches up near
the boundaries.  That also causes computational issues as the unconstrained
value heads off to + or - infinity.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Whassup with this simple bivariate normal model that's so damn slow and also throws weird exceptions?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Whassup with this simple bivariate normal model that's so damn slow and also throws weird exceptions?
messages.body_plain:
> On Mar 1, 2017, at 11:27 PM, Andrew Gelman <Gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>
>
>> On Mar 1, 2017, at 1:16 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>>
>> I don't know why it'd be slow with fixed Sigma.
>>
>> With variable Sigma, you should be using Cholesky factors,
>> or ideally, Cholesky factors of correlation matrices
>> with LKJ priors.
>
> I find that so confusing!  But I guess there's no way to simplify it in Stan so it looks to the user like a covariance matrix but is actually Cholesky under the hood?

A covariance matrix is actually Cholesky under the hood.  It's
just that pulling it back to a covariance matrix and applying
the Jacobian is arithmetically imprecise.  And then it just needs
to be factored again inside the multi-normal desnity.

>> The rounding errors may be running off to -0.5 or + 0.5, forcing
>> the unconstrained parameters try to run off to + or - infinity.
>>
>> I understand that you are assuming that the measurmeent is accurate
>> to +/- 0.5, but maybe loosening this assumption can help.
>
> It's not a matter of "accurate to +/- 0.5"; the assumption is that the continuous numbers are being rounded.

I got that, but that's the only error you're assuming, right?

>  For example, heights being recorded to the nearest inch.  But, sure, in practice there's continuous measurement error too:  "66 inches" is not really "65.5 to 66.5 inches," it's really "65.5 to 66.5 inches + error."

Isn't the continuous measurement error inside the rounding?  My point
was just that this will try to drive a value up against a hard boundary
if it really wants to be closer to the expected value.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
For probit, all you need to do is replace

  y ~ bernoulli_logit(theta);

with

  y ~ bernoulli(Phi(theta));

but that'll be a lot slower.

Ben added Phi_approx, but I think that's just a scaled inverse logit.

- Bob

>

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] questions around hierarchical ordered logit
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for all the answers so far! I never liked putting group hierarchies on the cut-points, that never seemed logical to me. So I have gone back and put the hierarchies on the linear predictor, roughly modeled after page 143 in stan reference 2.14 and gelman/hill 2007, chapter 13 (model attached).

The idea is the following: We have a group-specific vector of random effects, that we draw from a multivariate normal, modeling the across-group-within-random-effects variations and correlations in the Varcov matrix of this multivariate normal. Then, we draw class of outcome from an ordered logit where the combination of group-specific random effects is the linear predictor.

But, the model does not converge at all. Is there something obvious that I am missing?

Thanks again,

messages.subject_clean: Divergent transitions and low neff in Multinomial-Logistic Normal Model
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am trying to infer a (relatively simple) Multinomial-Logistic Normal model. I am however having trouble as my sampler continues to have many divergent transitions (~545 from 4 chains each sampling 1000 samples) despite an adapt_delta=0.99. The plot for the variance does appear to be somewhat funnel shaped, but I am not sure what to do about this. I thought this type of model was fairly common based on reading some forum posts.

I must admit, this is my first attempt at using stan and I am sorry if I am making a stupid mistake.

Thank you very much for any advice you can provide!!!
Justin Silverman

Hi Tobias,

When you say it's not converging at all, it actually helps to give more info:
- does it run quickly?
- does it not initialize?
- are the rhats ridiculous?

For me, convergence has a specific meaning and it's hard to tell if you also mean the same thing. And there are ways of dealing with it, depending on how you got there.

So... more info if you want help. We're happy to help if we know how.

Daniel

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Proposal to speed up grid-based GPs
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Proposal to speed up grid-based GPs
messages.body_plain:
It's trivial to precompute X' * X.

data {
  matrix[K, K] X;

transformed data {
  matrix[K, K] Xtr_X = X' * X;

But you didn't say what X_ was or how X_' * X_ relates
to X' * X.

- Bob

> On Mar 1, 2017, at 9:21 PM, Andrew Gelman <Gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>
> Regarding speed-ups, one thing I've been thinking about lately is the way that lme4 speeds up computation by pre-computing X^tX.
> In each step of the outer iteration, lme4 needs to compute X_*^tX_*, where X_* is an augmented version of X.  But in typical problems, most of this computation comes from the part of this that is X^tX.
>
> The thing that's bugging me, though, is that X^tX is part of the (analytic) solution of the conditional MLE but it's _not_ part of the likelihood computation.  So it's not quite clear how Stan could make use of this pre-computation.  And maybe it's not possible to do this at all.  But I'd like to think it is.
>
> A
>
>> On Mar 1, 2017, at 9:11 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>>
>> It's always a good idea to share repeated computations.
>>
>> The built in C++ functions can also include analytic gradients,
>> which can make things go faster.
>>
>> I hope someone who understands GPs better than me will have
>> a better idea what to do.
>>
>> What we really need to do is build some of these ideas into
>> the underlying matrix math efficiently.
>>
>> The problem we're facing now is how to control the sprawl of
>> specialized functions in Stan.
>>
>> - Bob
>>
>>> On Mar 1, 2017, at 7:18 AM, Mike Lawrence <mike....@gmail.com> wrote:
>>>
>>> Hi folks,
>>>
>>> I came up with an idea to speed up sampling on Gaussian Processes when X is sampled on a grid, in which case the pairwise distance matrix has high redundancy (nX unique distances repeated over (nX^2-nX)/2 cells of the matrix for the 1D X case). By pre-computing the unique pairwise distances and their indices in the full pairwise distance matrix, you can compute unique values for the subsequent covariance matrix then fill the full covariance matrix using the aforementioned indices.
>>>
>>> This ends up being about 2x faster than a standard GP (also faster than a GP where the pairwise distances are pre-computed, but uniqueness isn't considered) when the covariance matrix is computed by hand.
>>>
>>> Now, I will note that computing on the unique distances then filling the covariance matrix by hand *isn't* much faster than using the in-built cov_exp_quad() function. Well, I have observed a 30% speedup over cov_exp_quad() in some situations, but that's not much to rave about. But where I have no idea what magic is happening in cov_exp_quad() to make it so fast, I wonder if there might be room to achieve further speedups (in, say, a new cov_exp_quad_grid() function that takes in the unique distances & indices thereof) by combining my ideas with whatever sourcery cov_exp_quad() is doing internally.
>>>
>>> Thoughts?
>>>
>>> Oh, and here's gist demonstrating the unique-distances approach with comparison to cov_exp_quad() and the non-unique-but-pre-computed-differences approaches:
>>>
>>> https://gist.github.com/mike-lawrence/b56ac2d9450233837d426dd17fe20557
>>>
>>> Mike
>>>
>>> --
>>> Mike Lawrence
>>> Graduate Student
>>> Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
>>> Dalhousie University

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Divergent transitions and low neff in Multinomial-Logistic Normal Model
messages.body_plain:
I'd strongly suggest starting simpler in a new language.

You probably need a non-centered parameterization.  There's an
explanation of how to do that in the manual in the section
titled "Hierarchical Models and the Non-Centered Parameterization".

We don't have efficient Wisharts because we don't use them.
The problem is that cov_matrix by itself can be very unstable.
It's much more numerically stable and efficient to use Cholesky
factors instead.

- Bob

> On Mar 2, 2017, at 9:30 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>
> I doubt that these are the key issues, but:
> a.  I'd avoid the inverse Wishart; we like LKJ now.
> b.  There's some Cholesky thing that can make the mulltivariate normal thing go faster.
> A
>
>> On Mar 2, 2017, at 8:48 PM, Justin Silverman <jsil...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>
>> Hi all,
>>
>> I am trying to infer a (relatively simple) Multinomial-Logistic Normal model. I am however having trouble as my sampler continues to have many divergent transitions (~545 from 4 chains each sampling 1000 samples) despite an adapt_delta=0.99. The plot for the variance does appear to be somewhat funnel shaped, but I am not sure what to do about this. I thought this type of model was fairly common based on reading some forum posts.
>>
>> I must admit, this is my first attempt at using stan and I am sorry if I am making a stupid mistake.
>>
>> Thank you very much for any advice you can provide!!!
>> Justin Silverman

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] questions around hierarchical ordered logit
messages.body_plain:
As always, I'd suggest starting with a simpler model.  Lots
can go wrong in those ordinal models with cutpoints collapsing.
You don't have any priors to keep them from doing that, and you're
also letting them run between -infinity and infinity.  There's
often a translational non-identifiability in cutpoints when you
do that if you have an intercept in your model.

Did your program get garbled in transmission?  I'm seeing things
like this in it:

  for (k in 1:(n_waves-1)) {

  }

and then very oddly spaced code that I can't believe anyone intended:

 for(i in 1:N){
    real eta;

    eta =

beta_stat_race[race[i]]+
beta_stat_age[age[i]]+
beta_stat_education[education[i]]+
beta_stat_gender[gender[i]]
;

approval[i] ~ ordered_logistic(eta, c_approval[group[i]]);
  }

It might help to organize the code a bit better.

You can define

  vector[N] eta = beta_stat_race[race] + beta_stat_age[age] + ...;

and then use eta[n] in the loop.  We haven't gotten around to
vectorizing ordered_logistic yet.

You can declare/define now all at once so this:

  transformed data {
    real scale_const;
    real scale_dyn;

    scale_dyn =0.05;
    scale_const =5;
  }

can be just

  transformed data {
    real scale_const = 5;
    real scale_dyn = 0.05;
  }

- Bob

>>

Then, we draw class of outcome from an ordered logit where the combination of group-specific random effects is the linear predictor.

> On Mar 1, 2017, at 5:58 PM, John Hall <john.mic...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> I was able to get a one-dimensional PPCA working pretty well in some other constrained circumstances that would be applicable to some of my problems, but never was able to get it work (in the sense of having large N_eff for all variables and lp__) in a more general case that would work with any PPCA. Often, I would get a version working, then multiply the distribution by -1, re-run it, and get gibberish results.
>
> One of my takeaways is the connection of PPCA to finite mixtures: any {w, z} will be equivalent to {-w, -z}. This will cause the mean of z to have a bimodal symmetric distribution a lot of the time. Sometimes also with the mean of w, depending on the assumptions. It can get pretty tricky.
>
> I tend to think of it like: 50% of the time, the mean of w will be greater than or equal to zero, and w ~ N(mu(w+), sd_w), then the mean of z might be positive or negative depending on w, and z ~ N(mu(z(w+)), sd_z). And exactly the opposite the other 50% of the time.
>
> On Sun, Feb 19, 2017 at 10:38 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> You can  do that.  I think the 1/2 is a multiplicative
> term in the derivative before you take log, so it's
> just a constant and drops out.
>
> > On Feb 19, 2017, at 11:53 AM, John Hall <john.mic...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Thanks, I was a little confused about what you were saying because I figured you could put the distribution on y_raw instead of y.
>
> Yes, you can do put a distribution on y_raw instead of y.
>
> I'm thinking we should start thinking more about priors
> directly on the unconstrained scales.
>
> >
> > For the square root transformation, I got
> >
> >   target += -0.5 * log(sum(y));
>
> Ah, you're right---I mistakenly dropped the multiplicative
> 0.5 alng with the additive one.
> the multiplicative one
>
>  log sqrt'(x) = log( 0.5 * sqrt(x)^(-0.5) )
>
>               = log(0.5) - 0.5 * log(x)
>
> and you can drop the first log(0.5).
>
> - Bob
>
> >
> > On Saturday, February 18, 2017 at 6:54:40 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > Positive unit vectors can be coded using:
> >
> > parameters {
> >   simplex[K] y_raw;
> >
> > transformed parameters {
> >   vector<lower=0>[K] y = sqrt(y_raw);
> >
> > You have to take the Jacobian into account if you want to put
> > a distribution on y, but that's trivial for sqrt(), being
> > just |sqrt'(x)|, so on the log scale in Stan dropping constants
> > and vectorizing, it's just
> >
> >   target += -log(sum(y));
> >
> > though you should check my work on that.
> >
> > - Bob
> >
> >
> > > On Feb 17, 2017, at 8:30 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > Actually, positive_unit_vector is _much_ easier to implement
> > > than unit_vector as the half sphere is isomorphic to R^{n}.  Not
> > > sure if there’s enough use cases to warrant the work to include
> > > it in Stan, though.  Maybe a useful intro project for new devs.
> > >
> > >> On Feb 17, 2017, at 7:50 PM, John Hall <john.mic...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >>
> > >> +1 on the standardize function!
> > >>
> > >> In the early iterations I had tried non-centered parameterization for these, but not in the most recent version of the model. I have sufficient data so that there isn't much pooling going on. I calculate a lambda score using a formula in Gelman's book and it is near zero after fitting the model (I noticed that non-centered parameterization helps most when lambda is above 0.5, indicating lots of pooling).
> > >>
> > >> On unit_normal and standardizing: the issue with the way you present them is that the x_raw's don't get identified. As a result, the N_eff's will be near zero for those, which is not a big deal, but it is a big deal for lp__. I really like being able to use lp__ as a diagnostic. I don't typically print all the variables to the screen, just the hyperparamters and lp__. If lp__ is near zero, then at that point I would inspect what's going on with the other variables, If not, then I assume they are fine. When I was using those x_raws, I would get into a habit of ignoring the lp__, so other things could be going wrong in the model and I wouldn't realize it until much later. The only thing I could think of is if the calculation of N_eff for lp__ understands to ignore transformed variables that are not part of the final model.
> > >>
> > >> Also, I was very familiar with unit_vector. My point is that you can't say
> > >> unit_vector<lower=0>[N] w;
> > >> or some sort of
> > >> positive_unit_vector[N] w;
> > >>
> > >> What I did in the model was enforce an approximate unit vector that was always positive (I don't think I can get it exact with this approach because I get imaginary numbers). The reason I included it is that the sign of z and the sign of w weren't identified in any way. Sometimes the model would output w>0 and some z[i] > 0 and sometimes it would output w<0 with that z[i] <0. Forcing w > 0 helped keep it identified in a way that putting priors on the mean of z could not. I got much better results when I included this constraint vs. doing the analysis with just the unit_vector. Indeed, the problem of nailing down the sign seems similar to the issue discussed in the Stan manual under "Inference under Label Switching" in the "Finite Mixtures" section. Unlike finite mixtures, you may not have the information necessary to put a prior that enforces the constraint in a more general PPCA model.
> > >>
> > >> A more general approach would probably to be something like below. This ensures that the largest square value is always positive. I haven't tried it yet and I don't know how well Stan would handle it, but I think it would be more useful than the positive_unit_vector above since it would allow sign identification in all these PPCA models, not just my specific case where I know all the w's are positive.
> > >>
> > >> parameters {
> > >>      unit_vector[N] raw_w;
> > >> }
> > >> transformed parameters {
> > >>      unit_vector[N] w;
> > >>
> > >>      w = raw_w;
> > >>      if (abs(max(w)) < abs(min(w)))
> > >>           w = -w;
> > >> }
> > >>
> > >>
> > >>
> > >>
> > >> On Fri, Feb 17, 2017 at 6:09 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> > >> Thanks for reporting back.  That's great to know that it lines
> > >> up pretty closely in your application.
> > >>
> > >> Did you try non-centered parameterizations of z and w?  Not
> > >> sure if it'd be better or worse.
> > >>
> > >> We have a unit vector type.  If you declare
> > >>
> > >>   unit_vector[K] x;
> > >>
> > >> it ensures x' * x = 1 and the default distribution is uniform
> > >> over all unit vectors.
> > >>
> > >> The way it does it is as if we'd written it out by hand like this:
> > >>
> > >> parameters {
> > >>   vector[K] x_raw;
> > >>
> > >> transformed parameters {
> > >>   vector[K] x = x / dot_self(x);
> > >>
> > >> model {
> > >>   x_raw ~ normal(0, 1);
> > >>
> > >> This ensures that the distribution on x is uniform over
> > >> the unit vectors.  See:
> > >>
> > >> Marsaglia, G. (1972). Choosing a point from the surface of a sphere.
> > >> The Annals of Mathematical Statistics, 43(2):645–646.
> > >>
> > >> I'm not sure about a fully standardized type.  You might be
> > >> able to construct it the way we construct the unit vector.
> > >> The transform is just:
> > >>
> > >>   vector[K] x = (x - mean(x)) / sd(x);
> > >>
> > >> but it's not going to identify on the original y scale.  We
> > >> really need a function standardize(x) to replace that RHS with
> > >> efficient analytic derivatives.
> > >>
> > >> - Bob
> > >>
> > >>
> > >> > On Feb 17, 2017, at 5:48 PM, John Hall <john.mic...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >> >
> > >> > I have finally got to something that fits my data with reasonable N_eff using NUTS (300 of 1000 for lp__, 1000 of 1000 for all hyperparameters, rhats between 1 and 1.01) and thought I would share (below). ADVI also fits it reasonably well. Of the hyperparameters, sd_z was higher than NUTS and the standard deviations of mu_z and sd_z were bigger than NUTS. But overall, it looks like it fits it well.
> > >> >
> > >> > As many folks have noted, identification is very important for these PPCA-like models. What I really needed was a way to constrain w to be a positive unit normal vector. This isn't in Stan. However, I was able to make a close enough approximation by noting that var(w) should equal 1/N - mean(w)^2 for all unit vectors. The approach I took below uses this formula to constrain the mean. Since I didn't mind that w>0, it worked out pretty well. I also put a reasonably strong prior on the standard deviation of w, combined with constraints so mean(w) didn't have any imaginary variables in it.
> > >> >
> > >> > Another thing I tried was to constrain z to have mean of 0 AND standard deviation of 1. The Stan documentation does a good job explaining how to force mean of 0, but it's harder than you would think to also force standard deviation of 1 while having the whole thing be identified properly (The only way I was able to do it resulted in lp__ near zero because the raw z values were not identified. The approach usually fit the data well, but it can be hard to diagnose problems when you're not printing all the variables). I tried holding back a second data point and did the math so that it works out, but it's very easy to get imaginary terms that screw it all up. So I gave up on that.
> > >> >
> > >> > I would really love if Stan had better support for these kinds of constraints. Positive unit vectors seems do-able, but I don't know about forced unit normals.
> > >> >
> > >> > data {
> > >> >     int<lower=0> T;
> > >> >     int<lower=0> N;
> > >> >     vector[T] x[N];
> > >> > }
> > >> > transformed data {
> > >> >     real<lower=0> one_over_N;
> > >> >     real<lower=0> one_over_square_root_N;
> > >> >     real<lower=0> sd_w_prior;
> > >> >
> > >> >     one_over_N = 1.0 / N;

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] When does the data dominates the posterior distribution?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] When does the data dominates the posterior distribution?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Bob, thanks again for taking the time!

Regarding the triviality of my objective, I assure you that in my setting it makes sense! Basically, I'm modelling Zika virus epidemics in several areas using surveillance data. In epidemic situations, it is very important to be able to predict the outcome (duration, peak date, final attack rate) as early as possible. There are several methods for that, which are all frequentist or using flat priors. The thing is, it's an emerging epidemic, so we don't have much prior data. What I'm trying to do is to use previous Chikungunya epidemics in the same areas to build a prior distribution for the Zika epidemic, and to show that using this prior improves the epidemic assessment (i.e. its reliability at early stages of the epidemic). This is assuming that Zika and Chikungunya epidemics follow the same pattern (it's a pretty safe assumption as they are transmitted by the same mosquito in the same population, we already studied this issue and found no difference).

So there are several things at play:
- Does Chikungunya data allows for better prediction at early stages for Zika (I'll look into sharpness, thank you for that!)?
- At which point in time are the predictions reliable enough to translate into public health measures?
- Depending on the uncertainty on the prior, is there a point where the Chikungunya data does not influence the inference on Zika anymore?
- I have several parameters in the final model, so how does the prior on each of them influence prediction ?

Anyway, I don't think it is (that) trivial! :)

And thanks again for a stimulating conversation!
Cheers

>

-ssc uninstall stan-
download stan.ado from Github
save it in the ado folder / personal / s (see http://www.stata.com/support/faqs/programming/personal-ado-directory/)
restart Stata

Robert

Bob,

Kyosuke BUNJI.

messages.body_plain:
Thanks Jon, that's helpful. Ok, so you have a logistic regression with a model formula of

decision ~ condition * design + (condition |participant_id) + (condition | experiment_id)

which corresponds to a linear predictor that is a function of:

- a global intercept ((Intercept))
- a global "main effect" of condition (condition)
- a global "main effect" of design (designwithin)
- a global interaction term (condition:designwithin)
- shifts to the intercept and coefficient on condition specific to each participant_id (e.g. b[(Intercept) participant_id:1], b[condition participant_id:1])
- shifts to the intercept and coefficient on condition specific to each experiment_id (e.g. b[(Intercept) experiment_id:1], b[condition experiment_id:1])

and there will also be estimated covariance matrices for the multivariate normal prior on the participant-specific varying intercept/slope and for the experiment-specific varying intercept/slope.

That corresponds to what you're intending to do, correct?

Regarding the comparison of conditions across the two designs, I think preferable to focusing directly on the sign/magnitude of the interaction term would be to

(1) use your posterior distribution to predict a bunch of outcomes from the posterior predictive distribution under the various possible scenarios you have  (you can use posterior_predict to get the 0/1 outcomes themselves or posterior_linpred with transform=TRUE to get the posterior probabilities of the outcomes)

and then

(2) make the comparison of interest on the scale of the outcome via summaries of those predictions (rather than on the scale of the interaction coefficient).

I think that's generally much more intuitive than directly interpreting interaction coefficients (especially when the linear predictor is transformed by a non-linear inverse-link function) and also the implications for the outcome tend be what's of practical interest. What do you think?

Best,

Jonah

P.S. It might also be interesting to do this both with the model that has the interaction term explicitly included and for the same model but without the interaction term so that you can compare that too.

messages.body_plain:
Just to have it on record for anyone coming across this post in the future (especially for anyone not familiar with ggplot2), here's why setting inherit.aes=FALSE solves the problem. In the example in question

x <- example_mcmc_draws()
mcmc_hist(x, pars="beta[1]") + stat_function(fun=dnorm)

# Error in eval(expr, envir, enclos) : object 'density' not found

mcmc_hist creates a ggplot object with a particular so-called "aesthetic mapping". In this case the (binned) value of beta[1] is mapped to 'x' (i.e., displayed on the x-axis) and the density of the points in the bin is mapped to 'y'. We don't want to use the same mapping for stat_function but, unless it is called with inherit.aes=FALSE, the aesthetic mapping used by mcmc_hist will be inherited by stat_function and result in the error above.

Hi Luca, how were you specifying the initial values? It's possible you specified them in a way that is valid but that didn't correspond to what you were intending, in which case that wouldn't result in any warnings/errors. Or maybe it wasn't a valid specification and we need to fix something so an error or warning is thrown. If rstan is silently ignoring incorrectly specified inits then that's a bug.

>
> Re your suggestion to recode asym etc, that would be the same model, we are just moving them outside of the loop. It’s only an efficiency issue, correct?

Yeah that doesn't change the statistical model at all. What Bob's version gives you is cleaner code. It's probably more efficient too, but the loop you have isn't super inefficient. In general loops are pretty fast in Stan (it's ultimately C++). However, where you really do lose a lot efficiency by looping is when calls to the density functions are involved. When those can be vectorized you can get a big boost in efficiency.

Jonah

https://github.com/stan-dev/example-models/blob/feature/issue-72-stan-pkpdlib/misc/pkpd/oral_1cmt_mm.stan

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Left-hand side of sampling statement (~) may contain a non-linear transform of a parameter or local
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Left-hand side of sampling statement (~) may contain a non-linear transform of a parameter or local
messages.body_plain:
I'm afraid you can't actually code that model in Stan if I understand
your intent to make z work like a parameter.  You can code many related
models in Stan, but not models with latent count variables.  For example,
you could do something like this:

  ticks ~ poisson((1 - p) * lambda);

but you're going to find that hard to fit because you have a different lambda
for each tick value and so lambda[n] is just going to be driven to
ticks / (1 - p).

Stan's sampling statement only increments the log density, so that
program's not going to do what you think.  This confusion among users
is why we may wind up getting rid of "~" altogether in the future.  We've
tried to call this out clearly to the point of rearranging the user
manual to put it front and center, but it's a persistent source of
queries to this list.

Before you call y ~ foo(theta), both y and theta need to be defined (not
just declared).  The default initialization for an integer is the smallest
negative number (-2^31 or thereabouts).  So what you're saying in that loop
is equivalent to:

  for (n in 1:N)
     -2^31 ~ poisson(...);

which is presumably not what you want.  For a start, Poisson requires
positive variates.  So Stan should completely bomb out when you try to
run this model, not just when you compile it.

You could define your model in BUGS or JAGS (or even in PyMC3).
But for what it's worth, in BUGS and JAGS, the sampling statements
don't sample---they just construct a graphical model that's then
sampled using Gibbs, not literally by drawing the left hand side from
the right hand side of a ~.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Sounds like an issue with MKL config.  We don't do anything
that generates 16-bit applications---I didn't even know
there was such a thing.

MKL isn't going to help with Stan because we use Eigen for
all of our linear algebra and Boost for all of our math
computing.

- Bob

95% intervals require a lot of samples and are more sensitive
to priors than more central intervals, so use them with caution.

your example that seems ot have a lower value for 97.5% than 2.5%?
And there are two lines per variable.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hi Robert,
Thank you again for your consistent help. I installed the latest version of stan.ado. Now I can run the Bernoulli example successfully.
I have a new problem:
I tried to run a simple linear regression model using example from the stan reference document, and I received the following error message (in a pop-up dialog box):

stansummary.exe has stopped working
A problem caused the program to stop working correctly. Windows will close the program and notify you if a solution is available.

As a result. My program was terminated, and no results were shown.
I wasn't sure what caused the problem. Would you please take a look at my do and log files? Again, I appreciate your help very much!

Best
Jing

On Fri, Mar 3, 2017 at 6:15 AM, Robert Grant <email.r...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Jing, you found something important with the load option. I have fixed it (at least it works on my machine) and it's updated on Github (https://github.com/stan-dev/statastan) and I've sent it to Kit to upload to SSC. He'll probably have it up there later today. It now forms StataStan v1.2.3. Essentially, there are some internal data columns output by CmdStan and their names had changed a while back. The load option was still looking for one of the old names. This goes to show that I need to write a test script!
>
> If you want to run it now you'll have to:
> -ssc uninstall stan-
> download stan.ado from Github
> save it in the ado folder / personal / s (see http://www.stata.com/support/faqs/programming/personal-ado-directory/)
> restart Stata
>
> Much obliged to you for persisting, sharing the logs, and thus giving us the chance to fix problems.
>
> Robert
>
> On Wednesday, March 1, 2017 at 3:03:29 PM UTC, Jing Dong wrote:
> > Hi Robert,
> > Thanks again. I changed my cmdstandir and now I can run the program.
> > However, I cannot finish running the program-- most of the program steps were completed pretty fast. But the last step (now loading stan output into Stata) took more than 12 hours to run. So I forced the program to stop. Do you know what's the issue?
> > Please find attached STATA log file.
> >
> > Thank you very much
> > Best
> > Jing
> >
> > On Tue, Feb 28, 2017 at 4:51 PM, Robert Grant <email.r...@gmail.com> wrote:

> > >
> > > global cmdstandir "C:\Users\jdong\Documents\cmdstan-2.14.0"
> > > you might just be OK.
> > > I suspect the missing file error messages indicate that CmdStan has not run at all and line 13 would do that. A quick way to test is to remove any "mystanmodel.*" files from both the working directory and the cmdstandir, then run it again. If my hunch is right, there will be mystanmodel.stan but not .hpp or .exe - because it couldn't find the CmdStan binaries.
> > >
> > > Do let us know how it goes. If this is a different serious problem then I really want to know about it.

Hi, X_* and Sigma_* are defined in equation (14.24) of BDA3.  We can discuss more at Stan meeting perhaps.

>> On Mar 1, 2017, at 9:21 PM, Andrew Gelman <Gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>>
>> Regarding speed-ups, one thing I've been thinking about lately is the way that lme4 speeds up computation by pre-computing X^tX.
>> In each step of the outer iteration, lme4 needs to compute X_*^tX_*, where X_* is an augmented version of X.  But in typical problems, most of this computation comes from the part of this that is X^tX.
>>
>> The thing that's bugging me, though, is that X^tX is part of the (analytic) solution of the conditional MLE but it's _not_ part of the likelihood computation.  So it's not quite clear how Stan could make use of this pre-computation.  And maybe it's not possible to do this at all.  But I'd like to think it is.
>>
>> A
>>
>>> On Mar 1, 2017, at 9:11 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>>>
>>> It's always a good idea to share repeated computations.
>>>
>>> The built in C++ functions can also include analytic gradients,
>>> which can make things go faster.
>>>
>>> I hope someone who understands GPs better than me will have
>>> a better idea what to do.
>>>
>>> What we really need to do is build some of these ideas into
>>> the underlying matrix math efficiently.
>>>
>>> The problem we're facing now is how to control the sprawl of
>>> specialized functions in Stan.
>>>
>>> - Bob
>>>
>>>> On Mar 1, 2017, at 7:18 AM, Mike Lawrence <mike....@gmail.com> wrote:
>>>>
>>>> Hi folks,
>>>>
>>>> I came up with an idea to speed up sampling on Gaussian Processes when X is sampled on a grid, in which case the pairwise distance matrix has high redundancy (nX unique distances repeated over (nX^2-nX)/2 cells of the matrix for the 1D X case). By pre-computing the unique pairwise distances and their indices in the full pairwise distance matrix, you can compute unique values for the subsequent covariance matrix then fill the full covariance matrix using the aforementioned indices.
>>>>
>>>> This ends up being about 2x faster than a standard GP (also faster than a GP where the pairwise distances are pre-computed, but uniqueness isn't considered) when the covariance matrix is computed by hand.
>>>>
>>>> Now, I will note that computing on the unique distances then filling the covariance matrix by hand *isn't* much faster than using the in-built cov_exp_quad() function. Well, I have observed a 30% speedup over cov_exp_quad() in some situations, but that's not much to rave about. But where I have no idea what magic is happening in cov_exp_quad() to make it so fast, I wonder if there might be room to achieve further speedups (in, say, a new cov_exp_quad_grid() function that takes in the unique distances & indices thereof) by combining my ideas with whatever sourcery cov_exp_quad() is doing internally.
>>>>
>>>> Thoughts?
>>>>
>>>> Oh, and here's gist demonstrating the unique-distances approach with comparison to cov_exp_quad() and the non-unique-but-pre-computed-differences approaches:
>>>>
>>>> https://gist.github.com/mike-lawrence/b56ac2d9450233837d426dd17fe20557
>>>>
>>>> Mike

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Same model, different notation, different results
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Same model, different notation, different results
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jonah,
for this parameter:
    parameters {
        matrix[J,n_cond_int] inte;

this is the init that didn’t work and there were no warnings:
    "inte[,1]" = c(rep(2, sdata$J))

and this is what worked:
    inte = matrix(c(rep(2, sdata$J)), nrow = sdata$J, ncol = 1, byrow = FALSE)

It seems that RStan correctly returns error messages when the name of the parameter in the init list is correct but the values are not (number of values or data type are incorrect).

However, there are no error messages or warnings if the name of the parameter in the init list does not match any parameter in the Stan model; it could be something that one has tried (like in my case) or a typo and the init values are not passed and there are no warnings.
I think that in those cases it could be useful to have warnings saying that there is no matching parameter in the model for init “initname”.

Thank you,
Luca

On Friday, March 3, 2017 at 7:43:53 PM UTC-5, Jonah Gabry wrote:
> On Friday, March 3, 2017 at 4:03:50 PM UTC-5, Luca Campanelli wrote:
> > Thank you for your answer, Bob.
> > I finally found the problem. It was that my init values were correctly passed in model 1, but not in model 2 - and given the nature of the model without good init values things don’t work.
> > I was passing vectors while the parameters were matrices, and given the absence of warnings or errors messages I thought things were working. Then I looked at get_inits() and saw the problem.
>
> Hi Luca, how were you specifying the initial values? It's possible you specified them in a way that is valid but that didn't correspond to what you were intending, in which case that wouldn't result in any warnings/errors. Or maybe it wasn't a valid specification and we need to fix something so an error or warning is thrown. If rstan is silently ignoring incorrectly specified inits then that's a bug.
>
> >
> > Re your suggestion to recode asym etc, that would be the same model, we are just moving them outside of the loop. It’s only an efficiency issue, correct?
>
> Yeah that doesn't change the statistical model at all. What Bob's version gives you is cleaner code. It's probably more efficient too, but the loop you have isn't super inefficient. In general loops are pretty fast in Stan (it's ultimately C++). However, where you really do lose a lot efficiency by looping is when calls to the density functions are involved. When those can be vectorized you can get a big boost in efficiency.
>
> Jonah
>

> >> This ends up being about 2x faster than a standard GP (also faster than a GP where the pairwise distances are pre-computed, but uniqueness isn't considered) when the covariance matrix is computed by hand.
> >>
> >> Now, I will note that computing on the unique distances then filling the covariance matrix by hand *isn't* much faster than using the in-built cov_exp_quad() function. Well, I have observed a 30% speedup over cov_exp_quad() in some situations, but that's not much to rave about. But where I have no idea what magic is happening in cov_exp_quad() to make it so fast, I wonder if there might be room to achieve further speedups (in, say, a new cov_exp_quad_grid() function that takes in the unique distances & indices thereof) by combining my ideas with whatever sourcery cov_exp_quad() is doing internally.
> >>
> >> Thoughts?
> >>
> >> Oh, and here's gist demonstrating the unique-distances approach with comparison to cov_exp_quad() and the non-unique-but-pre-computed-differences approaches:
> >>
> >> https://gist.github.com/mike-lawrence/b56ac2d9450233837d426dd17fe20557
> >>
> >> Mike
> >>

> >> Graduate Student
> >> Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
> >> Dalhousie University
> >>
> >> ~ Certainty is (possibly) folly ~

messages.subject: Efficently using samples from a Stan fit in a different model (a discrete index variable?)
messages.subject_clean: Efficently using samples from a Stan fit in a different model (a discrete index variable?)
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
I am currently trying to replicate a model of gene expression I found in the literature. The original model uses custom Metropolis/Gibbs sampler, but I am trying to implement it in Stan to gain efficiency (also the original code is not available and I like Stan). The model deals with time series of gene expression and uses a Gaussian process prior on unobservable series to estimate parameters defining a non-linear ordinary differential equation (ODE) of gene regulation.

To be precise, there are two models used in succession: First, a transcription model that incorporates prior knowledge is fitted to estimate the (unobservable) levels of active protein over time. Every sample from the transcription model represents a possible time series of the estimated protein activity in 3 runs of the experiment (~100 time points each). Than a regulation model takes the posterior distribution (i.e. the actual samples) from the transcription model to infer ODE parameters of possible regulation of a target gene (repeatedly fitted for a large set of target genes).

I have managed to build the transcription model and I have the basics of the regulation model (it allows only a single protein time series to be given as input).

Since the regulation model needs to be fitted about 10^5 times with different data (but same input from the transcription model), marginalizing over all (~1000) samples from the transcription model in every likelihood calculation is a no-go (computing the likelihood involves numerically solving an ODE for each input sample). In the original paper, the authors instead introduce a discrete variable that indexes the array of possible samples. This reduces likelihood calculation to only solving a single ODE. The index variable is then updated with Gibbs steps. I believe that one of the reasons why this actually works and is reasonably fast is that the posterior samples from the transcription model are quite similar - there are usually only few classes where within each class, the differences are just small perturbations.

Now I am not sure how to replicate this in Stan. I checked this group for past discussions of discrete variables, and it seems that it is possible to interleave NUTS steps with Gibbs steps with a reasonable amount of C++ code. The main drawbacks cited is that convergence may be problematic since the Gibbs steps are unlikely to be accepted as the current continuous parameters will probably provide low likelihood when the discrete parameters change. (here: https://groups.google.com/d/topic/stan-users/aWChDDz1YFI/discussion and here: https://groups.google.com/d/topic/stan-users/rHrxlhL46KQ/discussion ). This might not be an issue in my case, since the posterior samples are often quite similar (though not enough to let me squeeze them into a simple distribution).

Another idea I had is to make the index variable continuous by turning it into a simplex with an entry for each sample and use weighed averaged of the samples to construct a profile I will use. Since averaging arbitrary transcription samples could be misleading, I would force the average to be close to one of the samples by adding a strong prior equivalent to something like
max(my_simplex) ~ normal(1, 0.001)
(a smooth approximation to the max function could be some of the L_n norms for a sufficiently large n).

Do you have some intuition why either of the approaches could break badly? Or are there other ways to achieve my intended goal?

Also wanted to say that using Stan has been smooth sailing so far, you guys made a great software and the mailing list is a very helpful resource...

Thanks for any hints

Martin

Thank you both very much for your help. In the end it was a combination of three things that solved the problem:

1) Using LKJ + Cauchy prior, rather than inverse wishart
2) Working with Cholesky Factorizations
3) Using a non-centered parameterization.

This brings up a question though:

I actually have fairly strong prior information regarding one of the covariance terms in my model. For the KxK matrix sigma I have estimates for each of the terms sigma_ij.  When I was working with the Inverse Wishart it was clear to me how to encode this prior information into the inverse wishart parameters. However with the LKJ prior I really have no idea, this is the first I have heard of this prior and unfortunately web searches have offered up little. How could you encode this information into an LKJ prior? Is there some decomposition of sigma that would allow my LKJ + Cauchy prior match my prior information for the expected value of sigma? Should I just be using the inverse wishart in this situation?

Thank you again!
Justin

When I was working with the Inverse Wishart it was clear to me how to encode this prior information into the inverse wishart parameters. However with the LKJ prior I really have no idea, this is the first I have heard of this prior and unfortunately web searches have offered up little. How could you encode this information into an LKJ prior? Is there some decomposition of sigma that would allow my LKJ + Cauchy prior match my prior information for the expected value of sigma? Should I just be using the inverse wishart in this situation?

The expectation of a LKJ-distributed correlation matrix is the identity matrix, and there is no way to change that within the LKJ framework. If you really want to provide the expectation, you could use the inverse Wishart and integrate the covariance matrix out

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverse-Wishart_distribution#Conjugate_distribution

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Efficently using samples from a Stan fit in a different model (a discrete index variable?)
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Efficently using samples from a Stan fit in a different model (a discrete index variable?)
messages.body_plain:
We haven't experimented with mixing Gibbs or other discrete
samplers with MCMC.  Better to marginalize them out in terms
of convergence.  But that's not going to save you computation (but
then neither would Gibbs if you had to evaluate the various categorical
probabilities).

You can fit ODEs directly in Stan---we have stiff and non-stiff
solvers.  GPs are hard to scale.  It's hard to imagine a Gibbs
sampler or Metropolis could've succeeded in robust inference on
this task.

If you try to set up a very narrow prior, it introduces a ridge
into the posterior geometry that can be very hard to sample---you
wind up needing very small step sizes to deal with the poor conditioning
assuming the rest of your model's not on the same scale.

I think the main reason mixing discrete parameters with HMC is going
to fail is that changing the discrete parameters messes with the
adaptation for HMC, which is very sensitive.

- Bob

> On Mar 6, 2017, at 7:35 AM, Martin Cerny <cer...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi,
> I am currently trying to replicate a model of gene expression I found in the literature. The original model uses custom Metropolis/Gibbs sampler, but I am trying to implement it in Stan to gain efficiency (also the original code is not available and I like Stan). The model deals with time series of gene expression and uses a Gaussian process prior on unobservable series to estimate parameters defining a non-linear ordinary differential equation (ODE) of gene regulation.
>
> To be precise, there are two models used in succession: First, a transcription model that incorporates prior knowledge is fitted to estimate the (unobservable) levels of active protein over time. Every sample from the transcription model represents a possible time series of the estimated protein activity in 3 runs of the experiment (~100 time points each). Than a regulation model takes the posterior distribution (i.e. the actual samples) from the transcription model to infer ODE parameters of possible regulation of a target gene (repeatedly fitted for a large set of target genes).
>
> I have managed to build the transcription model and I have the basics of the regulation model (it allows only a single protein time series to be given as input).
>
> Since the regulation model needs to be fitted about 10^5 times with different data (but same input from the transcription model), marginalizing over all (~1000) samples from the transcription model in every likelihood calculation is a no-go (computing the likelihood involves numerically solving an ODE for each input sample). In the original paper, the authors instead introduce a discrete variable that indexes the array of possible samples. This reduces likelihood calculation to only solving a single ODE. The index variable is then updated with Gibbs steps. I believe that one of the reasons why this actually works and is reasonably fast is that the posterior samples from the transcription model are quite similar - there are usually only few classes where within each class, the differences are just small perturbations.
>
> Now I am not sure how to replicate this in Stan. I checked this group for past discussions of discrete variables, and it seems that it is possible to interleave NUTS steps with Gibbs steps with a reasonable amount of C++ code. The main drawbacks cited is that convergence may be problematic since the Gibbs steps are unlikely to be accepted as the current continuous parameters will probably provide low likelihood when the discrete parameters change. (here: https://groups.google.com/d/topic/stan-users/aWChDDz1YFI/discussion and here: https://groups.google.com/d/topic/stan-users/rHrxlhL46KQ/discussion ). This might not be an issue in my case, since the posterior samples are often quite similar (though not enough to let me squeeze them into a simple distribution).
>
> Another idea I had is to make the index variable continuous by turning it into a simplex with an entry for each sample and use weighed averaged of the samples to construct a profile I will use. Since averaging arbitrary transcription samples could be misleading, I would force the average to be close to one of the samples by adding a strong prior equivalent to something like
> max(my_simplex) ~ normal(1, 0.001)
> (a smooth approximation to the max function could be some of the L_n norms for a sufficiently large n).
>
> Do you have some intuition why either of the approaches could break badly? Or are there other ways to achieve my intended goal?
>
> Also wanted to say that using Stan has been smooth sailing so far, you guys made a great software and the mailing list is a very helpful resource...
>
> Thanks for any hints
>
> Martin
>
>

I don't think we implemented rstandard(), but you can (and should) do something like this

PPD <- posterior_predict(fit) # use existing data by default
res <- sweep(PPD, MARGIN = 2, STATS = data$y)

That gives you an iterations x N matrix of raw residuals and maybe you want to normalize them by dividing by the conditional expectations:

res / posterior_linpred(fit, transform = TRUE)

Ben
