> Hi,
> I am currently trying to replicate a model of gene expression I found in the literature. The original model uses custom Metropolis/Gibbs sampler, but I am trying to implement it in Stan to gain efficiency (also the original code is not available and I like Stan). The model deals with time series of gene expression and uses a Gaussian process prior on unobservable series to estimate parameters defining a non-linear ordinary differential equation (ODE) of gene regulation.
>
> To be precise, there are two models used in succession: First, a transcription model that incorporates prior knowledge is fitted to estimate the (unobservable) levels of active protein over time. Every sample from the transcription model represents a possible time series of the estimated protein activity in 3 runs of the experiment (~100 time points each). Than a regulation model takes the posterior distribution (i.e. the actual samples) from the transcription model to infer ODE parameters of possible regulation of a target gene (repeatedly fitted for a large set of target genes).
>
> I have managed to build the transcription model and I have the basics of the regulation model (it allows only a single protein time series to be given as input).
>
> Since the regulation model needs to be fitted about 10^5 times with different data (but same input from the transcription model), marginalizing over all (~1000) samples from the transcription model in every likelihood calculation is a no-go (computing the likelihood involves numerically solving an ODE for each input sample). In the original paper, the authors instead introduce a discrete variable that indexes the array of possible samples. This reduces likelihood calculation to only solving a single ODE. The index variable is then updated with Gibbs steps. I believe that one of the reasons why this actually works and is reasonably fast is that the posterior samples from the transcription model are quite similar - there are usually only few classes where within each class, the differences are just small perturbations.
>
> Now I am not sure how to replicate this in Stan. I checked this group for past discussions of discrete variables, and it seems that it is possible to interleave NUTS steps with Gibbs steps with a reasonable amount of C++ code. The main drawbacks cited is that convergence may be problematic since the Gibbs steps are unlikely to be accepted as the current continuous parameters will probably provide low likelihood when the discrete parameters change. (here: https://groups.google.com/d/topic/stan-users/aWChDDz1YFI/discussion and here: https://groups.google.com/d/topic/stan-users/rHrxlhL46KQ/discussion ). This might not be an issue in my case, since the posterior samples are often quite similar (though not enough to let me squeeze them into a simple distribution).
>
> Another idea I had is to make the index variable continuous by turning it into a simplex with an entry for each sample and use weighed averaged of the samples to construct a profile I will use. Since averaging arbitrary transcription samples could be misleading, I would force the average to be close to one of the samples by adding a strong prior equivalent to something like
> max(my_simplex) ~ normal(1, 0.001)
> (a smooth approximation to the max function could be some of the L_n norms for a sufficiently large n).
>
> Do you have some intuition why either of the approaches could break badly? Or are there other ways to achieve my intended goal?
>
> Also wanted to say that using Stan has been smooth sailing so far, you guys made a great software and the mailing list is a very helpful resource...
>
> Thanks for any hints
>
> Martin
>

Hi,
thanks for the info. The paper is here: http://bmcsystbiol.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/1752-0509-6-53 but a better reference for the model is the supplementary material which has detailed description of both the model and the sampling procedure involved https://static-content.springer.com/esm/art%3A10.1186%2F1752-0509-6-53/MediaObjects/12918_2011_1007_MOESM1_ESM.pdf (kudos to the authors, most papers do not provide this level of detail). The relevant info is in chapters 2 & 4 of the supplementary material.

Bob: if I understand you correctly, you suggest that the only way to handle a distribution given by a set of samples is to either:
a) marginalize over all samples
b) avoid using the samples and use a different (approximate) approach
Is that correct?

I am aware of the built-in ODE solver, but in my case it messes up derivatives (using test_grad = TRUE gives errors on the order of 10^4 - I use RK45). At the same time the ODE can be analytically simplified to an integral that (given the nature of the data) can be accurately approximated with the trapezoid rule (implemented in Stan). This has so far been reasonably fast and accurate. I guess the problem with the built-in solver stems from the fact that the derivative is a function of the discretized protein profiles. This is OK with the trapezoid rule (I only use the time points where the protein profile is given), but RK45 needs to evaluate the derivative at arbitrary time points forcing me to interpolate the protein profile. The interpolation than probably messes up the derivatives (I need to use binary search to convert float time to the nearest int to perform a table lookup...).

I am however thinking whether there might be a good and general way to perform numerical integration in C++ with the Stan math library and somehow simplify the computation of gradients compared to the autodiff.

Thanks for quick replies, it is appreciated.

Martin

https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/rstan/vignettes/stanfit-objects.html#sampler-diagnostics

I think there may be an off-by-one error in the visualization as it certainly
looks like you’re saturating the tree depth, which would also account for
the exceedingly slow mixing.  It could also be caused by the intense
correlations of the weakly-identified posterior causing the NUTS criterion
to be prematurely satisfied.

Aside form increasing max_treedepth and seeing if that changes anything
you’ll want to look into putting some kind of sum-to-one constraint on the
fixed/random effects (typically be setting the last one to be 1 - sum of the
others) or using the QR decomposition as  recently discussed on the list
and I believe on in the manual.

> On Mar 7, 2017, at 10:38 AM, Jon Sjoberg <jon.s...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> I'm not sure how one finds the treedepth information, other than from shinystan,

https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/rstan/vignettes/stanfit-objects.html

All those different group intercepts plus a global intercept mean that the
model's only identified by the prior --- you can add to one group and subtract
from another with no difference in likelihood.

The program you provided is not non-centered, because sigma != 1.  You
only non-centered the location (necessary given that you have a global intercept)
and not the scale.   You could also try starting without the hierarchical structure
and see what you get.

You can also vectorize this

  for(n in 1:N)
    t[n] = a + ap[p[n]] + ac[c[n]] + as[s[n]] + acc[c_c[n]] + alc[lc[n]] + alf*lf[n] + aser*ser[n] +bme*m_e[n];

as

  t = a + ap[p] + ac[c] + as[s] + acc[c_c] + ... + aser * ser + bme * me;

assuming these are all defined as vectors rather than arrays.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Model for binary classification task with misclassification error
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Model for binary classification task with misclassification error
messages.body_plain:
For some hints on how to evaluate classifiers, you can check out
the case study on repeated binary trials.

http://mc-stan.org/documentation/case-studies/pool-binary-trials.html

We highly recommend testing on simulated data first.  And
starting with simple models then generalizing a step at a time.

Usually for measurement error models, the generative model is
that there's a true value, then a noisy measurement.  There are
examples in the measurement error chapter of the manual and in
the latent discrete parameters chapter for the Dawid and Skene
model for classification training data, which is probably closer
to what you want.

- Bob

> On Mar 6, 2017, at 3:50 AM, Marko <marko...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Dear Stan developers and experts,
> I am new to Stan and don't really have anyone from whom to get feedback on such questions in my immediate environment. I am thankful for any feedback from the list and hope that my question is not embarrassingly stupid.
>
> I want estimate P(x = 1) in a binary classification task which has some amount of misclassification error. For this I have two data sets.
> 1) The test data is a validation data set where for each unit a gold measure x (which I assume to represent the "true" values x) and the misclassified measure w is available. The test data set is *not* a representative sample of the population, so I cannot infer from the distribution of x in the test data to the distribution of x in the main data, but I am willing to assume that the misclassification process is the same in both data sets.
> 2) The main data is a representative sample of the population where only the misclassified measure w is available for each unit.
>
> I started by simplifying the cervix bugs example (https://github.com/stan-dev/example-models/tree/master/bugs_examples/vol2/cervix) to get the model described below. The basic idea is to estimate the misclassification probabilities phi from x and w in the test data set and q (P(x = 1) in the main data) from the misclassification probabilities and w in the main data. It is also possible to specify more informative priors on q or phi.
>
> From my layman's perspective, the model seems to be ok, but I never learned how to systematically evaluate such models. It would be great if someone could give me some feedback on whether the model is at all sensible.
> If the model in general makes sense, I would like to generalize the model to classification tasks with more than two categories. I would appreciate any pointers to resources that might be relevant for this.
>
> Thank you!
> Marko
>
>
> Stan model:
> data {
> int<lower=0> Nc; // Test data sample size (gold measure and misclassified measure are observed)
> int<lower=0> Ni; // Main data sample size (only misclassified measure is observed)
> int xc[Nc]; // gold measure in test data
> int wc[Nc]; // misclassified measure in test data
> int wi[Ni]; // misclassified measure in main data
> }
>
>
> parameters {
> real<lower=0,upper=1> phi[2]; // misclassification probabilities: phi[P(w = 1 | x = 0), P(w = 1 | x = 1)]
> real<lower=0,upper=1> q; // Probability of gold = 1 in main data, P(x = 1) <- quantity of interest
> }
>
>
> model {
> for (n in 1:Nc) { // for each case in test data:
>   wc[n] ~ bernoulli(phi[xc[n] + 1]); // estimate misclassification probabilities
> }
> for (n in 1:Ni) { // for each case with incomplete data:
>   wi[n] ~ bernoulli(phi[1] * (1 - q) + phi[2] * q); // estimate q
> }
> // Priors on q and/or phi possible, but not necessary
> // q ~ uniform(0, 1);
> // phi[1] ~ normal(.2, .05);  // Priors for misclassification probabilities
> // phi[2] ~ normal(.8, .05);  // Priors for misclassification probabilities
> }
>
>
>
>
> I also paste a simple simulation model in R to generate example data, in case this helps to evaluate the model:
> library(rstan)
> library(tidyverse); theme_set(theme_bw())
>
> # Simulated data
> # Sample sizes
> Nc = 200
> Ni = 1e3
>
>
> # Misclassification
> misclass = function(x, misclassification_matrix){
>   x = as.character(x)
>   sample(colnames(misclassification_matrix), size = 1, prob = misclassification_matrix[, x]) %>% as.integer
> }
> mcm = matrix(c(.7,.3,.1,.9), nrow = 2) # misclassification matrix (phi is in mcm[2, ])
> dimnames(mcm) = list(0:1,0:1)
> mcm
>
>
> xc = rbinom(Nc, 1, .5) # gold measure in test data; distribution != main data
> wc = sapply(xc, misclass, misclassification_matrix = mcm) # misclassified measure in test data
> xi = rbinom(Ni, 1, .2) # gold measure in main data, not observed
> wi = sapply(xi, misclass, misclassification_matrix = mcm) # misclassified measure in main data
>
>
> fm_stan = stan(model_code = stan_model, data = list(Nc = Nc, Ni = Ni, xc = xc, wc = wc, wi = wi), control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95))
>
>
>
>

messages.body_plain:
I think Michael meant sum-to-zero.  There's an explanation
in the manual in section 8.7, Parameterizing Centered Vectors.

- Bob

> On Mar 7, 2017, at 6:03 PM, Jon Sjoberg <jon.s...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Thanks for all the input! Increasing max_treedepth helped bring up the n_eff/iteration to ~.125 - ~.5, but the divergent transitions are still there.
>
> You don't happen to have an example of a sum-to-one constraint in a model like this? I have an idea of how I would implement it, but it always nice to have something to compare to so I haven't missed anything.
>
> Anyway, I will look into that and QR decomposition tomorrow, again, thanks for all the help!
>
> On Tuesday, 7 March 2017 16:57:18 UTC+1, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/rstan/vignettes/stanfit-objects.html#sampler-diagnostics
>
> I think there may be an off-by-one error in the visualization as it certainly
> looks like you’re saturating the tree depth, which would also account for
> the exceedingly slow mixing.  It could also be caused by the intense
> correlations of the weakly-identified posterior causing the NUTS criterion
> to be prematurely satisfied.
>
> Aside form increasing max_treedepth and seeing if that changes anything
> you’ll want to look into putting some kind of sum-to-one constraint on the
> fixed/random effects (typically be setting the last one to be 1 - sum of the
> others) or using the QR decomposition as  recently discussed on the list
> and I believe on in the manual.
>

> For some hints on how to evaluate classifiers, you can check out
> the case study on repeated binary trials.
>
> http://mc-stan.org/documentation/case-studies/pool-binary-trials.html
>
> We highly recommend testing on simulated data first.  And
> starting with simple models then generalizing a step at a time.
>
> Usually for measurement error models, the generative model is
> that there's a true value, then a noisy measurement.  There are
> examples in the measurement error chapter of the manual and in
> the latent discrete parameters chapter for the Dawid and Skene
> model for classification training data, which is probably closer
> to what you want.
>

>
>
> > On Mar 6, 2017, at 3:50 AM, Marko <marko...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Dear Stan developers and experts,
> > I am new to Stan and don't really have anyone from whom to get feedback on such questions in my immediate environment. I am thankful for any feedback from the list and hope that my question is not embarrassingly stupid.
> >
> > I want estimate P(x = 1) in a binary classification task which has some amount of misclassification error. For this I have two data sets.
> > 1) The test data is a validation data set where for each unit a gold measure x (which I assume to represent the "true" values x) and the misclassified measure w is available. The test data set is *not* a representative sample of the population, so I cannot infer from the distribution of x in the test data to the distribution of x in the main data, but I am willing to assume that the misclassification process is the same in both data sets.
> > 2) The main data is a representative sample of the population where only the misclassified measure w is available for each unit.
> >
> > I started by simplifying the cervix bugs example (https://github.com/stan-dev/example-models/tree/master/bugs_examples/vol2/cervix) to get the model described below. The basic idea is to estimate the misclassification probabilities phi from x and w in the test data set and q (P(x = 1) in the main data) from the misclassification probabilities and w in the main data. It is also possible to specify more informative priors on q or phi.
> >
> > From my layman's perspective, the model seems to be ok, but I never learned how to systematically evaluate such models. It would be great if someone could give me some feedback on whether the model is at all sensible.
> > If the model in general makes sense, I would like to generalize the model to classification tasks with more than two categories. I would appreciate any pointers to resources that might be relevant for this.
> >
> > Thank you!
> > Marko
> >
> >
> > Stan model:
> > data {
> > int<lower=0> Nc; // Test data sample size (gold measure and misclassified measure are observed)
> > int<lower=0> Ni; // Main data sample size (only misclassified measure is observed)
> > int xc[Nc]; // gold measure in test data
> > int wc[Nc]; // misclassified measure in test data
> > int wi[Ni]; // misclassified measure in main data
> > }
> >
> >
> > parameters {
> > real<lower=0,upper=1> phi[2]; // misclassification probabilities: phi[P(w = 1 | x = 0), P(w = 1 | x = 1)]
> > real<lower=0,upper=1> q; // Probability of gold = 1 in main data, P(x = 1) <- quantity of interest
> > }
> >
> >
> > model {
> > for (n in 1:Nc) { // for each case in test data:
> >   wc[n] ~ bernoulli(phi[xc[n] + 1]); // estimate misclassification probabilities
> > }
> > for (n in 1:Ni) { // for each case with incomplete data:
> >   wi[n] ~ bernoulli(phi[1] * (1 - q) + phi[2] * q); // estimate q
> > }
> > // Priors on q and/or phi possible, but not necessary
> > // q ~ uniform(0, 1);
> > // phi[1] ~ normal(.2, .05);  // Priors for misclassification probabilities
> > // phi[2] ~ normal(.8, .05);  // Priors for misclassification probabilities
> > }
> >
> >
> >
> >
> > I also paste a simple simulation model in R to generate example data, in case this helps to evaluate the model:
> > library(rstan)
> > library(tidyverse); theme_set(theme_bw())
> >
> > # Simulated data
> > # Sample sizes
> > Nc = 200
> > Ni = 1e3
> >
> >
> > # Misclassification
> > misclass = function(x, misclassification_matrix){
> >   x = as.character(x)
> >   sample(colnames(misclassification_matrix), size = 1, prob = misclassification_matrix[, x]) %>% as.integer
> > }
> > mcm = matrix(c(.7,.3,.1,.9), nrow = 2) # misclassification matrix (phi is in mcm[2, ])
> > dimnames(mcm) = list(0:1,0:1)
> > mcm
> >
> >
> > xc = rbinom(Nc, 1, .5) # gold measure in test data; distribution != main data
> > wc = sapply(xc, misclass, misclassification_matrix = mcm) # misclassified measure in test data
> > xi = rbinom(Ni, 1, .2) # gold measure in main data, not observed
> > wi = sapply(xi, misclass, misclassification_matrix = mcm) # misclassified measure in main data
> >
> >
> > fm_stan = stan(model_code = stan_model, data = list(Nc = Nc, Ni = Ni, xc = xc, wc = wc, wi = wi), control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95))

The paper is here: http://bmcsystbiol.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/1752-0509-6-53 but a better reference for the model is the supplementary material which has detailed description of both the model and the sampling procedure involved https://static-content.springer.com/esm/art%3A10.1186%2F1752-0509-6-53/MediaObjects/12918_2011_1007_MOESM1_ESM.pdf (kudos to the authors, most papers do not provide this level of detail). The relevant info is in chapters 2 & 4 of the supplementary material.
>
> Bob: if I understand you correctly, you suggest that the only way to handle a distribution given by a set of samples is to either:

Do you mean estimate the parameters of a distribution given a sample (set of draws)?

> a) marginalize over all samples
> b) avoid using the samples and use a different (approximate) approach
> Is that correct?

The usual approach is to either choose a general density function like
a Gaussian process or a parameteric density and fit it to the data
then use that.

I'm not sure how you want to make use of a set of draws.

> I am aware of the built-in ODE solver, but in my case it messes up derivatives (using test_grad = TRUE gives errors on the order of 10^4 - I use RK45).

> At the same time the ODE can be analytically simplified to an integral that (given the nature of the data) can be accurately approximated with the trapezoid rule (implemented in Stan). This has so far been reasonably fast and accurate. I guess the problem with the built-in solver stems from the fact that the derivative is a function of the discretized protein profiles. This is OK with the trapezoid rule (I only use the time points where the protein profile is given), but RK45 needs to evaluate the derivative at arbitrary time points forcing me to interpolate the protein profile. The interpolation than probably messes up the derivatives (I need to use binary search to convert float time to the nearest int to perform a table lookup...).

That's going to be a problem if the interpolation isn't smooth.  This is
why we're considering just getting rid of the ability to even branch on
parameters---it's why we don't have a real to int rounding function.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
When doing Bayesian inference, you want to look at the full distribution of the posterior, not just the mean (which is *not* analogous to a p-value in any event).

So you should do:

    summary(mean(extract(fit1)$theta1 < extract(fit1)$theta2))

and maybe

    hist(mean(extract(fit1)$theta1 < extract(fit1)$theta2))

If you're specifically interested in the hypothesis of zero difference between the probabilities, then you can see where zero falls relative to this distribution. If most of the mass is far away from zero, you can probably discount zero as a credible hypothesis.

--
Mike Lawrence
Graduate Student
Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
Dalhousie University

My guess is that you have some other package loaded that exports a traceplot() function. In

https://github.com/stan-dev/rstan/blob/develop/rstan/rstan/R/stanfit-class.R#L592

it tests whether there is a S4 generic function called traceplot before creating one.

If you start R with the --vanilla option, installation of rstan may work (although you should be able to install the binary version from CRAN rather than building from source).

Ben

messages.body_plain:
Hi Andrew, I changed the prior for alpha to N(0,1) and beta to lognormal(0,1),also I use vector calculation in model. First, I used only 3000 cases in my data(there are 14454 cases in my data), the # of iteration is 5000, it took me 3 hours. And then I used the whole data, it took me 96 hours. 14454 is about 5 times of 3000, so I think the time should also be 3 times. So could you please tell me why it took much longer to run the whole data?

On Sun, Feb 19, 2017 at 7:48 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:

> Hi, some quick comments:
> - parameterize in terms of tau, not tau_sq.
> - don't use inv-gamma priors
> - use stronger priors on alpha, beta, and make sure your problem is roughly on unit scale
> - your expression for eta1 needs no loop; just do:  eta1=beta[j1]*(theta[i1]-alpha[j1])
> - I don't know what W looks like, but if it has a constant term, you're going to have very weak identification of its coefficient along with the alphas.
> - Another source of weak identification is the multiplicative nonidentification of beta with theta,alpha.

messages.subject: Code to calculate delta_elpd and weights in model comparison
messages.subject_clean: Code to calculate delta_elpd and weights in model comparison
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

In case anyone might find it useful, I've put together a function to calculate delta in elpds and SEs as well as model weights during model comparison. It works with objects created by loo() and waic(). The function is heavily inspired by the compare() function in Richard McElreath's rethinking package (and requires the package to calculate model weights). Also, I used a bunch of code from loo::compare().

Function code: https://gist.github.com/matthewgthomas/de54079a5b94163f60761aff214fe7af#file-compare_models_delta-r

Example:

library(rstanarm)

source("https://gist.githubusercontent.com/matthewgthomas/de54079a5b94163f60761aff214fe7af/raw/21203cd6b91e2b7723bbce831ee43540197b1fb1/compare_models_delta.r")

# fit some example models from https://cran.rstudio.com/web/packages/rstanarm/vignettes/continuous.html
data(kidiq)
post1 <- stan_glm(kid_score ~ mom_hs, data = kidiq,
                  family = gaussian(link = "identity"),
                  chains = 1)
post2 <- update(post1, formula = . ~ mom_iq)
post3 <- update(post1, formula = . ~ mom_hs + mom_iq)

# Compare them with loo
loo1 <- loo(post1)
loo2 <- loo(post2)
loo3 <- loo(post3)

compare_models_delta(loo1, loo2, loo3)
compare_models_delta(loo1, loo2)  # check it's ok with only two objects

# compare with waic
waic1 <- waic(post1)
waic2 <- waic(post2)
waic3 <- waic(post3)

compare_models_delta(waic1, waic2, waic3)
compare_models_delta(waic1, waic2)  # check it's ok with only two objects

Cheers,
Matt

Hi Matthew,

There'e a reason why loo package doesn't give weights. The usual used way to compute them (and also how rethinking package computes them) gives weights which are too close to 0 and 1. We don't recommend using these weights. We have a draft paper describing better approach and experiments showing better results. We should get that paper in arXiv soonish, but it might still take couple weeks. After that, loo package will also return weights.

Aki

messages.body_plain:
Hi Craig,

I'm not familiar with the spBayes package, but I can make some guesses as to why to expect differences in efficiency. First, spBayes uses custom MCMC samplers written in C++ that are designed for spatial/spatiotemporal models (e.g., https://github.com/cran/spBayes/tree/master/src). Second, I'm not sure whether spBayes implements the bias adjusted predictive process that I was talking about (described in Finley et al. 2009: “Improving the performance of predictive process modeling for large datasets.” Computational statistics & data analysis 53.8 (2009): 2873-2884. <http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2743161/>). spBayes::spLM() may be implementing the predictive process model from a previous paper that did not include the bias adjustment (Banerjee et al. 2008: Gaussian predictive process models for large spatial data sets).

As for your other q's:

1. Why is setting the area range to [0,1]x[0,1] good?

This was easy to simulate - but is not necessary in practice. You should check to see whether your priors make sense given the range of spatial coordinates.

2. Would be using cov_matrix[m] Cstar be slower than just matrix[m,m] Cstar because of the checks?

As far as I know yes, but someone else may have a better sense for how costly these checks are.

In terms of other tricks - if your likelihood is normal you can marginalize over the spatial random effect w, which may or may not be helpful (see section 2.5 in Banerjee et al. 2008: Gaussian predictive process models for large spatial data sets). I would also expect that Bob might not approve of the prior for phi, which does not match the support of the parameter defined in the parameters block. If you do manage to increase efficiency - please do share here again!

The time the algorithm takes involves two factors:

1. time to evaluate density and gradient

This grows proportional to the data, modulo any issues with
memory throughput and caching.

2. number of density and gradient evaluations per iteration

This grows with the condition of the posterior, roughly
whether or not there are ridges with both flat and
steep components in different directions.  Then we need
smaller stepsizes to simulate the Hamiltonian, so we
require more density and gradient evaluations per iteration.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: Gaussian predictive process models for large-ish data
messages.body_plain:
I'm not an expert in computational linear algebra,
but rather than inverting and taking the Cholesky,
you want to take the Cholesky and then use matrix
division for triangular matrices.  Should be a lot faster.

>  inv_Cstar = inverse(Cstar);
>   w_star = cholesky_decompose(Cstar) * w_z;
>
>   // latent gp at sample locations
>   C_site_star = sigma_sq * exp(-D_site_star * phi); # covariance matrix at sites and knots
>   C_ss_inv_Cstar = C_site_star * inv_Cstar;
>   w = C_site_star * inv_Cstar * w_star; # transformed latent process at sites

Also, you don't ever want to do the same computation twice
as you do multiplying C_site_start * inv_Cstar.

Yes, declaring a transformed parameter as a cov_matrix
introduces overhead.  You probably don't want to save all
those transformed parameters, so you can just make them local
variables in the model block with no constraints.

Finally, we have some built-ins for computing squared exponential
covariance functions---see the manual.

- Bob

On Thursday, March 9, 2017 at 9:50:09 PM UTC+1, Maxwell Joseph wrote:
> Hi Craig,
>
> I'm not familiar with the spBayes package, but I can make some guesses as to why to expect differences in efficiency. First, spBayes uses custom MCMC samplers written in C++ that are designed for spatial/spatiotemporal models (e.g., https://github.com/cran/spBayes/tree/master/src). Second, I'm not sure whether spBayes implements the bias adjusted predictive process that I was talking about (described in Finley et al. 2009: “Improving the performance of predictive process modeling for large datasets.” Computational statistics & data analysis 53.8 (2009): 2873-2884. <http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2743161/>). spBayes::spLM() may be implementing the predictive process model from a previous paper that did not include the bias adjustment (Banerjee et al. 2008: Gaussian predictive process models for large spatial data sets).
>
> As for your other q's:
>
>
> 1. Why is setting the area range to [0,1]x[0,1] good?
>
> This was easy to simulate - but is not necessary in practice. You should check to see whether your priors make sense given the range of spatial coordinates.
>
> 2. Would be using cov_matrix[m] Cstar be slower than just matrix[m,m] Cstar because of the checks?
>
> As far as I know yes, but someone else may have a better sense for how costly these checks are.
>

> > >
> > > In trying to fit some spatial Gaussian process models with hundreds/thousands of spatial locations, I was running into prohibitively long run times, and ran across Gaussian predictive process models as described in the following:
> > >
> > > Finley, Andrew O., et al. 2009. "Improving the performance of predictive process modeling for large datasets." (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2743161/)
> > >
> > > Banerjee, Sudipto, et al. 2008. "Gaussian predictive process models for large spatial data sets." (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2741335/)
> > >
> > > For certain spatial models, these reduced rank predictive process models should scale much better to large n datasets. In case this is useful for others running into similar problems with spatial models or other Gaussian process models, here's a little write up: http://mbjoseph.github.io/2016/08/14/gpp.html, and here's the source code for a speed test experiment testing run times and efficiency between the full and reduced rank GP models: https://github.com/mbjoseph/gpp-speed-test. For an example of this approach in action, also see the following paper from Cameron Bracken that uses a reduced rank GP representation to model spatial dependence in the parameters of the generalized extreme value distribution with over 2000 point locations: http://arxiv.org/pdf/1512.08560
> > >
> > > Looking forward, many approaches for modeling large spatial data that have emerged in recent years rely heavily on sparse covariance matrix representations. When more sparse matrix functionality (particularly Cholesky decomposition) is added to Stan, that will be exciting for spatial applications.
> > >

Thanks.  We should be capturing ill-formed files and
throwing Stan exceptions, and that may be what's happening
before the other pieces of the puzzle get in between.  You'd
have to run directly from CmdStan to see what the output from
Stan itself was.

> On unrelated subject, I just finished the simulation of my PBPK model successfully and would like to contribute the model as a stan success story (assumed it adds value to community). The model is similar to the one in Gelman Bois paper but is about drug and much larger. Both blood concentration for 19 subjects and urine were fitted. I have supplied jacobian - it takes 24 hours to get 1200 draws (200 warmup). It has 10 parameters and 8 random effects. I had to use truncation since one parameter had multiple modes. And the model was a very stiff system of ODEs. If if adds value please guide me in the contribution process.
>
> I still thank some improvements can be done - like cholesky.
>
> With regards to truncation. I wanted all 10 parameters to be called theta so I put lower bound on the array theta. I have found that theta[6] had to be truncated - so I put truncation on the prior. If truncation doesn't cause convergence/speed/etc problems I would like to leave as is since it is more understandable - at least for me.

It can work if you get lucky or control initialization and there isn't any
probability mass near the boundary that you're not properly constraining.

We generally recommend making sure that any parameter values that
satisfy the declared constraints have a positive density (finite
log density).

Understandability is very much in the eye of the beholder.  The issue
I have with the way you're doing it is that there are unwritten constraints
that aren't apparent from looking at the model itself, at least not without
linking a bunch of the pieces.  That is, you're not treating theta homogeneously
in the model, but you're declaring it as a homogeneously constrained parameter.

- Bob

Along the same topic, I have some questions related to BDA3.  I have a hard time understanding the log of a "density" as a score because

1. Density functions are not dimensionless, but have a unit of 1/dy, so it's hard to interpret it.  If the sample contains many iid points, then p(y | theta) = product of p(y_i | theta), which would have a unit of 1/(y^n).

2. A density function could have point values greater than 1 (if it's narrow enough), meaning log(p|theta) can change sign.  That means removing 1 data point away from my y_i's could result in p(y | theta) changing sign.

3. In the broader context of KL divergence, it's hard to picture how the aforementioned sign change would impact the divergence value.  I can imagine situations where D(P || Q) ~ 0 when P and Q are discernibly distant from each other.

Thanks.

Best,

CW

On Friday, March 3, 2017 at 7:26:58 PM UTC-5, Jonah Gabry wrote:
> Hi Hamed,
>
> Some comments below:
>
> On Friday, March 3, 2017 at 12:17:53 PM UTC-5, Hamed Nikbakht wrote:
> > Hi all,
> >
> > I'm a newcomer in Stan. I wanted to implement the Stan on a toy example.
> > I want to make sure whether I'm on the right track.
>
> Welcome to Stan! It's definitely smart to try it out on toy examples before diving into more complicated models.
>
> > This is my Stan code:
> > data {
> >   int<lower=1> N;
> >
> > }
> > parameters {
> >   real x[N];
> > }
> > model {
> > for (n in 1:N)
> >   x[n] ~ normal(0, 1);
> > }
>
> Yes, that is a correct Stan program if the intent is to have an array x with N >= 1 elements that are independent and each is standard normal.
> It probably isn't essential for this toy example, but you can make it faster by replacing the loop in the model block with the vectorized form x ~ normal(0,1).
>
> > load('Ufile.mat');  // Load my initial states which is the vector of ux
> > N = length(ux);
> > MCMC_dat = struct('N',N);
> > initial = struct('x',ux');
> > fit = stan('file','MC.stan','data',
> > MCMC_dat,'chains',1,'iter',10,'init',initial,'algorithm','NUTS','sample_file','output-6.csv');
> > %print(fit)
>
> I'm not actually familiar with the syntax for specifying these things using MatLabStan (we have a bunch of interfaces to Stan and I haven't actually used the one for MatLab). If you're trying to run 1 Markov chain for 10 iterations (I assume only 1 chain and 10 iter just as a test) with initial values for that 1 chain given by the values in ux then it looks ok to me! But hopefully someone who knows the MatLab interface can let you know if that's actually the right way to specify that.
>
> Best,
>
> Jonah
>
>

messages.body_plain:
It is the part of a technique to estimate the small failure probabilities in high dimensions.

This method expresses probability of failure (Pf) as a product of conditional probabilities that are significantly larger than Pf. These conditional probabilities are estimated by application of Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling.

These samples are used as “seeds” for generating additional samples conditional on F1 (based on figure) at simulation level 1.

The seeds -which are the initial values as I mentioned before - for generating conditional samples at Level i are discarded after use. This provides some convenience in sample accounting and analysis of the failure
probability estimate. It also reduces the correlation between the samples at different simulation levels.

I attach the figure for more clarification about the technique.

My toy example is very similar to example 4.1.1 250-dimensional multivariate normal (MVN) in the paper of Hoffman & Gelman: The No-U-Turn Sampler:…..

But with this difference that I have the initial values as I mentioned above and my problem's dimension is 1000.

So, based on above explanation, Do you think my Matlab and Stan code is correct?

Thank you very much for your consideration.

Regards,

Hamed

On Saturday, March 4, 2017 at 4:57:23 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> I didn't understand what you meant by
>
> "which i set it as the initial values of my problem for the HMC NUTS sampling."
>
> You can initialize parameters, but you almost never need to in Stan.
>
> The best way to write that program is:
>
> data {
>   int<lower=0> N;
> }
> model { }
> generated quantities {
>   real y[N];
>   for (n in 1:N) y[n] = normal_rng(0, 1);
> }
>
> Then each iteration gives you a random draw from a normal.
> It's a Monte Carlo approach rather than a Markov chain
> Monte Carlo (MCMC) approach, which is always better if you
> can pull it off.    But it's not going to generalize to cases
> where you are fitting data.
>
> - Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Using of log predictive density rather than log posterior for measuring predictive accuracy
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Using of log predictive density rather than log posterior for measuring predictive accuracy
messages.body_plain:
> 1. Density functions are not dimensionless, but have a unit of 1/dy, so it's hard to interpret it.  If the sample contains many iid points, then p(y | theta) = product of p(y_i | theta), which would have a unit of 1/(y^n).

Correct — the only well-posed calculation in probability theory are expectations
which reduce to integration.  The dimensionality washes away when you integrate
a density over some region of parameter space.

> 2. A density function could have point values greater than 1 (if it's narrow enough), meaning log(p|theta) can change sign.  That means removing 1 data point away from my y_i's could result in p(y | theta) changing sign.

Yes, log p(y | theta) can oscillate between signs as more or less data is considered.
And the exact nature of that oscillation will depend on the parameterization and
hence density that you have chosen.  There’s nothing wrong with that provided
you keep (1) in mind.

> 3. In the broader context of KL divergence, it's hard to picture how the aforementioned sign change would impact the divergence value.  I can imagine situations where D(P || Q) ~ 0 when P and Q are discernibly distant from each other.

The KL divergence, really any of the divergences from information theory, are
parameterization-invariant — they are maps between probability distributions
to a number, not densities.  More operationally, all of the odd paramterization-
dependent properties of densities cancels out when you evaluate the
divergence (or you can write it purely measure-theoretically using
Radon-Nikodym derivatives, if you’re into that kind of thing).  Really this has
to be true according to (1).

Now all of this gets muddied when people try to argue about quantifying
predictive performance.  The explicit values of the “log predictive density”
score depends on the parameterization, but importantly the _ordering_
of the log predictive density from different models is preserved.  When
the literature discusses log densities as valid “scores” they ultimately are
referring to its ability to determine the ordering between models up to
certain technical assumptions.

Many gory details at https://arxiv.org/abs/1506.02273.

messages.body_plain:
Because you're using parameters/model instead of just the rng in generated quantities it is doing MCMC instead of just MC. That's ok, but because the inits are random here and because you basically have no warmup period you can still end up with some divergences because no auto-tuning of the sampler parameters has happened. I doubt you would see any post-warmup divergences if you gave it more warmup time.

Jonah

Hi All -- I wanted to provide an update on this effort. I implemented Rob's code (thanks Rob!) and it has mostly been good, the one major challenge has been that I couldn't achieve good sampling -- Rhat always high, n-eff very low. I suspect that this is linked to the large region in the grid where I have no observations. The fix I have come to so far is to add fake observations to fill this part of the grid, each of these set to the mean of the other observations. The attached shows a heatmap of the surface I am fitting, and the additional points in red. I have tried to keep these additional points away from the real observations so they don't bias the estimation, but obviously this is a hack.

Anyway, I wanted to see whether this raises any obvious flags, or if there are other better solutions I might try.

As a side note, are there any approaches to GPs based on taxi-cab distance rather than euclidian distance? My reason for asking is that this would greatly reduce the number of discrete distances involved, which I assume could speed the matrix calculations.

Thanks again for the help -- Nick

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] @Michael Betancourt: are your slides from the Stan Conference 2017 available online?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] @Michael Betancourt: are your slides from the Stan Conference 2017 available online?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Michael,

thanks a lot for the link to your paper! This was exactly what I needed for developing a better understanding. My background is physics and your explanation of the analogy of HMC to gravitational systems in phase space was very helpful. It also makes clear to me now what the word “Hamiltonian” means in that context. I still need to read more and your references in that paper are on my reading list now :)

I understand that NUTS is a variant/improvement of HMC, but otherwise the same “rules” apply for HMC as for NUTS. Is there any reason to continue to use the HMC sampler in Stan rather than NUTS?

If this analogy with the gravitational system is right then I have a question about multi-modal distributions. If I take the analogy that in a multi modal system it could happen that there are more than one stable orbits, e.g. a stable orbit around earth plus a stable orbit around the moon. Will HMC/NUTS find all of the orbits or do I have to be careful in such scenarios? Would R_hat still be a valid “problem indicator” in such a scenario? I guess that R_hat would be different from 1 if two different chains find two different orbits? So my question would be how to deal with multi-modal systems?

My original problem that I try to solve that put me on the track of your video is a mixture model of shifted gammas. This is not a real world problem, but just an exercise that I’ve chosen for myself in order to learn MCMC techniques. My problem with this exercise is described here: http://stackoverflow.com/questions/42735489/fit-a-mixture-model-of-two-shifted-gamma-distributions-in-pymc3

And I created a PyMC3 version and a Stan version as gists on github: https://gist.github.com/cs224/36482b4f52885310cec6ef975fd20184

I guess I am making more fundamental mistakes than “just” trying to fit a multi-modal model, but nevertheless my question would be how to do something like this best in Stan?
Thanks for any further hints that help me find my way into the world of MCMC.

Thanks,
Christian

messages.body_plain:
Hello Michael,

I have another side question to your talk at StanCon. I simply quote two passages from your talk:

-- snip start --
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DJ0c7Bm5Djk&feature=youtu.be&t=4h45m20s
Statistics was this menagerie of techniques and approaches and there was not unified theory underneath all of this all. In Bayesian inference there is really only two steps, there is the modeling step where you chose the prior and the likelihood and there is the computation step where you compute expectations with respect to the posterior. … how is that computation trying to do an integral. If it’s not clear how your computational algorithm is trying to do an integral, probably a good sign of doing something weird.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DJ0c7Bm5Djk&feature=youtu.be&t=5h00m00s
Now what’s nice about this is that you can invert the logic and using it to evaluate all of the algorithms you might know about. Statistical computation is all about computing integrals and computing integrals is all about quantifying this typical set. That must mean that all of this statistic algorithms are just different ways of quantifying this typical set. And indeed you can analyse them all from this perspective and start seeing why they fail.
-- snip end --

I could not have summarized my own problem with traditional statistics any better than you did! And this is also my main attraction to the Bayesian approach, because it is from a conceptional perspective clean and clear.

Do you have pointers that show how you analyse traditional statistical algorithms from this perspective of computing integrals? I would be very much interested in reading more about this.

Thanks a lot!
Christian

That is supposed to work the same way in posterior_predict() as it does in predict.merMod(). I believe you just do something like

messages.body_plain:
> On Mar 13, 2017, at 2:09 AM, Christian Schuhegger <christian....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi Michael,
>
> thanks a lot for the link to your paper! This was exactly what I needed for developing a better understanding. My background is physics and your explanation of the analogy of HMC to gravitational systems in phase space was very helpful. It also makes clear to me now what the word “Hamiltonian” means in that context. I still need to read more and your references in that paper are on my reading list now :)
>
> I understand that NUTS is a variant/improvement of HMC, but otherwise the same “rules” apply for HMC as for NUTS. Is there any reason to continue to use the HMC sampler in Stan rather than NUTS?

Only for comparison and for use as bits of other algorithms.

> If this analogy with the gravitational system is right

Potential = negative log density
Kinetic = random standard normal at start of iteration

The algorithm then uses the leapfrog integrator to simulate the
Hamiltonian and draws point along trajectory.    NUTS then
just controls how long the Hamiltonian is simulated forward
and backward in time and how a point is selected from along
the trajectory for the next draw.

> then I have a question about multi-modal distributions. If I take the analogy that in a multi modal system it could happen that there are more than one stable orbits, e.g. a stable orbit around earth plus a stable orbit around the moon. Will HMC/NUTS find all of the orbits or do I have to be careful in such scenarios?

No.  Nothing will.  If there's only a few, finding them
won't be the big problem---deciding how much time to spend
on each will be.

> Would R_hat still be a valid “problem indicator” in such a scenario? I guess that R_hat would be different from 1 if two different chains find two different orbits? So my question would be how to deal with multi-modal systems?

Rhat will explode if the different chains fall into different modes.
That's one thing we use it to diagnose.

> My original problem that I try to solve that put me on the track of your video is a mixture model of shifted gammas. This is not a real world problem, but just an exercise that I’ve chosen for myself in order to learn MCMC techniques.

You probably want to read Michael's case study (see our web site
under DOCS) on mixture models.

> My problem with this exercise is described here: http://stackoverflow.com/questions/42735489/fit-a-mixture-model-of-two-shifted-gamma-distributions-in-pymc3
>
> And I created a PyMC3 version and a Stan version as gists on github: https://gist.github.com/cs224/36482b4f52885310cec6ef975fd20184
>
> I guess I am making more fundamental mistakes than “just” trying to fit a multi-modal model, but nevertheless my question would be how to do something like this best in Stan?

There aren't really any good techniques for fitting general multimodal
models.  Mixture models we usually code directly and they wind up not
being so multimodal on their paramters.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
The ensemble samplers go in the "doesn't scale well with dimension"
category.  We implemented the Goodman and Weare sampler, and it
fared as poorly in high dimensions as we expected it would.  So
we left it on a branch rather than encouraging our users to waste
time on it.

The problem is that interpolating between two points in the typical set
is unlikely to fall back in the typical set in high dimensions,
because you'll be in a thin shell around the mode.

It's tempting to speed up these poor algorithms because they're
easy to parallelize.  It's a good example of the "streetlight effect"
(colloquially, "drunk under a lamp post"):

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Streetlight_effect

- Bob

But all of this will not help if (talking in your geometrical picture) this affine-invariant ensemble sampler cannot deal with high dimensional spaces in a conceptual “good” way like HMC does. What is your view on this?

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] @Michael Betancourt: are your slides from the Stan Conference 2017 available online?
messages.body_plain:
> On Mar 13, 2017, at 2:11 AM, Christian Schuhegger <christian....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> ...

> Do you have pointers that show how you analyse traditional statistical algorithms from this perspective of computing integrals? I would be very much interested in reading more about this.

MCMC methods were defined to compute integrals.  Specifically,
expectations of functions over densities.  The typical set's just
the set over which you need to integrate to compute expectations
w.r.t. a density.  In Bayes, the densities are posteriors of parameters
conditioned on data.

Event probabilities are expectations of indicator functions over params.
Bayesian estimates in the form of posterior means are expectations
of the parameters themselves.  Predictive inference is just another
integral of one of these forms depending on how you're doing prediction.

They approximate
the posterior density in the typical set and the typical set is
the region you need to integrate over to get the right result (by
definition).

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] hyper prior doesn't converge
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] hyper prior doesn't converge
messages.body_plain:
You're model's not well identified well here.   You usually
want to allow a scale parameter for hi.  And you might be
better off with a non-centered parameterization.

If you unfold it into standard normal components (the
non-centered parameterization) its easy to see where
the identifiability issues arise:

   h_raw ~ normal(0, 1);
  hi_raw ~ normal(0, 1);
  hi = 1 + h_raw + hi_raw;

There is only one h_raw and presumably many hi_raw, so they're
not symmetric.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
You might find it better to use CmdStan to profile Stan.
Much less going on and RStan's just a relatively thin
wrapper around R's memory and Stan.  The time's still all
spent in computing gradients.  So if you want to optimize,
that's where to put your attention.

messages.subject_clean: Using external software inside Stan
messages.body_plain:
I think this question has been asked a lot, but I wanted to clarify.

I've got a small custom HMC code that does Bayesian inference for a structural mechanics problem.

I'd like to do inferences on it in Stan so I can take advantage of the Stan samplers and use the Stan modeling language for the priors and stuff. However:

1. The problem, at the end of the day, reduces to a big eigenvalue solve. I need control over the eigenvalue solve beyond what Stan currently offers (generalized eigenvalue solve, only need the few smallest eigenvalues)

2. The actual mechanics are kinda black box too. I could conceivably code up some of the matrix assembly stuff in Stan, but it isn't terribly practical, and in the near future I might be needing some other software to do the assembly for me anyway.

Either way, I can provide my stuff as a black box. So it takes in parameters, and spits out some stuff that corresponds roughly to data I'm measuring. I can also provide the gradients for this as well.

So if I want to implement the 'mechanics_solve' thing in something like:

data ~ normal(mechanics_solve(parameters), sigma);

And I have my forward function evaluation as well as my gradients, where's the best place for me to start? I use PyStan, if that changes anything.

>From what I've dug up on the mailing list, I go here: https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Contributing-New-Functions-to-Stan, find a function that looks reasonably like what I want in the Stan Math library, and plug away?

Ben

messages.body_plain:
If you can write up a C++ function that does what you want,
then we can help you plug it together.  If you have analytic
gradients, you can just plug them in using:

stan_math/stan/math/rev/core/stored_gradient_vari.hpp

That is, you want your function to be something like this:

  std::vector<var> mechanics_solve(const std::vector<var>& v) {
     copy args into double structure
     compute values and gradients
     use stored_gradient_vari to create return vars
     return them
  }

You need to use our built in allocation memalloc_.allocate_array<T>(size)
to generate the pointer arrays to pass into the stored gradients so
there are no memory leaks.

I should write this up in the how to write functions.

Then just add it to symbol table and you're good to go (assuming you
can build it into PyStan or use it from CmdStan).

- Bob

> 1. The problem, at the end of the day, reduces to a big eigenvalue solve. I need control over the eigenvalue solve beyond what Stan currently offers (generalized eigenvalue solve, only need the few smallest eigenvalues)

Stan cannot autodiff through complex generalized eigenvalues, which is why we currently only support eigenvalues of symmetric matrices. Even if your small eigenvalues happen to be real, if complex arithmetic is used, it will probably segfault. I have some stuff on a branch that mitigates some of these problems using what Eigen calls a pseudo-eigendecomposition that only uses real arithmetic but it doesn't do anything partial like finding the few smallest generalized pseudo-eigenvalues.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] @Michael Betancourt: are your slides from the Stan Conference 2017 available online?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] @Michael Betancourt: are your slides from the Stan Conference 2017 available online?
messages.body_plain:
> I understand that NUTS is a variant/improvement of HMC, but otherwise the same “rules” apply for HMC as for NUTS. Is there any reason to continue to use the HMC sampler in Stan rather than NUTS?

I refer to Hamiltonian Monte Carlo as the general mathematical method.
NUTS is an implementation of that method.  So is “static HMC” of “vanilla
HMC” which is to how the original implementation of the algorithm.

There is no reason to use static HMC unless you know that your target
distribution is very very very close to a Gaussian.

> If this analogy with the gravitational system is right then I have a question about multi-modal distributions. If I take the analogy that in a multi modal system it could happen that there are more than one stable orbits, e.g. a stable orbit around earth plus a stable orbit around the moon. Will HMC/NUTS find all of the orbits or do I have to be careful in such scenarios? Would R_hat still be a valid “problem indicator” in such a scenario? I guess that R_hat would be different from 1 if two different chains find two different orbits? So my question would be how to deal with multi-modal systems?

HMC can do okay for weakly multimodal problems, but if the modes are
well separated then it will not perform well.  R_hat with multiple chains is
a critical diagnostic.

To tackle multimodal problems you have to either make them unimodal
or consider algorithms in development, https://arxiv.org/abs/1405.3489.

> My original problem that I try to solve that put me on the track of your video is a mixture model of shifted gammas. This is not a real world problem, but just an exercise that I’ve chosen for myself in order to learn MCMC techniques. My problem with this exercise is described here: http://stackoverflow.com/questions/42735489/fit-a-mixture-model-of-two-shifted-gamma-distributions-in-pymc3

This is not a great model for learning MCMC as multimodal pathologies
are relatively advanced.  In any case, http://mc-stan.org/documentation/case-studies/identifying_mixture_models.html.

messages.body_plain:
Just an update: I did managed to improve the speed by about 30% by replacing

  inv_Cstar = inverse(Cstar);
  w_star = cholesky_decompose(Cstar) * w_z;

with

  Cstar_L = cholesky_decompose(Cstar);
  w_star = Cstar_L * w_z;
  inv_Cstar = multiply_lower_tri_self_transpose(mdivide_left_tri_low(Cstar_L,  diag_matrix(rep_vector(1,m)));

In addition, I fixed the prior for phi by constraining the parameter directly without prior assignment,

  real<lower = 0.25, upper = 10> phi;

On Thursday, March 9, 2017 at 9:50:09 PM UTC+1, Maxwell Joseph wrote:

> Hi Craig,
>
> I'm not familiar with the spBayes package, but I can make some guesses as to why to expect differences in efficiency. First, spBayes uses custom MCMC samplers written in C++ that are designed for spatial/spatiotemporal models (e.g., https://github.com/cran/spBayes/tree/master/src). Second, I'm not sure whether spBayes implements the bias adjusted predictive process that I was talking about (described in Finley et al. 2009: “Improving the performance of predictive process modeling for large datasets.” Computational statistics & data analysis 53.8 (2009): 2873-2884. <http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2743161/>). spBayes::spLM() may be implementing the predictive process model from a previous paper that did not include the bias adjustment (Banerjee et al. 2008: Gaussian predictive process models for large spatial data sets).
>
> As for your other q's:
>
>
> 1. Why is setting the area range to [0,1]x[0,1] good?
>
> This was easy to simulate - but is not necessary in practice. You should check to see whether your priors make sense given the range of spatial coordinates.
>
> 2. Would be using cov_matrix[m] Cstar be slower than just matrix[m,m] Cstar because of the checks?
>
> As far as I know yes, but someone else may have a better sense for how costly these checks are.
>
> In terms of other tricks - if your likelihood is normal you can marginalize over the spatial random effect w, which may or may not be helpful (see section 2.5 in Banerjee et al. 2008: Gaussian predictive process models for large spatial data sets). I would also expect that Bob might not approve of the prior for phi, which does not match the support of the parameter defined in the parameters block. If you do manage to increase efficiency - please do share here again!
>
>
> On Thursday, March 9, 2017 at 9:45:03 AM UTC-7, Craig Wang wrote:
> > Perhaps a few additional questions I encounter when I browsed similar problems:
> >

> > > First, big thanks to the stan-dev team for creating and continuing to improve Stan.
> > >
> > > In trying to fit some spatial Gaussian process models with hundreds/thousands of spatial locations, I was running into prohibitively long run times, and ran across Gaussian predictive process models as described in the following:
> > >
> > > Finley, Andrew O., et al. 2009. "Improving the performance of predictive process modeling for large datasets." (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2743161/)
> > >
> > > Banerjee, Sudipto, et al. 2008. "Gaussian predictive process models for large spatial data sets." (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2741335/)
> > >
> > > For certain spatial models, these reduced rank predictive process models should scale much better to large n datasets. In case this is useful for others running into similar problems with spatial models or other Gaussian process models, here's a little write up: http://mbjoseph.github.io/2016/08/14/gpp.html, and here's the source code for a speed test experiment testing run times and efficiency between the full and reduced rank GP models: https://github.com/mbjoseph/gpp-speed-test. For an example of this approach in action, also see the following paper from Cameron Bracken that uses a reduced rank GP representation to model spatial dependence in the parameters of the generalized extreme value distribution with over 2000 point locations: http://arxiv.org/pdf/1512.08560
> > >
> > > Looking forward, many approaches for modeling large spatial data that have emerged in recent years rely heavily on sparse covariance matrix representations. When more sparse matrix functionality (particularly Cholesky decomposition) is added to Stan, that will be exciting for spatial applications.

On Tuesday, March 14, 2017 at 3:06:48 PM UTC, Guillaume Bal wrote:
>
> Dear stan users,
>
> I recently started using STAN hoping it may help obtaining reasonably fast convergence for a mixture growth model compared to using JAGS.
>
> This model aims at estimating the proportion of 1, 2 and 3+ years old fish and their corresponding weight from weight at capture data. I implemented a Von Bertalanffy growth model as a guide to how mean weights change with increasing age. I did not want to go for a broken stick approach as my goal will be to make this model hierarchical later on. Error on weight is assumed gamma (best option so far to get realistic weight estimates together with allowing the variance to be proportional to the mean).
>
>
> I tend to run 3 chains and I usually get:
>   2 chains with mean weights about 2, 4 and 6 kg and proportion of ages about 0.70, 0.25, 0.05 for ages 1, 2 and 3 respectively. This is quite realistic biologically.
>   1 chain stuck with values of .7, 2.2 and 4.5 for mean weights and proportions of 0, .7 and .3. This gives reasonable fit to the data but it is clearly not realistic ecologically and the Log posterior values distribution associated is significantly lower than is the previous case.
>
> This happens with giving rather informative starting values to the different chains. I thus wonder if I could improve things using different priors. I have the feeling that this could be the issue but any other suggestion you may have would also be very welcome.
>
> If you have hints about how to change the code to make it faster that would be great too.
>
>
> My R and Stan codes are provided below and a subset of the data is attached
>
>
> Thanks in advance for your help.
>
>
> Best
>
>
> Guillaume
>
>
> Stan model
>
> Enter code here...
> data {
>   int<lower=0> n_fish; // number of fish
>   int<lower=1> n_ages; // number of age classes in the model
>   real<lower=0> weight[n_fish]; // weight of fish
> }
>
> parameters {
>   real<lower=7500> weight_inf; // asymptotic weight
>   real<lower=0.1> k; // growth rate
>   real t_zero; // curve shifting
>   real<lower=1.5> b; // weight length exponent factor
>   real<lower=0> beta; // component of gamma likelyhood
>   simplex[n_ages] p_ages; // age proportions, ie mixture
> }
>
> transformed parameters {
>   real<lower = 0> mu_weight_ages[n_ages]; // mean weight of an age class
>   real<lower = 0> alpha_ages[n_ages]; // component gamma likelyhood
>   for(a in 1:n_ages){
>    // Von Bertalanffy growth equation
>    mu_weight_ages[a] = weight_inf * pow(1 - exp(-k * (a - t_zero)), b);
>    alpha_ages[a] = mu_weight_ages[a] * beta;
>   }
> }
>
> model {
>   real ps[n_ages];
>   weight_inf ~ normal(30000, 3000);
>   k ~ cauchy(0, 1);

>   b ~ normal(2.84, 0.2); # informative prior

>   for(f in 1:n_fish){

>           ps[a] = log(p_ages[a]) + gamma_lpdf(weight[f] |alpha_ages[a], beta);

>       target += log_sum_exp(ps);

> }

Hi Daniel,

Thank you very much for your prompt reply.

We can not use the Monte Carlo simulation. because, its main drawback, however, is that it is not suitable for finding small failure probabilities (Pf < 10^-3),
because, the number of samples, and hence the number of system analyses required to achieve a given accuracy, is proportional to 1/Pf.
Essentially, finding small failure probabilities requires information from rare samples corresponding to failure, and on average it would requires many samples before a failure occurs.

I attach both Matlab and Stan files for both CW-MCMC and NUTS via this email.

Thank you very much in advance for your time and consideration.
Hamed

messages.body_plain:
To answer the original question, when you have a purely conjugate i.i.d.
model like yours, Gibbs reverts to pure Monte Carlo (MC) sampling, which is more
efficient than using NUTS to do Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC).  You can code up
pure Monte Carlo in Stan, too, using the generated quantities block.  Then it should
be just as efficient up to the normal RNGs being used.

More below.

> On Mar 14, 2017, at 1:07 PM, Hamed Nikbakht <hamednik...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> ...

> We can not use the Monte Carlo simulation. because, its main drawback, however, is that it is not suitable for finding small failure probabilities (Pf < 10^-3),

Right.  Then you can't use MCMC either, which is even slower
to find small failures.  It usually takes multiple MCMC
iterations to get the same power as a single MC iteration.

> because, the number of samples, and hence the number of system analyses required to achieve a given accuracy, is proportional to 1/Pf.

It's more that you only get about one useful draw for the tail
per 1 / Pf effective sample size.

You're going to have to either use some kind of truncation or
inverse CDF or something to code up tail probabilities.

- Bob

> On Mar 14, 2017, at 1:16 PM, Marko <marko...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Dear Bob, dear list,
> Thank you again for the reference to the Dawid and Skene model. It provides a very helpful framework for my problem.
> I work in communication research, where a typical content analysis usually works in two steps. First, you train the annotators and let them classify the same test units. The Dawid and Skene model can then be used to estimate the category proportions (pi_test in the following model code) and the misclassification matrices for all annotators (theta). Second, each unit in the actual study sample is only classified by one annotator.
> My idea is to use the estimate of misclassification in the test data to correct the estimate of the category proportions in the main study (pi_study) - with the necessary assumption that misclassification in the test and in the actual study are the same.

You can do that.  But even better, do full Bayesian inference
on all the data and parameters jointly.  It's perfectly OK for
there to be only one (or even no) annotators per item.  That's the only way
to properly propagate your uncertainty and it has the side
benefit of using all of your data efficiently.

> I have added the parts of the study data to the model and it seems to work well with simulated data. However, it is still quite likely that a made a stupid mistake somewhere along the way.

Maybe, but this kind of thing is almost impossible to debug just by
squinting at it.

You should be able to vectorize many of those loops.  We still need
to go back and update all of our old model examples.

I need to write the Dawid and Skene model up with the Raykar et al.
JMLR model (it trains a logistic regression for prevalence rather
than just having a categorical distribution---or in machine learning
terms, trains a model for the problem and the annotation model at
the same time).

- Bob

Thank you very much for the useful points that you mentioned.

I didn't get your point when you are pointing out "you can't use MCMC either, which is even slower

to find small failures.  It usually takes multiple MCMC iterations to get the same power as a single MC iteration."

In order to overcome the inefficiency of the Monte Carlo method in estimating small failure probabilities,
while maintaining its independency on the number of random variables, a method named Subset Simulation suggested by Au & Beck (which I'm using this technique) has been implemented.

This method express Pf as a product of conditional probabilities that are significantly larger than Pf. These conditional probabilities are estimated by application of MCMC sampling.
It should be noted that Subset Simulation has been studied in the mathematical literature under the surrogate terms Sequential Monte Carlo and Generalized Splitting.

THE POINT IS THAT the efficiency and accuracy of Subset Simulation depends of the ability of the applied MCMC algorithm to estimate accurately the conditional probabilities with minimum number of samples.

That's why I'm gonna recruit the NUTS sampling to see whether it can be improved with respect to the efficient sampling.

(The variance of the estimates of the conditional probabilities depend on the correlation of the Markov chains simulated by MCMC algorithm)

And My Matlab code is based on this subset simulation technique. I attach the figure for clarifying conceptually the subset simulation technique).

Your kind help on this is very much appreciated.

Hamed

I meant don't compute the inverse at all---you only use
it as an intermdiate quantity.

Best place to define something is in transformed data if
it doesn't depend on parameters.

Where to put a quantity that depends on parameters:

  if it's used in the model:
    if you want to save it:
      * transformed parameters
    else
      * local variable in model
  else
    * generated quantities

It's not always possible to satisfy this if there are complex
dependencies among the parameters.  Then it's usually more
efficient to make everything a local variable in the model and
redefine quantities to save as generated quantities.  The generated
quantities are very cheap as there are no gradients and they're only
calculated once per iteration rather than once per leapfrog step.

- Bob

> On Mar 14, 2017, at 10:48 AM, Craig Wang <craigw...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Just an update: I did managed to improve the speed by about 30% by replacing
>
>
>   inv_Cstar = inverse(Cstar);
>   w_star = cholesky_decompose(Cstar) * w_z;
>
> with
>
>   Cstar_L = cholesky_decompose(Cstar);
>   w_star = Cstar_L * w_z;
>   inv_Cstar = multiply_lower_tri_self_transpose(mdivide_left_tri_low(Cstar_L,  diag_matrix(rep_vector(1,m)));
>
>
> In addition, I fixed the prior for phi by constraining the parameter directly without prior assignment,
>
>   real<lower = 0.25, upper = 10> phi;

We recommend leaving variables unconstrained up to physical constraints
(such as phi > 0 being a requirement for the model to be well-defined).
Then just use a prior that concentrates most of the mass where you think
it has to be, like here, say a normal(5, 1) or normal(5, 2) if you want
support at zero or something zero-avoiding like a gamma otherwise.  This
will be more robust in the face of data that tries to force phi up against
one of its boundaries.

- Bob

> >
> > It's more that you only get about one useful draw for the tail
> > per 1 / Pf effective sample size.
> >
> > You're going to have to either use some kind of truncation or

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] NUTS through Stan running slower than traditional component wise MCMC in Matlab
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] NUTS through Stan running slower than traditional component wise MCMC in Matlab
messages.body_plain:
We answered that one already.  It's because "componentwise"
reduces to elementwise Monte Carlo in this case.

If you want to do pure Monte Carlo sampling in Stan, it
looks like this:

data {
  int<lower=0> N;
}
model { }
generated quantities {
  vector[N] x;
  for (n in 1:N) x[n] = normal_rng(0, 1);
}

If that runs at different speed, it comes down to Boost's Normal RNG
vs. whatever package you're using.  Make sure you're getting the right
results before comparing speed.

- Bob
