messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Cutpoint Priors
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Cutpoint Priors
messages.body_plain:
In theory, you won't ever get exactly collapsed cut points
in the posterior, but that doesn't mean that in practice you
won't get close enough to cause underflow and other problems.

Same as if you start drawing theta ~ beta(1e-10, 1e-10).  Sure,
you shouldn't draw theta = 0 or theta = 1 in theory, but that's
what's going to happen with floating point arithmetic on computers.
You can get around that problem with just a little stronger prior.

- Bob

> On Mar 13, 2017, at 5:59 PM, Andrew Gelman <Gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>
> Collapse if cutpoints can occur with point estimation but should not occur with full Bayes.
>
>> On Mar 13, 2017, at 3:47 PM, Tobias Konitzer <tobias....@gmail.com> wrote:
>>
>> I am wondering how to derive cut-points with only using prior counts in the different categories, but no information from the data other than that. It sounds like Bob's approach above does this, but how do I go from K (assuming K= number of categories) prior probabilities to K-1 cut-points? Does the above not estimate the first cut-point? In that case, we would calculate the predicted probability of k=1 as 1-sum(prob k=k), akin to estimating the probability of falling into the maximum category in standard ordinal logistic regression?
>>
>> And, would that approach, without some scale taken from predictors, be good enough to avoid collapse?
>>
>> Thanks,
>> Tobi
>>
>> On Thursday, April 14, 2016 at 1:53:28 PM UTC-7, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>> The transform for the simplex uses stick-breaking.  but
>> there's no ordering --- what do you mean by ordering of
>> the cutpoints?  The usual thing to do here is take the
>> cumulative sums, so you get an increasing sequence to scale:
>>
>> parameters {
>>   simplex[K] theta;     // gaps between cutpoints
>>   real<lower=0> kappa;  // scale for cutpoints
>>
>> transformed parameters {
>>   ordered[K] cutpoints;
>>   cutpoints <- cumulative_sum(theta) * kappa;
>>
>> model {
>>   theta ~ dirichlet(rep_vector(alpha, K));
>>
>> Then if you put a Dirichlet prior on theta, with alpha >> 1, it'll keep
>> the cutpoints apart.  And it's best to define that vector as
>> transformed data.
>>
>> - Bob
>>
>> > On Apr 14, 2016, at 12:11 AM, Dustin Tran <dustinv...@gmail.com> wrote:
>> >
>> > What about a truncated stick breaking prior? The size-biasedness of TSB priors will
>> > (1) force an ordering for the cutpoints;
>> > (2) make draws of cutpoints live on [0,1] which you can scale willy-nilly;
>> > (3) reinforce what Ben said on adding prior information via pseudocounts in the parameters of a Dirichlet prior (here, use Beta stick-breaking priors, which is what Ben essentially does based on the running sum in the make_cutpoints function).
>> >
>> > Dustin
>> >> On Apr 13, 2016, at 11:43 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>> >>
>> >> HI, are you saying that a simple flat prior on the cutpoints won’t work?  Or a super-weak prior such as normal(0,10)?
>> >>
>> >> I’m surprised that you get “cutpoint collapse” if you’re doing full Bayes (as opposed to maximum likelihood).
>> >>
>> >> If you want to put some prior info as below, I recommend putting the normal priors on the _differences_ between the cutpoints, not the cutpoints themselves.  Otherwise you have this weird thing going on where the cutpoints are all being pulled toward each other.
>> >>
>> >> A
>> >>
>> >>> On Apr 13, 2016, at 9:38 AM, Lei Zhang <bnuzhan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>> >>>
>> >>> Sorry to bring this up again. I am (still) facing the cutpoint-collapse problem when fitting an ordered-logistic model. After reading this thread and several others, I am still not sure (1) how to properly specify the prior of the cutpoint parameters, and (2) is there a way to model the cutpoint hierarchically like below? I tried something before but it seems that it doesn't guarantee that c[n,k+1] > c[n,k], hence it won't compile. I would highly appreciate any suggestions!
>> >>>
>> >>> ordered[K] c_mu;
>> >>> vector<lower=0>[K] c_sd;
>> >>> ordered[K] c[N];
>> >>>
>> >>> for (n in 1:N)
>> >>>    for (k in 1:K)
>> >>>        c[n,k] ~ normal(c_mu[k], c_sd[k]);
>> >>>
>> >>>
>> >>>
>> >>>
>> >>> On Wednesday, May 20, 2015 at 8:27:28 PM UTC+2, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>> >>> Cool.  I like that idea.
>> >>>
>> >>> Just ordering obviously isn't enough for the uniform distribution
>> >>> on an ordered vector to be proper.
>> >>>
>> >>> What does happen for reasons I still don't fully understand is
>> >>> that
>> >>>
>> >>>   ordered[K] cutpoints;
>> >>>
>> >>>   cutpoints ~ normal(0, 5);
>> >>>
>> >>> provides the same distribution for cutpoints as
>> >>>
>> >>>   vector[K] cutpoints_raw;
>> >>>
>> >>>   cutpoints_raw ~ normal(0, 5);
>> >>>
>> >>>   cutpoints <- sort(cutpoints_raw);
>> >>>
>> >>> You can put a prior directly on the gaps with
>> >>>
>> >>>   vector[1] cutpoint0;
>> >>>   vector<lower=0>[K - 1] cutpoint_gaps;
>> >>>
>> >>>   cutpoint_gaps ~ normal(0, 2);
>> >>>
>> >>>   ordered[K] cutpoints;
>> >>>
>> >>>   cutpoints <- append_col(cutpoint, cutpoint + cutpoint_gaps);
>> >>>
>> >>> I'm not sure how to constraint the lowest cut point, cutpoint0.
>> >>>
>> >>> - Bob
>> >>>
>> >>>
>> >>>
>> >>>
>> >>> > On May 19, 2015, at 10:53 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:
>> >>> >
>> >>> > One of the reasons the paper is unwritten is because I think it is better to bring the prior information through the parameters of a Dirichlet prior on the conditional probabilities of being in each category given that the predictors are at the sample means. In code, it would look like
>> >>> >
>> >>> > functions {
>> >>> >   vector make_cutpoints(vector probabilities, real scale) {
>> >>> >     vector[rows(probabilities)-1] cutpoints;
>> >>> >     real running_sum;
>> >>> >     running_sum <- 0;
>> >>> >     for(c in 1:(rows(cutpoints))) {
>> >>> >       running_sum <- running_sum + probabilities[c];
>> >>> >       cutpoints[c] <- logit(running_sum);
>> >>> >     }
>> >>> >     return scale * cutpoints;
>> >>> >   }
>> >>> > }
>> >>> > data {
>> >>> >   int<lower=1> N;            # observations
>> >>> >   int<lower=1> K;            # predictors
>> >>> >   int<lower=3> C;            # outcome categories
>> >>> >   matrix[N,K]  X;            # "standardized" predictor matrix
>> >>> >   vector[K] xbar;            # vector of predictor means
>> >>> >   int<lower=1,upper=C> y[N]; # ordinal outcome
>> >>> >   vector[C] pseudocounts;    # prior value for concentrations in Dirichlet prior
>> >>> >   real<lower=0> nu;          # scale for Cauchy priors
>> >>> > }
>> >>> > transformed data {
>> >>> >   matrix[K,K] middle;
>> >>> >   middle <- xbar * transpose(xbar);
>> >>> > }
>> >>> > parameters {
>> >>> >   vector[K] beta_raw;        # coefficients
>> >>> >   simplex[C] probabilities;  # of falling in each category given xbar
>> >>> > }
>> >>> > transformed parameters {
>> >>> >   vector[K] beta;
>> >>> >   vector[C-1] cutpoints;
>> >>> >   for (k in 1:K) beta[k] <- nu * tan(pi() * (Phi(beta_raw[k]) - 0.5));
>> >>> >   cutpoints <- make_cutpoints(probabilities, sqrt(quad_form(middle, beta) + 1));
>> >>> > }
>> >>> > model {
>> >>> >   vector[N] eta;
>> >>> >   eta <- X * beta;                                          # linear predictor
>> >>> >   for(n in 1:N) y[n] ~ ordered_logistic(eta[n], cutpoints); # likelihood
>> >>> >   probabilities ~ dirichlet(pseudocounts);                  # our intuitive prior
>> >>> >   beta_raw ~ normal(0,1); # prior implies beta ~ cauchy(0,nu)
>> >>> > }
>> >>> >
>> >>> > Ben
>> >>> >
>> >>> > On Tuesday, May 19, 2015 at 8:25:50 PM UTC-4, Andrew Gelman wrote:
>> >>> > Hi, Ben and I actually have an (unwritten) paper on this.  The short answer is that we do think there’s a place for a weakly informative prior here.  One challenge is that the scale of the cutpoints themselves is hard to know ahead of time, so we were talking about setting up a prior by putting in a small bit (possibly a fractional bit) of pseudo-data in each bin.
>> >>> >
>> >>> > > On May 19, 2015, at 5:46 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>> >>> > >
>> >>> > > Is there a natural prior for cut points (specifically in
>> >>> > > an ordered logistic regression) or is the ordered constraint
>> >>> > > sufficiently strong that the uniform prior is well-posed?

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Using Gaussian Copulas for hierarchical priors
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Using Gaussian Copulas for hierarchical priors
messages.body_plain:
Usually you work on the unconstrained scale and then map
back to the constrained scale.

So if you have y = (y[1], y[2]), where y[1] is unconstrained
and y[2] is constrained to be positive, then you model

 (y_raw[1], y_raw[2])

as having a multivariate normal structure and define

 y[1] = y_raw[1]

 y[2] = exp(y_raw[2])

Same deal if some are probabilities (use inverse logit
instead of exp).

- Bob

One model I'm currently looking has something like this going on.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] convergence / prior for finite mixture growth model
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] convergence / prior for finite mixture growth model
messages.body_plain:
See inline.

> On Mar 14, 2017, at 11:06 AM, Guillaume Bal <guillaum...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Dear stan users,
>
> I recently started using STAN hoping it may help obtaining reasonably fast convergence for a mixture growth model compared to using JAGS.
>
> This model aims at estimating the proportion of 1, 2 and 3+ years old fish and their corresponding weight from weight at capture data. I implemented a Von Bertalanffy growth model as a guide to how mean weights change with increasing age. I did not want to go for a broken stick approach as my goal will be to make this model hierarchical later on. Error on weight is assumed gamma (best option so far to get realistic weight estimates together with allowing the variance to be proportional to the mean).
>
>
>
> I tend to run 3 chains and I usually get:
>
> 	•   2 chains with mean weights about 2, 4 and 6 kg and proportion of ages about 0.70, 0.25, 0.05 for ages 1, 2 and 3 respectively. This is quite realistic biologically.
> 	•   1 chain stuck with values of .7, 2.2 and 4.5 for mean weights and proportions of 0, .7 and .3. This gives reasonable fit to the data but it is clearly not realistic ecologically and the Log posterior values distribution associated is significantly lower than is the previous case.

Michael just wrote a case study on mixture models:

  http://mc-stan.org/documentation/case-studies/identifying_mixture_models.html

The problem is that you can't jump between the modes you're
finding.

If you start near the solution you want and keep the initial
step size low, it'll be less likely to randomly jump away to start.

This is only going to be kosher if you know the probabiliy mass
around the other mode is low (it can be high with low density values
if it covers a lot of raw Euclidean volume).

> This happens with giving rather informative starting values to the different chains. I thus wonder if I could improve things using different priors.

A prior that avoids the weights going to zero might
help.  Something like

  p_ages ~ dirichlet(alpha_p_ages);

where alpha_p_ages is rep_vector(a, K) where K is the size
of p_ages and a >> 1.

> I have the feeling that this could be the issue but any other suggestion you may have would also be very welcome.
>
> If you have hints about how to change the code to make it faster that would be great too.

See below.

>
>
> Enter code here...
> data {
>   int<lower=0> n_fish; // number of fish
>   int<lower=1> n_ages; // number of age classes in the model
>   real<lower=0> weight[n_fish]; // weight of fish
> }
>
> parameters {
>   real<lower=7500> weight_inf; // asymptotic weight

We don't recommend these hard cutoffs, but recommend priors.
It's a big problem if you wind up with mass near the boundaries.

Also, keeping params unit scale will help.  For example, take
the parameter to be

  real<lower=0> weight_raw;

and then scale it manually as a transformed parameter:

  weight_inf = 7500 * weight_raw;

>   real<lower=0.1> k; // growth rate

Same comment.

>   real t_zero; // curve shifting
>   real<lower=1.5> b; // weight length exponent factor

Same comment.

>   real<lower=0> beta; // component of gamma likelyhood
>   simplex[n_ages] p_ages; // age proportions, ie mixture
> }
>
> transformed parameters {
>   real<lower = 0> mu_weight_ages[n_ages]; // mean weight of an age class
>   real<lower = 0> alpha_ages[n_ages]; // component gamma likelyhood
>   for(a in 1:n_ages){
>    // Von Bertalanffy growth equation
>    mu_weight_ages[a] = weight_inf * pow(1 - exp(-k * (a - t_zero)), b);

This can be unstable with exp inside of pow, especially if b is large.

>    alpha_ages[a] = mu_weight_ages[a] * beta;

Vectorize this.

>   }
> }
>
> model {
>   real ps[n_ages];
>   weight_inf ~ normal(30000, 3000);

weight_inf_raw ~ normal(0, 1);

weight_inf = 30000 + weight_inf_raw * 3000;

>   k ~ cauchy(0, 1);
>   t_zero ~ normal(0, 1);
>   b ~ normal(2.84, 0.2); # informative prior
>   beta ~ cauchy(0, 1);

The Cauchy's can be too fat---see how far beta and k are moving
out into the tails.

>   for(f in 1:n_fish){
>       for(a in 1:n_ages){
>           ps[a] = log(p_ages[a]) + gamma_lpdf(weight[f] |alpha_ages[a], beta);

Precomputing and saving log(p_ages) will save recomputing it.

>       }
>       target += log_sum_exp(ps);
>   }
> }
>

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] sampling poorly-constrained shape parameter for gamma distribution
messages.body_plain:
With a low step size (0.01) and high adapt delta (0.99), I don't
get any divergent transitions and everything seems to work in your simple
example.  I added an MC simulation for comparison:

generated quantities {
  real shape2 = lognormal_rng(0, 1);
  real y2 = gamma_rng(shape2, shape2);
}

and get this with 4 chains of 10K iterations total (half warmup each):

        mean se_mean   sd  2.5%   25%   50%   75% 97.5% n_eff Rhat
shape   1.64    0.03 2.00  0.14  0.52  1.01  1.96  7.11  3357    1
y       1.00    0.01 1.34  0.00  0.25  0.70  1.30  3.92  8246    1
shape2  1.66    0.02 2.25  0.14  0.51  1.00  1.96  7.21 20000    1
y2      0.99    0.01 1.30  0.00  0.24  0.69  1.28  3.94 20000    1

You can see that the intervals are very close even if the sd is
a bit off (sampling error, not a bug).

The pairs plot does look like a pretty awful L shape on the constrained
scale --- I'm not good enough at R to figure out how to do the pairs() plot
on the unconstrained scale, which is the only scale that matters for
sampling.

Maybe someone else will have a better idea of how to reparameterize.
It's not a simple location-scale family, so the obvious non-centered
approach won't work.  I also have no idea if you can integrate out that
shape parameter.

- Bob

> On Mar 14, 2017, at 12:50 PM, David J. Harris <harr...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> (sorry for the double-post. I think my wording may have been unclear on one point: I meant to say that my VG model has strong correlations & BFMI warning, which could indicate an additional problem not found in this example)
>

> On Tuesday, March 14, 2017 at 12:33:01 PM UTC-4, David J. Harris wrote:
> I'm working with the variance-gamma (VG) process, which is a Lévy process where the increments between t and t+1 are conditionally Gaussian with gamma-distributed variance (as opposed to Student t's _inverse_ gamma).  I'm getting really bad behavior from the gamma distribution's shape parameter, and I was wondering about possible reparameterizations of the gamma distribution.
>

messages.body_plain:
I should be a little more specific.

I am working with the following type of model:

Y ~ Multinomial(pi)
pi = softmax(eta)
eta ~ DLM()

were "eta ~ DLM()"  is a model of the form

eta = F_t' * theta_t + v_t ;  v_t ~ N(0, V_t)
theta_t = G_t * theta_t-1 + w_t ; w_t ~ N(0,W_t)

I am using the Kalman filter to marginalize over the state variables (to reduce the burden on Stan's sampler) as appears to be done here <http://www.juhokokkala.fi/blog/posts/kalman-filter-style-recursion-to-marginalize-state-variables-to-speed-up-stan-inference/> and for gaussian_dlm_obs_log <https://github.com/stan-dev/math/blob/0e44f625d4b8a366670b4fd18059fc2cbc054d21/stan/math/prim/mat/prob/gaussian_dlm_obs_log.hpp>. However this marginalization makes it difficult to see how to create a non-centered parameterization and I was hoping for some help.

Thank you very much!!
Justin Silverman

messages.body_plain:
Everywhere you see

x ~ N(mu, sigma)

replace it with

x_tilde ~ N(0, 1)
x = mu + sigma * x_tilde

In other words, for your updates

eta = F_t' * theta_t + V_t * v_t ;  v_t ~ N(0, 1)
theta_t = G_t * theta_t-1 + W_t * w_t ; w_t ~ N(0, 1)

What you have is already half-way to a non-centered
parameterization.  It would be fully centered if you had

theta_t ~ N(G_t * theta_t-1, W_t)
eta ~ N(F_t' * theta_t, V_t)

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I coded the Modified Metropolis algorithm for sampling from pi(x | y) in both Matlab and R and it works well.
But, Conceptually i have a problem applying that in Stan, in which block "model"  or "generated quantities"? and how can i implement that?

The following is the Matlab code which I want to transfer it into Stan:

%-------------------------------------------------------------------------
 % Modified Metropolis algorithm for sampling from pi(x | F_L)
 for j=1:nc
 for m=1:ns
 % Step 1:
 for k=1:d
 a=z(k,j,m)+randn; % Step 1(a)
 r=min(1,normpdf(a)/normpdf(z(k,j,m))); % Step 1(b)
 % Step 1(c):
 if rand<r
 q(k)=a;
 else
 q(k)=z(k,j,m);
 end
 end
 % Step 2: applying the conditional part
 if sum(q)>Y(L) % q belongs to F_L
 z(:,j,m+1)=q;
 else
 z(:,j,m+1)=z(:,j,m);
 end
 end
 end
%-------------------------------------------------------------------------

Thank you very much in advance for your help.
Hamed

messages.subject_clean: avoid bi-modal posterior distribution for Phi_approx(normal)?
messages.body_plain:
On Thursday, April 21, 2016 at 10:03:36 AM UTC-4, Lei Zhang wrote:

>
> Hi Stan,
>
>
> I am modeling a discounting factor (hence lies in the range [0,1]) in a hierarchical fashion. I first used Matt Trick (non-centered reparameterization) for sampling from a normal distribution and then transform them into the [0 1] range with Phi_approx. Code as below.
>
> real disc_mu_pr;
> real<lower=0> disc_sd;
>
> vector[nSubjects] disc_raw;
> vector<lower=0,upper=1+1e-10>[nSubjects] disc;
>
> for (s in 1:nSubjects) {
>   disc[s] <- Phi_approx( disc_mu_pr + disc_sd * disc_raw[s] );
> }
>
> disc_mu_pr ~ normal(0,1);
> disc_sd    ~ cauchy(0,5);
> disc_raw   ~ normal(0,1);
>
>
> The fitting result shows a bi-modal posterior distribution of the disc parameter for nearly all the participants. I wonder it might because that the group level disc_sd is too large, such that the transformed disc parameter is pushed to both ends (0 and 1). I noticed that the R-hat values are actually not bad (all below 1.02, most are 1.00). I paste some of the summaries and I attach the density and pairs plot in case you may want to have a look.
>
> My question is, is there a way to avoid such a bi-modal posterior distribution? Should I use a more restricted prior for disc_sd (eg. half-normal(0,2)), or should I model the disc parameter as beta distribution and discard the Matt Trick?
>
> I appreciate any suggestions. Thanks!
>
> Lei
>
>
> 4 chains, each with iter=2000; warmup=1000; thin=1;
> post-warmup draws per chain=1000, total post-warmup draws=4000.
>
>           mean se_mean    sd 2.5%  25%  50%  75% 97.5% n_eff Rhat
> disc_mu   0.55    0.01  0.18 0.21 0.43 0.56 0.68  0.87  1036 1.01
> disc_sd   9.34    1.05 14.45 1.11 3.06 5.08 9.37 51.72   190 1.02
> disc[1]   0.56    0.01  0.41 0.00 0.07 0.67 0.99  1.00  1814 1.00
> disc[2]   0.65    0.01  0.39 0.00 0.27 0.84 1.00  1.00  1280 1.00
> disc[3]   0.73    0.01  0.32 0.00 0.53 0.87 1.00  1.00  2721 1.00
> disc[4]   0.54    0.01  0.41 0.00 0.08 0.61 0.98  1.00  4000 1.00
> disc[5]   0.85    0.00  0.22 0.16 0.77 0.96 1.00  1.00  2088 1.00
> disc[6]   0.57    0.01  0.41 0.00 0.09 0.69 0.99  1.00  2293 1.00
> disc[7]   0.42    0.01  0.40 0.00 0.01 0.30 0.88  1.00  4000 1.00
> disc[8]   0.41    0.01  0.42 0.00 0.00 0.23 0.89  1.00   814 1.00
> disc[9]   0.64    0.01  0.38 0.00 0.30 0.80 0.99  1.00  4000 1.00
> disc[10]  0.25    0.01  0.31 0.00 0.00 0.10 0.41  1.00  2022 1.00
>
>

Hi all,

I found this post after observing some strange behavior with this same transformation (i.e. Phi_approx transformation after using the Matt trick).

In summary, I think this issue may be caused by the prior, which is placing a large mass on the extremes of the parameter bounds after the probit transformation is applied. I have attached code below (plot_priors.R) that can be used to draw samples from the prior distribution for a parameter being sampled in this way. The code can be modified by changing the distribution of the scale parameter from a cauchy to a normal (line 7), and you can also change the other values used in the sampling (e.g. the hyper_sd scale on line 11). Using the same parameterization as in the model you have attached, I get prior distributions of the form shown in image_1.png (attached). The image shows what the prior looks like both with (left) and without (right) the probit transformation being applied. On the left, you can see that the prior mass is heavily localized around the parameter bounds. On the right, the prior looks like what you would expect (Note that I am "zooming in" by limiting the x axis between -200 and 200, else you cannot see the form). I think this may explain why bimodal posteriors are common when using this type of parameterization? But I could be wrong–I wanted to post here to see what everyone else thinks.

Interestingly, when the scale parameter on the cauchy distribution is set very low, the prior distribution over the probit transformed space becomes relatively uniform. image_2.png shows an example of the prior when the scale parameter in the cauchy is set to 0.001 as opposed to 5. Also, the right panel now appears more or less normally distributed.

So, I guess my question is now this–what is the best way to approach this problem? Can the scale parameter for the cauchy be set low, or will this not allow for individual level differences in that parameter estimate (in the case of Lei's example code, differences among disc)? Another potential solution would be to truncate the parameter being estimated so that values under 0.01 and over 0.99 are not allowed (using the code example above; see image_3.png for a visual depiction):

 vector<lower=0.01,upper=0.99>[nSubjects] disc;

However, I understand that hard constraints like this are not ideal. I guess the problem then is coming up with a good soft constraint.

If anyone has information on the best steps to take in this situation, it would be greatly appreciated. Please let me know if anything is unclear.

Best,
Nate

messages.body_plain:
No, that's not what I meant.  If you have uniform priors on the distances between the cutpoints, and you have a bit of data, then your posterior won't be collapsed near 1e-10 or even near 0.001.  That sort of collapsing behavior can occur with point estimates, and it can occur with hierarchical models (the "funnel") but it should not hold with flat priors.  If you happen to have zero data in some cells, maybe you'll get the difference between cutpoints to be estimated at 0.01 or something like that.
A

> On Mar 15, 2017, at 2:43 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
> In theory, you won't ever get exactly collapsed cut points
> in the posterior, but that doesn't mean that in practice you
> won't get close enough to cause underflow and other problems.
>
> Same as if you start drawing theta ~ beta(1e-10, 1e-10).  Sure,
> you shouldn't draw theta = 0 or theta = 1 in theory, but that's
> what's going to happen with floating point arithmetic on computers.
> You can get around that problem with just a little stronger prior.
>
> - Bob
>
>> On Mar 13, 2017, at 5:59 PM, Andrew Gelman <Gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>>
>> Collapse if cutpoints can occur with point estimation but should not occur with full Bayes.
>>
>>> On Mar 13, 2017, at 3:47 PM, Tobias Konitzer <tobias....@gmail.com> wrote:
>>>
>>> I am wondering how to derive cut-points with only using prior counts in the different categories, but no information from the data other than that. It sounds like Bob's approach above does this, but how do I go from K (assuming K= number of categories) prior probabilities to K-1 cut-points? Does the above not estimate the first cut-point? In that case, we would calculate the predicted probability of k=1 as 1-sum(prob k=k), akin to estimating the probability of falling into the maximum category in standard ordinal logistic regression?
>>>
>>> And, would that approach, without some scale taken from predictors, be good enough to avoid collapse?
>>>
>>> Thanks,
>>> Tobi
>>>
>>> On Thursday, April 14, 2016 at 1:53:28 PM UTC-7, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>>> The transform for the simplex uses stick-breaking.  but
>>> there's no ordering --- what do you mean by ordering of
>>> the cutpoints?  The usual thing to do here is take the
>>> cumulative sums, so you get an increasing sequence to scale:
>>>
>>> parameters {
>>>  simplex[K] theta;     // gaps between cutpoints
>>>  real<lower=0> kappa;  // scale for cutpoints
>>>
>>> transformed parameters {
>>>  ordered[K] cutpoints;
>>>  cutpoints <- cumulative_sum(theta) * kappa;
>>>
>>> model {
>>>  theta ~ dirichlet(rep_vector(alpha, K));
>>>
>>> Then if you put a Dirichlet prior on theta, with alpha >> 1, it'll keep

>>> transformed data.

>>> - Bob

>>>> On Apr 14, 2016, at 12:11 AM, Dustin Tran <dustinv...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>>>
>>>> What about a truncated stick breaking prior? The size-biasedness of TSB priors will
>>>> (1) force an ordering for the cutpoints;
>>>> (2) make draws of cutpoints live on [0,1] which you can scale willy-nilly;
>>>> (3) reinforce what Ben said on adding prior information via pseudocounts in the parameters of a Dirichlet prior (here, use Beta stick-breaking priors, which is what Ben essentially does based on the running sum in the make_cutpoints function).
>>>>
>>>> Dustin

>>>>>>>    real running_sum;

messages.subject: Stan Math Library - Newbie Question on AutoDiff Operator Overloading
messages.subject_clean: Stan Math Library - Newbie Question on AutoDiff Operator Overloading
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am trying to use the autodiff functionality in the Stan Math Library to compute the Jacobian as part of a complex energy optimization. I have a reasonable understanding of how the autodiff approach works in theory.

The complication I have is that some of the variables in one energy term are non-trivial and whose derivatives are hidden within a 3rd party library (and are not trivial to calculate from first principles). They are related to change on curvature of patches representing a surface.

As an example, lets call two of the variables u and v which are 3x1 vectors, which I am trying to optimize over. For known u and v, the API can return the (first, second, third derivatives) i.e. du, dv, duu, dvv, duv, etc.....so I am able to know ascertain these in addition to my current u and v values.

So my question if it is possible to overload a simple as example e.g.

std::math::var lp = 0.5 * cross(u,v)
lp.grad() ;
std::cout << " d.f / d.u = " << u.adj() << " d.f / d.v = " << v.adj() << std::endl;

such that when the Stan Math Library tries to find the partial derivatives of u and v, rather than attempting to perform a standard differentiation on what appears to be a simple pair of variables u and v, but replaces the nodes in the graph by either my known du and dv values (or a function which calls the API to get them).

I presume if you can, it is via some sort of overloading of the stan::math::var type (the type you normally define your standard variables as) ?

Thanks in advance,

Adam

Yup, understood.  The MLE will actually collapse the boundaries
into each other if there's no data, whereas the Bayesian one
will never get there.

Now we're just guessing how close the cut points will go
to each other in some of the posterior draws, which will
depend on the prior and how much data there is in the other
bins.  I haven't fit one of these in a while, so I may be
misremembering how bad the numerical issues will be.
Either way, the distance on the unconstrained scale needs
to go to -infinity to get it exponentiation to zero, so it
can cause issues if you get lots of data in the other bins.

Of course, instead of a uniform on the inter-cut-point distances,
you can use something that avoids zero like a gamma with the
appropriate params.

- Bob

> No, that's not what I meant.  If you have uniform priors on the distances between the cutpoints, and you have a bit of data, then your posterior won't be collapsed near 1e-10 or even near 0.001.  That sort of collapsing behavior can occur with point estimates, and it can occur with hierarchical models (the "funnel") but it should not hold with flat priors.  If you happen to have zero data in some cells, maybe you'll get the difference between cutpoints to be estimated at 0.01 or something like that.
> A

I think we're just talking about the math lib, not using
Stan for sampling, so much of that doc won't be relevant.

To plug in an external black box function for use with the rest of
our autodiff, you need to be able to compute its value
and its Jacobian.

An alternative, is to convert the double types to stan::math::var
types and make sure all the operations bottom out in functions the
Stan math library supports (all the C++ built-ins plus a lot more).

You want to check out the arXiv paper for details on how
our reverse-mode autodiff works:

https://arxiv.org/abs/1509.07164

It's very thoroughly tested.

Forward mode isn't nearly as thoroughly tested.

- Bob

There should be a named list called stanmodels containing compiled stanmodel objects that is in your package's namespace but not exported. The names of the list elements are the same as the files in the exec/ directory but without the .stan extension. You can pass any of those to sampling(), optimizing(), or vb().

Ben

messages.body_plain:
> On Mar 16, 2017, at 10:38 AM, Guillaume Bal <guillaum...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Dear Bob and Michael,
>
> First thanks a lot for your answers. I really appreciate them and I am going to try them out very soon.
>
> In particular, I'll vectorize the code a bit mode, will use more informative priors when possible and try to get the scale units comparable.
>
> Here are a few more elements/ question following your comments:
>  - I get the idea that starting near the 'right answer' lead to small jumps. Just for my information, is there a way to increase the jump size ?
>    I guess it is probably possible to do it through arguments within control but it is a bit obscure to me.

stepsize sets initial step size and adapt_delta gives you target acceptance
rate---closer to 1 that is, the smaller the stepsize required.  Or you can
just fix it, but then you need to use a default mass matrix until a release or
two from now.

> -  about the two kind of convergence I mentioned, the second one, tending to go toward a binomial mixture, is not 'a complete aberration' ecologically speaking.

Then the model's wrong if it has way less probability mass
than the other mode (with three components).

>    Nonetheless according to expert knowledge, it is sub-optimal and that does reflect on the lp__ values as well.

The lp__ values are about density---what you care about is
probability mass, which is density integrated over a volume.

>  - About the cauchy being to fat, do you mean to much of a tail ?

Yes.

> If yes I think it might be right. Indeed the k and beta posteriors are centered on 0.18 (sd =  0.01) and  3.3e-03(sd =2.4 e-4).
>    A tighter prior may be better and maybe going for a half normal would also improve things.

>  - I looked at your link and I think the model I wrote should be alright as the growth model implies some ordering
>  - about the problem with the power factor, there is quite on informative prior centered on 2.84. I guess this should limit the issue you mentioned

It can still be easy to fall into a mode and not escape if
the density in between the modes is too low.  You can try
initializing around the mode you know is right and starting
stepsize low.  You'll get the right answer if and only if
there's roughly no probability mass in the other modes (again,
I want to stress this is mass, not density).

- Bob

On Friday, March 17, 2017 at 1:03:03 AM UTC-4, Nathaniel Haines wrote:
> Hi all,
>
> I am posting a new topic, but this question is related to a previous post which I actually wrote most of this comment out in: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/stan-users/_D6MlTNQZxk/ . I am posting a new topic because I am not sure if older posts will get attention.
>
> The problem I am encountering is this–my colleagues and I have been using a non-centered parameterization to estimate parameters in a hierarchical model. This parameterization follows the form:
>
> real mu_parameter;
> real<lower=0> sigma;
>
> vector[N] parameter_raw;
> vector<lower=0,upper=1>[N] parameter;
>
> for (i in 1:N) {
>   parameter[i] <- Phi_approx( mu_parameter + sigma * parameter_raw[i] );
> }
>
> mu_parameter  ~ normal(0,1);
> sigma         ~ cauchy(0,5);
> parameter_raw ~ normal(0,1);
>
> As you can see, we transform the parameter to [0,1] with the Phi_approx function (the parameters are rates, which justifies this transformation).
>
> Referring back to the post I linked above (https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/stan-users/_D6MlTNQZxk/), this can sometimes lead to bimodal posterior estimates, where the posterior mass is largely clustered around the parameter bounds. Advice in the linked post was assuming that this may be due to the parameter actually being bimodal, but I am not sure this is the case. My reasoning is outlined below.
>
> In summary, I think this issue (bimodality) may be caused by the prior, which is (I think) placing a large mass on the extremes of the parameter bounds after the probit transformation is applied. I have attached code below (plot_priors.R) that can be used to draw samples from the prior distribution for a parameter being sampled in this way. The code can be modified by changing the distribution of the scale parameter from a cauchy to a normal (line 7), and you can also change the other values used in the sampling (e.g. the hyper_sd scale on line 11). Using the same parameterization as in the example code above, I get prior distributions of the form shown in image_1.png (attached). The image shows what the prior looks like both with (left) and without (right) the probit transformation being applied. On the left, you can see that the prior mass is heavily localized around the parameter bounds. On the right, the prior looks like what you would expect (Note that I am "zooming in" by limiting the x axis between -200 and 200, else you cannot see the form). I think this may explain why bimodal posteriors are common when using this type of parameterization? But I could be wrong–I wanted to post here to see what everyone else thinks.
>
> Interestingly, when the scale parameter on the cauchy distribution is set very low, the prior distribution over the probit transformed space becomes relatively uniform. image_2.png shows an example of the prior when the scale parameter in the cauchy is set to 0.001 as opposed to 5.
>
> So, I guess my question is now this–what is the best way to approach this problem? Can the scale parameter for the cauchy be set low, or will this not allow for individual level differences in that parameter estimate (in the case of the example code, differences among parameter)? Another potential solution would be to truncate the parameter being estimated so that values under 0.01 and over 0.99 are not allowed (using the code example above; see image_3.png for a visual depiction of the constraint):
>
>  vector<lower=0.01,upper=0.99>[N] parameter;
>
> However, I understand that hard constraints like this are not ideal. I guess the problem then is coming up with a good soft constraint.
>
> If anyone has information on the best steps to take in this situation, it would be greatly appreciated. Please let me know if anything is unclear.
>
> Best,
> Nate

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Bounded transformations after non-centered parameterization (i.e. Matt Trick)
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: Bounded transformations after non-centered parameterization (i.e. Matt Trick)
messages.body_plain:
If a in (-inf, inf) then Phi(a) in (0, 1).  No need to bound
a below at zero.  (inv_logit, the inverse CDF of the logistic
distribution, is a bit more efficient, and is the basis of
the Phi_approx function.)

Usually if there's a problem like this, it's because
the data are pulling your parameters toward the boundary.

I had a hard time following all those things with "parameter"
in the name, but in general,  if

  y ~ normal(0, 1)

then

  Phi(y) ~ uniform(0, 1)

If y ~ normal(0, sigma) for sigma > 1, then it's bimodal at the
extremes, whereas if sigma < 1, then it's unimodal.

Similarly, if

  y ~ logistic(0, 1)

then

  inv_logit(y) ~ uniform(0, 1)

You can't do what you're trying to do with constraints.  What you
can do, but which we don't recommend (because if the data's causing
a pileup near the boundary, moving the boundary will just exacerbate
the problem), is to do this:

  0.98 * Phi(y) + 0.01

to generate values in the (0.01, 0.99) range.

- Bob

> Nate

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Can we simply sample from the joint gaussian distribution using NUTS in Stan?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Can we simply sample from the joint gaussian distribution using NUTS in Stan?
messages.body_plain:
Yes, but ti's a bad idea.  Just draw independent samples
from the multi-normal if that's all you're trying to do.

The Stan program to draw from a multivariate normal using
NUTS is trivial:

data {
  int N;
  vector[N] mu;
  cov_matrix[N] Sigma;
}
parameters {
  vector[N] y;
}
model {
  y ~ multi_normal(mu, Sigma);
}

But it's far far better to do this:

generated quantities {
  vector[N] y = multi_normal_rng(mu, Sigma);
}

to draw independent samples.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Yes and no.  It'd reject values below 0, but it's a
terrible way to code this.

Instead, declare y[2] with a lower bound of zero.  If
the other y don't have constraints, paste together
a vector of unconstrained and constrained variables.

Anything else will kill sampling performance.  Stan programs
should have finite density for any values of the parameters
that satisfy the declared constraints.  Otherwise, they may
just devolve to simple random walks.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hi Ben,

I have a problem with RStudio crashing that seems like it might be to do with this. I started using rstan a few weeks ago and it's been great -- I've had no problems with it crashing RStudio at all. However, ever since I started calling stan() from inside a new function, this problem has appeared: the function runs fine the first time, it compiles the code and runs the chains and it's all lovely. Then I call the function again, with exactly the same arguments, and it crashes RStudio. I restart RStudio and everything works (pretty much) fine from then on. Sporadically it will fail after the first time, but I can generally run the function as many times as I like without it crashing.

I'm generating a new .stan file each time (I know you don't like me doing this, but I need to allow the user to specify general nonlinear models and I can't think of a good way to precompile). The function goes something like:

1) generate mymodel.stan from user-supplied character strings and save to working directory
2) run fit <- stan("mymodel.stan",...)
3) compute some stuff
4) return(list(fit=fit,...))

Is there something obvious about this approach that would cause problems with the way the DSO is reloaded, but only after I first compile the model and only if I try to quickly re-run it?

Thanks,
Will

> On Thursday, March 17, 2016 at 8:49:15 AM UTC-4, Craig Wang wrote:
> > NOTE: it only re-compiles if I do not assign the output to a name, i.e. foo.out<-fecr_stan(...) does not re-compile while fecr_stan(...) does.

If a stanfit or stanmodel object is assigned to a symbol (that can easily be found), then calling the same Stan program does not recompile the model and instead fishes the compiled model out of the existing stanfit or stanmodel object. Otherwise, it has to recompile because loading the same dynamic shared object off of the disk crashes R.
>
> Ben

messages.body_plain:
Sorry for being unclear.

I have a function, f(u,v), hidden in a 3rd party API, which I don't have access to the core of what it is calculating and returns a [3,1] vector of values. There are also methods within the 3rd party API called GetFirstDerivatives(u,v), which returns partial derivative of f(u,v) i.e. du and dv, and GetSecondDerivatives(u,v), which returns duu, dvv, duv. Thus,

du is the partial derivative of f with respect to u.
dv is the partial derivative of f with respect to v.

duu is the second order partial derivative of f with respect to u
etc

Say I have a function K = (EP - F*F),

where

E = dot(du,du)
F = dot(du,dv)
G = dot(dv,dv)

Which is all fine.

However, now I want to create the Jacobian of K, which will obviously require combinations of 2nd order partial differentials (which I can numerically get from the function mentioned above). The autodiff library as it stands would obviously not be able to cope with this because it won't know what the partial differential of u, let alone du...as the base formula for f(u,v) is hidden from us.

So say when it comes to calculating the Jacobian of K, there is going to be need somewhere in the graph to calculate things like d/du (F), which written out in full will be duu * dv + du * dvu.

Autodiff won't know how to calculate duu or dvu. So there are going to be nodes in the graph I need to overload with special operators, such in this example GetSecondDerivatives(u,v) is called in order to insert the known value of duu or dvv.

Can I do this with a two dimensional array?

Thank you in advance

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Can we simply sample from the joint gaussian distribution using NUTS in Stan?
messages.body_plain:
It won't work.  HMC visits tail regions proportional to
their probability mass (assuming the tails aren't too fat).
It just does it more slowly than independent samplers.

- Bob

>

>
> I think directly sampling from the multi-normal distribution quite often visiting the typical set space, which computationally it might not be reasonable.
>
>
>
> - Hamed

>
>
>
> On Friday, March 17, 2017 at 7:51:12 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Yes, but ti's a bad idea.  Just draw independent samples
> from the multi-normal if that's all you're trying to do.
>
> The Stan program to draw from a multivariate normal using
> NUTS is trivial:
>
> data {
>   int N;
>   vector[N] mu;
>   cov_matrix[N] Sigma;
> }
> parameters {
>   vector[N] y;
> }
> model {
>   y ~ multi_normal(mu, Sigma);
> }
>
> But it's far far better to do this:
>
> generated quantities {
>   vector[N] y = multi_normal_rng(mu, Sigma);
> }
>
> to draw independent samples.
>
> - Bob

Aki

We're always looking for contributors. A few things:
1. Please start a new thread
2. Functions that make it into the Stan language need the function evaluation and gradients; hopefully you know how to compute the gradients of the kernels you're interested in (that's the gradient of each element of the kernel matrix with respect to each argument of the function)

That said, we're always happy to help. Before diving too deep, it would help to scope out what you're thinking and determine if what you're thinking is feasible. Computing gradients in a numerically stable way is a skill that you'll need if you don't have it already.

Daniel

messages.body_plain:
My ultimate goal is a least squares optiminization, via Levenberg-Marquart method, thus I need to form the Jacobian of a cost function. The cost function I am using includes a term which is the difference of Gaussian Curvature. For the other terms I have the actual function defined in a traditional way that fits with AutoDiff, but for the difference of Gaussian Curvature I don't have access to the underlying function.

Gaussian Curvature can be defined as a combination of First and Second Fundamental Forms of a Surface.

K = (e*g - f^2) / (E*G - F^2)

where

N = cross(du,dv) / norm(du,dv)
e = dot(N, duu)
f = dot(N,duv)
g = dot(N, dvv)

E = dot(du,du)
F = dot(du,dv)
G = dot(dv,dv)

where for example du is partial differential of a hidden function f(u,v) with respect to u etc as stated before.

http://mathworld.wolfram.com/FundamentalForms.html

So I want to incorporate the Jacobian of this function in my LM optimization.

I am using Pixar's OpenSubDiv library to model a surface. I have modified this set of functions, such that it returns upto 3rd Derivs. However, I don't have access to the base function f(u,v), only the ability to call a function which returns things like du, duv, ...

http://graphics.pixar.com/opensubdiv/docs/doxy_html/a00048.html

What it does is a little bit more complicated, but for ease of explanation lets say that it effectively takes a set of triples (faceId,u,v) and from which you can return the values of the partial first, second and third order derivations. The faceId isn't important, just think of it as a function f(u,v). The exact function is a blackbox hidden in OpenSubDiv (it is actually different functions depending on various conditions, which is why I don't want to open the blackbox up directly to AutoDiff).

So what I want to do is override some operators in Stan that effectively says when it is trying to calculate the Jacobian and will differentiate K, for all the partial diffs that will be required I know what the value is and insert that into the graph directly.

As stated in my last post, Adept appears to have exactly this function built-in called  append_derivative_dependence, which is explained in Section 2.7 of their documentation with an example not a million miles from what I am trying to achieve.

>

messages.body_plain:
You are overcomplicating the problem, which is already
complicated enough.

First, let’s assume that you are studying a surface that
admits a global coordinate system so that the Gaussian
curvature equations can be defined self-consistently
everywhere.

Then you can write your cost function as

C : R^N \times R^N -> R
(u, v) \mapsto K(u) - K(v)

The function K can be written entirely in terms of the
first and second-order coordinate surface tangents
made available by this third-party library.

Then you can compute the gradient of f analytically
in terms of the first, second, and third-order surface
tangents which you claim to also be available.

So now you have equations for C and its gradient
and you can evaluate them using information provided
by the third-party library.

_This_ is what you implement as a function in the Stan
Math Library.  If you cannot provide that gradient
analytically and can’t or won’t open up the black box
then we literally do not have the information necessary
to try to compute the gradient automatically.

required components.  Thanks for figuring this out and responding!

harder if you need second-order derivatives, because we need a templated
first-order derivative function in order to write our mixed mode
reverse nested in forward mode for second-order derivatives.

that parallel's that section of the Adept doc (thanks for the pointer).

higher-order derivatives.  The problem we have is that there's not an easy
way to implement a forward-mode function.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Iterations start fast but become very slow
messages.body_plain:
If you have the default 50% warmup, what you're probably seeing
is that as Stan adapts the mass matrix (essentially scale of each
parameter), it is having to take a very small step size and the
number of steps go up.  This is usually because there's some
parameter bumping up against a boundary (which forces it to try to
run off to positive or negative infinity on the unconstrained scale
where Stan samples), or because there's very high curvature in some
regions of the posterior.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] avoid bi-modal posterior distribution for Phi_approx(normal)?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] avoid bi-modal posterior distribution for Phi_approx(normal)?
messages.body_plain:
Thanks---that's right.  The Cauchy always has fat tails, but you
can keep most of the mass more central and avoid getting a U-shaped
result.

Truncating won't help as it'll just pile up against the truncation
points, and still be problematic.  You need to control where the
parameters get estimated.

- Bob

> On Mar 15, 2017, at 4:26 PM, Nathaniel Haines <nathane...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
>
>
> On Thursday, April 21, 2016 at 10:03:36 AM UTC-4, Lei Zhang wrote:
>
> Hi Stan,
>
>
>
> I am modeling a discounting factor (hence lies in the range [0,1]) in a hierarchical fashion. I first used Matt Trick (non-centered reparameterization) for sampling from a normal distribution and then transform them into the [0 1] range with Phi_approx. Code as below.
>
> real disc_mu_pr;
> real<lower=0> disc_sd;
>
> vector[nSubjects] disc_raw;
> vector<lower=0,upper=1+1e-10>[nSubjects] disc;
>
> for (s in 1:nSubjects) {
>   disc[s] <- Phi_approx( disc_mu_pr + disc_sd * disc_raw[s] );
> }
>
> disc_mu_pr ~ normal(0,1);
> disc_sd    ~ cauchy(0,5);
> disc_raw   ~ normal(0,1);
>
>
> The fitting result shows a bi-modal posterior distribution of the disc parameter for nearly all the participants. I wonder it might because that the group level disc_sd is too large, such that the transformed disc parameter is pushed to both ends (0 and 1). I noticed that the R-hat values are actually not bad (all below 1.02, most are 1.00). I paste some of the summaries and I attach the density and pairs plot in case you may want to have a look.
>
> My question is, is there a way to avoid such a bi-modal posterior distribution? Should I use a more restricted prior for disc_sd (eg. half-normal(0,2)), or should I model the disc parameter as beta distribution and discard the Matt Trick?
>
> I appreciate any suggestions. Thanks!
>
> Lei
>
>
>
> 4 chains, each with iter=2000; warmup=1000; thin=1;
> post-warmup draws per chain=1000, total post-warmup draws=4000.
>
>           mean se_mean    sd 2.5%  25%  50%  75% 97.5% n_eff Rhat
> disc_mu   0.55    0.01  0.18 0.21 0.43 0.56 0.68  0.87  1036 1.01
> disc_sd   9.34    1.05 14.45 1.11 3.06 5.08 9.37 51.72   190 1.02
> disc[1]   0.56    0.01  0.41 0.00 0.07 0.67 0.99  1.00  1814 1.00
> disc[2]   0.65    0.01  0.39 0.00 0.27 0.84 1.00  1.00  1280 1.00
> disc[3]   0.73    0.01  0.32 0.00 0.53 0.87 1.00  1.00  2721 1.00
> disc[4]   0.54    0.01  0.41 0.00 0.08 0.61 0.98  1.00  4000 1.00
> disc[5]   0.85    0.00  0.22 0.16 0.77 0.96 1.00  1.00  2088 1.00
> disc[6]   0.57    0.01  0.41 0.00 0.09 0.69 0.99  1.00  2293 1.00
> disc[7]   0.42    0.01  0.40 0.00 0.01 0.30 0.88  1.00  4000 1.00
> disc[8]   0.41    0.01  0.42 0.00 0.00 0.23 0.89  1.00   814 1.00
> disc[9]   0.64    0.01  0.38 0.00 0.30 0.80 0.99  1.00  4000 1.00
> disc[10]  0.25    0.01  0.31 0.00 0.00 0.10 0.41  1.00  2022 1.00
>
>
>
> Hi all,
>
> I found this post after observing some strange behavior with this same transformation (i.e. Phi_approx transformation after using the Matt trick).
>
> In summary, I think this issue may be caused by the prior, which is placing a large mass on the extremes of the parameter bounds after the probit transformation is applied. I have attached code below (plot_priors.R) that can be used to draw samples from the prior distribution for a parameter being sampled in this way. The code can be modified by changing the distribution of the scale parameter from a cauchy to a normal (line 7), and you can also change the other values used in the sampling (e.g. the hyper_sd scale on line 11). Using the same parameterization as in the model you have attached, I get prior distributions of the form shown in image_1.png (attached). The image shows what the prior looks like both with (left) and without (right) the probit transformation being applied. On the left, you can see that the prior mass is heavily localized around the parameter bounds. On the right, the prior looks like what you would expect (Note that I am "zooming in" by limiting the x axis between -200 and 200, else you cannot see the form). I think this may explain why bimodal posteriors are common when using this type of parameterization? But I could be wrong–I wanted to post here to see what everyone else thinks.
>
> Interestingly, when the scale parameter on the cauchy distribution is set very low, the prior distribution over the probit transformed space becomes relatively uniform. image_2.png shows an example of the prior when the scale parameter in the cauchy is set to 0.001 as opposed to 5. Also, the right panel now appears more or less normally distributed.
>
> So, I guess my question is now this–what is the best way to approach this problem? Can the scale parameter for the cauchy be set low, or will this not allow for individual level differences in that parameter estimate (in the case of Lei's example code, differences among disc)? Another potential solution would be to truncate the parameter being estimated so that values under 0.01 and over 0.99 are not allowed (using the code example above; see image_3.png for a visual depiction):
>
>  vector<lower=0.01,upper=0.99>[nSubjects] disc;
>

> However, I am not sure if this is an appropriate way to do this.

>
> If anyone has information on the best steps to take in this situation, it would be greatly appreciated. Please let me know if anything is unclear.
>
> Best,
> Nate
>

The first place to look is the manual chapter on ragged and sparse
data.  Until we get ragged arrays, you have to code everything up
in simpler data structures and then slice it out.  This is much easier
now with the array slicing (e.g., a[3:7]) than it used to be, but
the manual chapter may not have been updated and may still use older
slicing functions.

If you still have questions after that, let us know and we can help
further.

- Bob

> On Fri, Mar 17, 2017 at 7:25 PM Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> > If a in (-inf, inf) then Phi(a) in (0, 1).  No need to bound
> > a below at zero.  (inv_logit, the inverse CDF of the logistic
> > distribution, is a bit more efficient, and is the basis of
> > the Phi_approx function.)
> >
> > Usually if there's a problem like this, it's because
> > the data are pulling your parameters toward the boundary.
> >
> > I had a hard time following all those things with "parameter"
> > in the name, but in general,  if
> >
> >   y ~ normal(0, 1)
> >
> > then
> >
> >   Phi(y) ~ uniform(0, 1)
> >
> > If y ~ normal(0, sigma) for sigma > 1, then it's bimodal at the
> > extremes, whereas if sigma < 1, then it's unimodal.
> >
> > Similarly, if
> >
> >   y ~ logistic(0, 1)
> >
> > then
> >
> >   inv_logit(y) ~ uniform(0, 1)
> >
> > You can't do what you're trying to do with constraints.  What you
> > can do, but which we don't recommend (because if the data's causing
> > a pileup near the boundary, moving the boundary will just exacerbate
> > the problem), is to do this:
> >
> >   0.98 * Phi(y) + 0.01
> >
> > to generate values in the (0.01, 0.99) range.

messages.subject: Re: CFA with four factors: problem in covariance matrix (I think)
messages.subject_clean: CFA with four factors: problem in covariance matrix (I think)
messages.body_plain:
With this type of parameterization, you need multi_normal_cholesky to use a cholesky factor of a covariance matrix, but you're feeding it a cholesky factor of a correlation matrix.

messages.body_plain:
You're talking about something like below.

parameters {
    vector[N] alpha;
    vector<lower=0>[N] beta;
    ...
}
transformed parameters {
    vector[N] gamma[2];
    ...

    gamma[1] = alpha;
    gamma[2] = beta;
    ...
}
model {
    gamma ~ multi_normal(mu_gamma, sigma_gamma);
    ...
}

The only problem I can see is that it becomes complicated to implement something like this with a multivariate reparameterization. Would something like the below work? In the more general case, I would be fitting a prior to mu and L_sigma, so delta[2]'s lower bounds would depend on those. That gets complicated.

parameters {
    vector[N] delta[2];
    ...
}
transformed parameters {
    vector[N] alpha;
    vector<lower=0>[N] beta;
    vector[N] gamma[2];
    ...

    gamma = mu_gamma + L_sigma_gamma * delta;
    alpha = gamma[1];
    beta = gamma[2];
    ...
}
model {
    delta ~ normal(0, 1);
    ...
}

It’s not that there is a trade off between divergences and low E-BFMI,
rather the divergences are masking a low E-BFMI.  Remember that
divergences indicate that you’re not able to explore the entire target
distribution, and that incomplete exploration can give you inaccurate
E-BFMI estimates.  Only when you increase adapt_delta and the
exploration becomes more accurate does the accurate E-BFMI
emerge!

messages.body_plain:
What derivatives of G do you want?  With respect to x and y?

As I was trying to say before, you need to nest the other way,
following the way Hessians work, but interposing the extra
operation in between.

So it's going to look something like this:

  var xv = x;
  var yv = y;

  fvar<var> a(x, 1);
  fvar<var> b(y, 0);

  fvar<var> fab = f(a, b);

  var dfab_da = fab.tangent();
  var gab = square(xv) * dfab_da;

  vector<double> grad;
  vector<var> args;
  args.push_back(xv);
  args.push_back(yv);
  gab.grad(grad, args);

and grad will hold the gradient you're after.  There may be
some missing steps in there---I haven't tested it.

- Bob

The small E-BFMI typically indicate heavy tails, so it could

continuous spaces where something like Stan could be used, but those
embeddings introduce their own pathologies which obstruct efficient
computation.  Ultimately this is all due to the fact that we don’t know how
to efficiently move through even structured discrete spaces.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Chang,

Variables declared in the model block are only available in the model block. One thing you can do is declare and define the variable in the transformed parameters block (in which case it will be available both in the model and generated quantities blocks), but then that variable will be saved (unlike in the model block). Instead, what I typically do in a case like this is define a function in the functions block that returns the quantity I need and then I use that function in both the model block and generated quantities blocks (instead of copying and pasting the code in both blocks).

Jonah

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Stan for MC sampling of Ising states
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Stan for MC sampling of Ising states
messages.body_plain:
There's a cottage entire industry devoted to fitting Ising models.
That's precisely because nobody knows how to fit them reliably.
They're NP-complete, in general, so there's good reason to believe
they're fundamentally intractable (no polynomial algorithm in the number
of states exists to solve them):

  https://www.siam.org/pdf/news/654.pdf

You probably don't want to reinvent the wheel here, but I don't
know which packages to recommend for special cases that might be
tractable or that provide heuristic approximations to the intractable
general case.

Just pulling out a naive discrete sampler (either Metropolis or Gibbs)
isn't going to work due to the stability of local optima and the combinatorial
number of states requiring exploration, no matter how much parallel computing
power you throw at it.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] unbalanced panel with autocorrelation
messages.body_plain:
I don't see the ragged data in your example, so I misunderstood
your first question.

I'm afraid I'm going to recommend the manual again, this
time for non-centered parameterizations.  And for efficient
ways to code.  But I'll provide some hints inline below.

> On Mar 20, 2017, at 9:04 PM, Luis G <luism....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi Bob,
>
> Sorry for bugging you again. Thanks for your answer (and for the work you have done developing Stan!), I had gone through the manual but did not expect that the answer would be there!
>
>  I have now managed to get the program compiled and running well. Unfortunately, the markov chain does not converge (it is apparent when examining the diagnostics).
>
> Here is my code:
>
>     data{
>
>       int<lower = 0> N;// #observations
>       int<lower=0> K; // #individuals
>       int T[K]; // #observations/periods per individual
>       vector[N] y; // observations
>     }
>     parameters{
>       vector[N] x; // latent factor
>       real<lower = 0> mu[K];//average
>       real<lower = 0> sigma_eta;//variance of temporary shock
>       real<lower = 0> sigma_eps;//variance of permanent shock
>     }
>     model{

You probably want priors.

>       int iter;
>       iter = 1; // create an iterator to go through the vector
>       for (k in 1:K){//outerloop to iterate through each individual
>         //Define initial values for the individual
>         x[iter] ~ normal (mu[k], sigma_eta);

You are defining p(x[1] as follows:

  p(x[1]) propto PROD_{k in 1:K} normal(x[1] | mu[k], sigma_eta)

This is unlikely to be what you want.  If you did want it, you could
vectorize as

   x[iter] ~ normal(mu, sigma_eta) if mu is K elements long.

>         y[iter] ~ normal (x[iter], sigma_eps);
>         iter = iter +1;//one step ahead since
>
>         for(time_ind in 2:T[k]){//innerloop to iterate through periods
>           x[iter] ~ normal (x[iter-1], sigma_eta);//transition equation
>           y[iter] ~ normal (x[iter], sigma_eps);// measurement equation
>         }

Now you define x[2]  using (T[2] - 2 + 1) different priors, again not
what you probably want.

If you had wanted to do it, a better way to code this for efficiency
is with vectorization:

  x[2:T[k]] ~ normal(x[1:(T[k] - 1)], sigma_eta);

>         iter = iter + 1;//jump to next

Did you really want to increment iter twice in each loop?

> My guess is that it does not converge because sampling the x[K] factors makes it particularly intensive computationally.

That's part of the problem, but probably not why you think.  The problem
here is the measurement model and the fact that you're probably overspecifying
priors here in a way that doesn't make sense.

> The parameters I am truly interested in, however, are sigma_eps and sigma_eta, which I would like to model in a more sophisticated way -based on covariates or period specific- in future stages. Do you have any suggestion? Perhaps re-parametrizing the model in some fashion it would be computationally feasible?

I think you need to sort out the distributions---I don't think they're
right in this specification.

- Bob

failure diagnostics.

messages.subject: Explicitly Correlated Parameters
messages.subject_clean: Explicitly Correlated Parameters
messages.body_plain:
There are already a few threads on the subject, but I'm not interested in a particular model. Rather, I'm just observing that models with explicitly correlated parameters are a bit quirky in Stan. I'm curious if people out there have a lot of success with explicitly correlated parameters versus the implicit case. I'm also curious about best practices on when to use them and when to not use. My thoughts are below.

By explicitly correlated parameters, I mean a model that contains something like what is in Section 26.6 of the documentation under Multivariate Reparameterizations, rather than the previous section that handles the univariate case.

With Gibbs sampling and Metropolis-Hastings, you have to include a multivariate distribution or the posterior distribution would be almost forced to have uncorrelated parameters. I believe the situation was similar with BUGS/JAGS. I suspect the focus in those techniques is why there is a decent amount of focus in the Stan documentation on models with correlated parameters.

In Stan, my experience with correlated parameters in Stan has been rather frustrating. I almost always get worse results (in terms of having divergences, low N_eff, time to estimate, etc.) compared to univariate models. With a univariate prior on sets of parameters, the resulting posterior distribution on parameters might have some correlation when you look at them together, or maybe they won't. The only downside is that if you have some new observation, then you might need to make some assumptions in order to make predictions about it.

I suspect that this is driven by the restrictions imposed by the multivariate normal prior. For instance, one model I'm estimating is a linear regression on some panel data, each regressed on one common time series variable with parameters varying cross-sectionally on the intercepts, slopes, and std. deviations (hierarchical priors on each of these three). If you leave the priors on the varying parameters univariate, it fits pretty well, pretty quickly, all things considered. By contrast, if you explicitly impose any kind of correlated parameters (centered or non-centered on the slopes and intercepts), then you get divergences or low N_eff and it takes forever way longer.

To understand why this is, I focused on the posterior distribution of the parameters in the univariate case. Upon inspection, the slope looks a more log-normal than normal and the relationship of the intercept and the slope (or the slope and the standard deviations) looks non-linear. Thus, I suspect that imposing the linear correlation in the multivariate normal prevents the Stan sampler from finding the non-linear result.

Another potential explanation is sort of brought up in the wiki section on priors
https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Prior-Choice-Recommendations
under "Boundary-avoiding priors for modal estimation". I'm not sure it entirely applies, but it discusses the varying slope and intercept model and discusses the potential for a correlation of 1. Well, my example above often had a correlation near -1 between the intercepts and slopes. But, I'm not sure if this is a product of the divergences though.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Explicitly Correlated Parameters
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Explicitly Correlated Parameters
messages.body_plain:
It's not so much a Stan problem as a general problem.
There's no way to tweak multivariate proposals in Gibbs unless
you block them, and they tend not to work in Metropolis unless
you know the curvature (second derivative matrix) explicitly and
it doesn't vary around the posterior.  What you may be finding
is just that Stan's much better at exploring out the boundaries of
parameter space and reporting when it gets into trouble.

To see this for yourself, we recommend simulating data from a model
that looks like what you want and trying to fit in various systems
and look at the boundaries on 80% or 90% intervals you're getting
(95% or higher will be too noisy without a high effective sample size).
But you need to use Stan's posterior summary tools, which are also
more conservative than Coda or other tools often applied to BUGS
or JAGS models.

It's not the correlation that causes so much of a problem as
when the curvature (second derivative matrix aka Hessian) varies
around the posterior, as in the funnel example.

For arithmetic stability, we recommend using Cholesky factors
of correlation matrices with LKJ priors and then scaling (a
less ad hoc version of what Gelman and Hill recommend in
their regression book.

And yes, correlations near -1 or 1 are going to be problematic
no matter what sampler you use.  This is largely a fact of the
way floating point arithmetic works.  You can represent numbers
like 1e-300 --- in other words, get very close to zero, but the
closest you can get to 1 or -1 in floating point is around 1 - 1e-15.
If there's nothing stopping you from wanting to get closer, you're
going to get divergences because you just can't even represent a number
that's closer to 1 or -1 without rounding error to 1 or -1, which in
turns makes the covariance matrix singular.

But this is just what Andrew calls the "folk theorem".  If your
inferences want a correlation near 1 or -1, you have two linearly
redundant parameters in your regression and you probably just want
to get rid of one.  Otherwise, they're only going to be identified
by the prior (see the manual section on problematic priors for a simple
example using two intercepts, which is just an extreme case of
the same problem).

- Bob

> On Mar 21, 2017, at 3:58 PM, John Hall <john.mic...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> There are already a few threads on the subject, but I'm not interested in a particular model. Rather, I'm just observing that models with explicitly correlated parameters are a bit quirky in Stan. I'm curious if people out there have a lot of success with explicitly correlated parameters versus the implicit case. I'm also curious about best practices on when to use them and when to not use. My thoughts are below.
>
> By explicitly correlated parameters, I mean a model that contains something like what is in Section 26.6 of the documentation under Multivariate Reparameterizations, rather than the previous section that handles the univariate case.
>
> With Gibbs sampling and Metropolis-Hastings, you have to include a multivariate distribution or the posterior distribution would be almost forced to have uncorrelated parameters. I believe the situation was similar with BUGS/JAGS. I suspect the focus in those techniques is why there is a decent amount of focus in the Stan documentation on models with correlated parameters.
>
> In Stan, my experience with correlated parameters in Stan has been rather frustrating. I almost always get worse results (in terms of having divergences, low N_eff, time to estimate, etc.) compared to univariate models. With a univariate prior on sets of parameters, the resulting posterior distribution on parameters might have some correlation when you look at them together, or maybe they won't. The only downside is that if you have some new observation, then you might need to make some assumptions in order to make predictions about it.
>
> I suspect that this is driven by the restrictions imposed by the multivariate normal prior. For instance, one model I'm estimating is a linear regression on some panel data, each regressed on one common time series variable with parameters varying cross-sectionally on the intercepts, slopes, and std. deviations (hierarchical priors on each of these three). If you leave the priors on the varying parameters univariate, it fits pretty well, pretty quickly, all things considered. By contrast, if you explicitly impose any kind of correlated parameters (centered or non-centered on the slopes and intercepts), then you get divergences or low N_eff and it takes forever way longer.
>
> To understand why this is, I focused on the posterior distribution of the parameters in the univariate case. Upon inspection, the slope looks a more log-normal than normal and the relationship of the intercept and the slope (or the slope and the standard deviations) looks non-linear. Thus, I suspect that imposing the linear correlation in the multivariate normal prevents the Stan sampler from finding the non-linear result.
>
> Another potential explanation is sort of brought up in the wiki section on priors
> https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Prior-Choice-Recommendations
> under "Boundary-avoiding priors for modal estimation". I'm not sure it entirely applies, but it discusses the varying slope and intercept model and discusses the potential for a correlation of 1. Well, my example above often had a correlation near -1 between the intercepts and slopes. But, I'm not sure if this is a product of the divergences though.
>

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] unbalanced panel with autocorrelation
messages.body_plain:
Hi Luis,

This model looks pretty poorly identified, so I'd expect bad sampling performance. Do you expect the individuals to be correlated within time periods? If so it might be worth specifying the latent factor model at the level of the hyperprior, then the x_it would be distributed around that. Something like:

// time an integer[] with the time period, T the number of time periods, N number of observations

parameters {
  vector[N] x;
  vector[T] mu;
// also int, sigma, slope
}
model {

mu[1] ~ prior for starting value

// dynamic model for hyperprior
for(t in 2:T) {
  // I normally use AR(P) models for time-varying parameters, as you
  // can simulate (many of) them into the future without the process exploding
  // you can also include things like seasonality here by taking fourier transforms of time or whatnot
  mu[t] ~ normal(int + slope *mu[t-1], sigma);

}

// then your data-level model

for(n in 1:N) {
  // your individual latent parameters are centered around the latent parameters for each time
  x[n] ~ normal(mu[time[n]], some scale parameter with tight prior);
  // your data model
  y[n] ~ normal(x[n], scale);
}

}

That should probably work better.

Jim

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Feature suggestion: check for unused parameters
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Feature suggestion: check for unused parameters
messages.body_plain:
Just ran into a similar problem with unused transformed parameters. In the process of modifying a model I ended up with something like:

data {
  int n;
}
parameters {
  vector[n] x;
}
transformed parameters {
  vector[n] foo;
}
model {
  x ~ normal(0, 1);
}

Which samples, but returns an error only after sampling (which takes ~3 days in my case):

Error in validObject(.Object) :
  invalid class “stanfit” object: The following variables have undefined values:  foo[1],The following variables have undefined values:  foo[2],The following variables have undefined values:  foo[3],The following variables have undefined values:  foo[4],The following variables have undefined values:  foo[5]...

 Maybe this has already been proposed elsewhere, but it might be worth raising a warning or error when checking or compiling a model if a *transformed* parameter is declared but never assigned a value or used. I can't think of an instance when I would want to declare a transformed parameter but never assign value(s) to it, but I could be overlooking a case where this would be useful.

On Friday, May 27, 2016 at 12:03:47 PM UTC-6, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> It's surprisingly tricky to do this right with string search.
> There are quoted strings, substrings, operators and functions,
> comments, declaration and use scope, and identifier
> type.
>
> Having said that, it'd be really great to build something
> along the lines of Google's cpplint program, which we
> use ourselves.  It's a Python program that runs over
> C++ code looking for various kinds of coding problems.
> You can get pretty far with string matching and also
> detect other kinds of problems.
>
> - Bob
>
>
> > On May 27, 2016, at 11:51 AM, Mike Lawrence <mike....@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Let's say we have the following stan code:
> >
> >     data{
> >         int<lower=1> N ;
> >         vector[N] Y ;
> >     }
> >     parameters{
> >         real mu ;
> >         real sigma ;
> >     }
> >     model{
> >         Y ~ normal(mu,1)
> >     }
> >
> > The parameter sigma is never actually used. Maybe it was at some point during model development but then the user decided to hard-code the SD of the gaussian to 1 for some reason, but forgot to take out sigma. Presumably it should be relatively trivial to use simple string searches before compilation to check for variables that are initialized but then never appear in any sampling or transforms.
> >
> >
> > On Fri, May 27, 2016 at 11:47 AM, Krzysztof Sakrejda <krzysztof...@gmail.com> wrote:

messages.subject: Divergent transitions, relationships to other diagnostics and noncentered parameterizations
messages.subject_clean: Divergent transitions, relationships to other diagnostics and noncentered parameterizations
messages.body_plain:
Hi

I have a question on divergent transitions. I fit a complex nonlinear model, and get an eyewatering number of divergent transitions (3000 divergent transitions when I run three chains of 1500 warmup and 1500 sampling).

Despite this, the Rhat statistic is great (all parameters 1.02 or less), and the mcse / posterior sd are all around 0.03-0.05. The n_eff/n  aren't great though, hovering between 6% and 20% for all parameters, so there is some autocorrelation. My traceplots are little oscillatory, and occasionally sticky, but it doesn't appear to be major.

A posterior predictive check reveals no major problems. My data are very noisy, but as a sanity check, if I were to fit the parameters 'by eye' I would choose similar values to those outputted from the model.

Something tells me that despite this, something is wrong if there are this many divergent transitions. Should I be worried? I've tried to understand the complexities of HMC but I'm very much an applied researcher and not a great physicist, so I don't understand how these divergent transitions influence the samples.

I've read this great summary:
http://mc-stan.org/documentation/case-studies/divergences_and_bias.html
but it's difficult to test sensitivity to adapt_delta when the models take 5 hours to run each time, even with a small subset of the dataset. I've tried a couple of different values for the subset, but it's not really feasible to try all of this for the large dataset.

My next step is to try the 'non-centered parameterization', but I'm a little unclear exactly how to do the rescaling. Is there a good summary of that somewhere? I've attached my model, in case someone has time for specific tips. (please don't laugh at the likelihood, I know it's a tricky one)

Thanks everyone

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Feature suggestion: check for unused parameters
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Feature suggestion: check for unused parameters
messages.body_plain:
If you declare a transformed param and don't assign to it, it should
have a NaN value (which would violate any constraint, but be OK in
the unconstrained case).  Where does the problem arise?  Are you trying
to use it in generated quantities?

We could probably stand to check even the unconstrained values aren't
NaN.  It's hard to know what to do in some of these cases because we
don't want to mess with the underlying IEEE numerics more than we need
to and none of those crash when fed NaN---they just keep returning NaN.
But some of our functions from Boost and that we wrote themselves, will
throw exceptions.

We do suggest always running a few real iterations before setting things
off for days.

- Bob
