>
> My mistake was that there was no possibility of assignment anywhere (not even in a conditional statement) - just a declaration at the beginning of the transformed parameter block. This seems like it may be a separate (mis)use case.
>
>
>
> On Wednesday, March 22, 2017 at 10:16:28 AM UTC-6, Jonah Gabry wrote:
> On Wednesday, March 22, 2017 at 10:56:59 AM UTC-4, Maxwell Joseph wrote:
>  I can't think of an instance when I would want to declare a transformed parameter but never assign value(s) to it, but I could be overlooking a case where this would be useful.
>
> It can be useful when there's the possibility of a zero-length transformed parameter. For example,
>
> data {
>  ...
>  int<lower=0,upper=1> flag;
> }

> transformed parameters {

>   if (flag) {
>     // do something with x only if flag==1
>   }

messages.body_plain:
On Wednesday, March 22, 2017 at 11:45:38 PM UTC-4, Olivier Ma wrote:
> But the prediction is nothing like the observed values. I have 7 different classes, and here are the observed values:
>
> > table(d$response)
>    1    2    3    4    5    6    7
> 1274  909 1071 2323 1462 1445 1446
>
> And the predicted values are all in a much smaller range:
>
> > range((m113_sample$y_p))
> [1] 2.673227 4.953754
>
> What am I doing wrong here?

Not drawing from the posterior predictive distribution. You don't want to compare d$response to some real number than only reflects uncertainty in the coefficients and cutpoints; you want to compare d$response to what distribution the model implies d$response should be. So, rather than storing those probabilities in the generated quantities block, you want to store draws from a categorical distribution that is evaluated at those posterior probabilities. Then --- assuming your model is reasonable --- you have an apples-to-apples comparison with d$response.

Ben

On Thursday, March 23, 2017 at 12:08:14 PM UTC-4, Tobias Konitzer wrote:
> 1) I am running a simple logit regression (not displayed), and am trying to generate a linear predictor for a new data.frame with 3,091,493 rows in the generated quantities block. The model runs fine, but crashes upon generated quantities. Am I misusing the purpose of the block? i.e.

It looks OK at first glance. What is the error message? Your model block should change the likelihood from

  gender ~ bernoulli(inv_logit(eta));

to

  gender ~ bernoulli_logit(eta);

for numerical stability.

> 2) I am trying to run a very large logistic regression model with some random effects, and two very large matrices of linear predictors drawn from N~(0, var), with 13,024 predictors each (model attached). I can get the model to run, but barely (for example, init='random' fails due to memory). Is such a problem too big for stan, or does it make sense to go down routes of sparse matrix representations, which I know are possible now with stan?

The stan_glmer() function in the stanarm package represents such models in the same way that lme4 does, i.e.

eta = X * beta + Z * b

where the Z matrix is sparse and the X matrix is dense by default. There is a sparse = TRUE option to encode X as sparse, but sparse matrix multiplication by a vector in Stan is very slow (it is really only good for the case where RAM binds before patience). Moreover, it is usually better to specify QR = TRUE to reparameterize the model as

eta = Q * R * beta + Z * b = Q * theta + Z * b

where theta = R * beta and stan_glmer() automatically recovers the posterior distribution of beta by pre-multiplying each draw of theta by R^{-1}. However, in that case Q is dense even if X has a lot of zeros.

If you need the posterior predictive distribution or the posterior distribution of eta, you can obtain that using posterior_predict() or posterior_linpred() (possibly with transform = TRUE to get the posterior distribution mu) so you don't have to generate such things in the generated quantities block.

Ben

Ben

> > 1) I am running a simple logit regression (not displayed), and am trying to generate a linear predictor for a new data.frame with 3,091,493 rows in the generated quantities block. The model runs fine, but crashes upon generated quantities. Am I misusing the purpose of the block? i.e.
>
> It looks OK at first glance. What is the error message? Your model block should change the likelihood from
>
>   gender ~ bernoulli(inv_logit(eta));
>
> to
>
>   gender ~ bernoulli_logit(eta);
>
> for numerical stability.
>
> > 2) I am trying to run a very large logistic regression model with some random effects, and two very large matrices of linear predictors drawn from N~(0, var), with 13,024 predictors each (model attached). I can get the model to run, but barely (for example, init='random' fails due to memory). Is such a problem too big for stan, or does it make sense to go down routes of sparse matrix representations, which I know are possible now with stan?
>
> The stan_glmer() function in the stanarm package represents such models in the same way that lme4 does, i.e.
>
> eta = X * beta + Z * b
>
> where the Z matrix is sparse and the X matrix is dense by default. There is a sparse = TRUE option to encode X as sparse, but sparse matrix multiplication by a vector in Stan is very slow (it is really only good for the case where RAM binds before patience). Moreover, it is usually better to specify QR = TRUE to reparameterize the model as
>
> eta = Q * R * beta + Z * b = Q * theta + Z * b
>
> where theta = R * beta and stan_glmer() automatically recovers the posterior distribution of beta by pre-multiplying each draw of theta by R^{-1}. However, in that case Q is dense even if X has a lot of zeros.
>
> If you need the posterior predictive distribution or the posterior distribution of eta, you can obtain that using posterior_predict() or posterior_linpred() (possibly with transform = TRUE to get the posterior distribution mu) so you don't have to generate such things in the generated quantities block.
>
> Ben

messages.body_plain:
append_col(a, append_col(b, c))

will append three vectors (or matrices) by column.

The next version of Stan (2.15) will let you construct
vector and matrix literals.  It'll look like:

  real a;
  row_vector[3] x = [ 1, 2, a ];
  vector[3] xt = [ 1, 2, a ]';  // note transpose
  matrix[3, 3] = [ [ 1, 2, 3],
                   [4, 5, 6],
                   [7, 8, 9] ];

Arrays use { 1, 2, 3 } instead of [1, 2, 3].

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] weighted regression
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] weighted regression
messages.body_plain:
Instead of, say

  y ~ normal(x * beta, sigma);

in a regression, you want to first unfold

  for (n in 1:N)
    y[n] ~ normal(x[n] * beta, sigma);

then switch to incrementing

  for (n in 1:N)
    target += normal_lpdf(y[n] | x[n] * beta, sigma);

and then you can weight

  for (n in 1:N)
    target += w[n] * normal_lpdf(y[n] | x[n] * beta, sigma);

It's as if you had w[n] count rather than a count of 1 for
that item.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
gamma_p is not the pgamma function from R.  For that, you need
gamma_cdf.  gamma_p is the incomplete gamma function, which you
don't want to be using here.

We don't recommend those truncated priors on the parameters (lower
and upper bounded) unless those are physical requirements of
the model.  Softer proper priors work better both statistically
(don't introduce bias due to truncation point) and computationally (don't
get jammed up against a boundary and try to head off to +/-
infinity on the unconstrained scale on which Stan samples).

Try fitting the model with data simulated from the model before
trying it on real data---real data for which the model's badly
misspecified can also cause big problems.

- Bob

messages.subject: Help fitting a simple Bayesian Generalized Method of Moments (GMM) model
messages.subject_clean: Help fitting a simple Bayesian Generalized Method of Moments (GMM) model
messages.body_plain:
For those not familiar with bayesian generalized method of moments (GMM), the basic idea is really simple:
1) construct estimating equations u for parameters of interest theta
> we are interested in solving u=0 to obtain estimates of theta
2)  then the sample mean U = 1/N * sum(u_1,....,u_N) will be asymptotically normal with mean 0 and covariance which is consistently estimated by Sigma_hat (formula is given in Yin's paper).
3) Apply a normal likelihood function to U (with mean 0 and covariance Sigma_hat) and flat priors for theta, then use MCMC to estimate the posterior distribution for all parameters of interest

 <http://projecteuclid.org/download/pdf_1/euclid.ba/1340370272>
Yin's 2009 paper <http://projecteuclid.org/download/pdf_1/euclid.ba/1340370272> proposed the Bayesian GMM which I am trying to fit in STAN.  Essentially the model I'm trying to fit is a Bayesian anlog to the frequentist GEE model using an indepdence working correlation structure.  I simulated some simple data which consists of N 2-person families, thus we do not have independent subjects since the response (Y) will be correlated within each family.  However, GMM can be used to conduct valid inference on the mean parameters despite the fact that our working independent correlation structure is wrong.

I attached some simple simulated data and my current .stan file.  Lastly, here is my R code to fit the model in Rstan:
library(rstan)
load("GEE1data1.RData")
data=list(Y=simdata$Y,X1=simdata$X1,N=length(table(simdata$famID)),N2=100.0)
fit = stan(file = "stan_GEE1_ind.stan",data = data, cores = 1, chains = 1, iter = 10)

However the model fails to fit.  Specifically, it appears the main problem is with the final line in my .stan file where i attempt to define the multivariate normal likelihood from step (3):
target += -0.5*U'*inverse(Sigma)*U;

 Any help getting this model to fit would be greatly appreciated!! I will note that I was unable to get this model to fit in JAGS, and I'm now trying to decide if it's possible to fit bayesian GMM models in STAN.

Thanks

Thank you very much Bob for the advise about prior selection!

Your direction solves the problem! But I still have few concerns:

But first of all, I am not sure why you say my priors are improper. According to Stan-reference 2.14.0, page 124, section "Proper Uniform Priors: Interval Constraints", I have both upper and lower limits specified on the parameters, which, I guess, should gives me proper uniform priors. Of course, you are the one who knows what is really going on there. I only want to present you my confusion.

Secondly, the problem I was reporting is that I can not use gamma_cdf() or gamma_p() as a regular math function. If I replace the gamma_p with gamma_cdf, with parameters changed accordingly, the same problem remains. But if I replace it with normal_cdf, things work fine.

Anyway, following your suggestions, I removed the boundaries on parameter k and theta, and replaced them with specified gamma priors. Then the calculation returns to its normal speed, and sampling no longer gets stuck. My problem solved!
parameters {
  real k;
  real theta;

}
transformed parameters {
  real<lower=0,upper=1> prob[N];

  for (j in 1:N) prob[j] = gamma_cdf(D[j], k, 1/theta);
}
model {
  k ~ gamma(2, 0.1);
  theta ~ gamma(2, 0.1);
  ntcp ~ bernoulli(prob);
}

But I get exceptions below from running the model. How could I get negative parameters, given my priors are gamma distributions with positive support?

Exception thrown at line 13: gamma_cdf: Scale parameter is -0.100042, but must be > 0!                   1
Exception thrown at line 13: gamma_cdf: Scale parameter is -0.107527, but must be > 0!                   1

   real<lower=0> k;
   real<lower=0> theta;

Btw, the parameterization of gamma_cdf in the user reference is gamma_cdf(reals y, reals alpha, reals beta), using beta(rate parameter) instead of theta (scale parameter). While in the exception message, Scale parameter is reported.

Thanks again! I would appreciate to learn your thoughts if you have the time.

John

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Explicitly Correlated Parameters
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Explicitly Correlated Parameters
messages.body_plain:
Some good points. I wanted to take some time to digest. A few comments:

"To see this for yourself, we recommend simulating data from a model
that looks like what you want"

The simulations I have used in the past often simulate the parameters as effectively multivariate normal. There are relatively fewer problems with the model in these cases because the model assumes multivariate normal and that's how the parameters are distributed when simulated. I get more problems when I switch to the actual data set and the parameters are no longer multivariate normal.

"For arithmetic stability, we recommend using Cholesky factors
of correlation matrices with LKJ priors and then scaling (a
less ad hoc version of what Gelman and Hill recommend in
their regression book."

I read and re-read the Stan documentation more regularly than I should admit...I followed a lot of the best practices, like LKJ priors.

"And yes, correlations near -1 or 1 are going to be problematic
no matter what sampler you use.  This is largely a fact of the
way floating point arithmetic works.  You can represent numbers
like 1e-300 --- in other words, get very close to zero, but the
closest you can get to 1 or -1 in floating point is around 1 - 1e-15.
If there's nothing stopping you from wanting to get closer, you're
going to get divergences because you just can't even represent a number
that's closer to 1 or -1 without rounding error to 1 or -1, which in
turns makes the covariance matrix singular."

I've been fitting the model with OLS and no pooling and comparing it to the results to Stan's output. So for instance, I can plot the distribution of intercepts vs. slopes in OLS and compare that to what the mean intercepts and slopes are from Stan. The correlation of the intercepts to the slopes from the OLS output is probably closer to -0.6. So it's modest, but it's not that extreme. I think the issue more is that Stan will move towards that +1 or -1 and then get stuck there. Also, the Stan plots looks much more like a multivariate normal than the OLS plots do. I suspect this is because of the divergences.

"But this is just what Andrew calls the "folk theorem".  If your
inferences want a correlation near 1 or -1, you have two linearly
redundant parameters in your regression and you probably just want
to get rid of one.  Otherwise, they're only going to be identified
by the prior (see the manual section on problematic priors for a simple
example using two intercepts, which is just an extreme case of
the same problem)."

I've made that mistake of effectively putting in two intercepts before...One thing that would make life a little easier is if divergences can be printed at the end of each chain or perhaps an option to exit early if there is a divergence (for instance, equivalent to a field that indicates success or failure in an optimization). Beyond that, I don't know if it would be possible for someone to write a program that parses a Stan model and it warns you if there are problems, at least for simple things like identification.

Anyway, this part of your post caused me to go back and run a few more models. After double-checking, the divergences problem was showing up with explicitly multivariate normal intercepts/slopes, regardless of whether I used a constant standard deviation or varying standard deviations by group. However, I also realized that under some conditions, I would also get divergences when I did the model with varying intercepts, slopes, and standard deviations (which I don't think I had realized before double-checking). I could avoid these with some simple changes, like having 2 of 3 vary or changing the priors (for my data, varying standard deviations was more important than varying intercepts).

There are two separate points I want to address with respect to the model being wrong:

1) The multivariate case. The idea that the model is wrong makes some sense since the empirical distribution of the OLS parameters I discussed above aren't REALLY multivariate normal. So there may be computational problems because I'm forcing a distribution to be multivariate normal, when it is really more complicated than that. In my case, I had wanted the intercepts and slopes to vary by individual. I knew from looking at the OLS results that individuals with high slopes tended to have low intercepts, so I assumed it was important to explicitly model the correlation with a multivariate normal. But I almost always had worse results when I did that. That's what I find intuitive. The model isn't wrong with separate univariate normal priors, but it becomes wrong with a multivariate normal one.

2) Varying intercepts/slopes/standard deviations. Stan can fit a univariate model with an intercept, slope, and standard deviation. And it can fit a no pooling version of that with many separate individuals each having their own intercepts, slopes, and standard deviations. But give all those parameters hierarchical priors and you get divergences. I don't find this intuitive. Why has the model become wrong?

On Tue, Mar 21, 2017 at 4:25 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> It's not so much a Stan problem as a general problem.
> There's no way to tweak multivariate proposals in Gibbs unless
> you block them, and they tend not to work in Metropolis unless
> you know the curvature (second derivative matrix) explicitly and
> it doesn't vary around the posterior.  What you may be finding
> is just that Stan's much better at exploring out the boundaries of
> parameter space and reporting when it gets into trouble.
>
> To see this for yourself, we recommend simulating data from a model
> that looks like what you want and trying to fit in various systems
> and look at the boundaries on 80% or 90% intervals you're getting
> (95% or higher will be too noisy without a high effective sample size).
> But you need to use Stan's posterior summary tools, which are also
> more conservative than Coda or other tools often applied to BUGS
> or JAGS models.
>
> It's not the correlation that causes so much of a problem as
> when the curvature (second derivative matrix aka Hessian) varies
> around the posterior, as in the funnel example.
>
> For arithmetic stability, we recommend using Cholesky factors
> of correlation matrices with LKJ priors and then scaling (a
> less ad hoc version of what Gelman and Hill recommend in
> their regression book.

>
> And yes, correlations near -1 or 1 are going to be problematic
> no matter what sampler you use.  This is largely a fact of the
> way floating point arithmetic works.  You can represent numbers
> like 1e-300 --- in other words, get very close to zero, but the
> closest you can get to 1 or -1 in floating point is around 1 - 1e-15.
> If there's nothing stopping you from wanting to get closer, you're
> going to get divergences because you just can't even represent a number
> that's closer to 1 or -1 without rounding error to 1 or -1, which in
> turns makes the covariance matrix singular.
>
> But this is just what Andrew calls the "folk theorem".  If your
> inferences want a correlation near 1 or -1, you have two linearly
> redundant parameters in your regression and you probably just want
> to get rid of one.  Otherwise, they're only going to be identified
> by the prior (see the manual section on problematic priors for a simple
> example using two intercepts, which is just an extreme case of
> the same problem).
>
> - Bob
>
>
> > On Mar 21, 2017, at 3:58 PM, John Hall <john.mic...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > There are already a few threads on the subject, but I'm not interested in a particular model. Rather, I'm just observing that models with explicitly correlated parameters are a bit quirky in Stan. I'm curious if people out there have a lot of success with explicitly correlated parameters versus the implicit case. I'm also curious about best practices on when to use them and when to not use. My thoughts are below.
> >
> > By explicitly correlated parameters, I mean a model that contains something like what is in Section 26.6 of the documentation under Multivariate Reparameterizations, rather than the previous section that handles the univariate case.
> >
> > With Gibbs sampling and Metropolis-Hastings, you have to include a multivariate distribution or the posterior distribution would be almost forced to have uncorrelated parameters. I believe the situation was similar with BUGS/JAGS. I suspect the focus in those techniques is why there is a decent amount of focus in the Stan documentation on models with correlated parameters.
> >
> > In Stan, my experience with correlated parameters in Stan has been rather frustrating. I almost always get worse results (in terms of having divergences, low N_eff, time to estimate, etc.) compared to univariate models. With a univariate prior on sets of parameters, the resulting posterior distribution on parameters might have some correlation when you look at them together, or maybe they won't. The only downside is that if you have some new observation, then you might need to make some assumptions in order to make predictions about it.
> >
> > I suspect that this is driven by the restrictions imposed by the multivariate normal prior. For instance, one model I'm estimating is a linear regression on some panel data, each regressed on one common time series variable with parameters varying cross-sectionally on the intercepts, slopes, and std. deviations (hierarchical priors on each of these three). If you leave the priors on the varying parameters univariate, it fits pretty well, pretty quickly, all things considered. By contrast, if you explicitly impose any kind of correlated parameters (centered or non-centered on the slopes and intercepts), then you get divergences or low N_eff and it takes forever way longer.
> >
> > To understand why this is, I focused on the posterior distribution of the parameters in the univariate case. Upon inspection, the slope looks a more log-normal than normal and the relationship of the intercept and the slope (or the slope and the standard deviations) looks non-linear. Thus, I suspect that imposing the linear correlation in the multivariate normal prevents the Stan sampler from finding the non-linear result.
> >
> > Another potential explanation is sort of brought up in the wiki section on priors
> > https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Prior-Choice-Recommendations
> > under "Boundary-avoiding priors for modal estimation". I'm not sure it entirely applies, but it discusses the varying slope and intercept model and discusses the potential for a correlation of 1. Well, my example above often had a correlation near -1 between the intercepts and slopes. But, I'm not sure if this is a product of the divergences though.

messages.body_plain:
Let me just add to this discussion that there's nothing wrong at all about identifying parameters with the prior!  Suppose you have a regression with two collinear predictors and you have some prior information on the coefficients.  Then include the prior information!  No need to throw predictors out of the model just because of some scruple that prior info is cheating.
A

> On Mar 23, 2017, at 6:27 PM, John Hall <john.mic...@gmail.com> wrote:
>

> Some good points. I wanted to take some time to digest. A few comments:
>
> "To see this for yourself, we recommend simulating data from a model
> that looks like what you want"
>
> The simulations I have used in the past often simulate the parameters as effectively multivariate normal. There are relatively fewer problems with the model in these cases because the model assumes multivariate normal and that's how the parameters are distributed when simulated. I get more problems when I switch to the actual data set and the parameters are no longer multivariate normal.
>
> "For arithmetic stability, we recommend using Cholesky factors
> of correlation matrices with LKJ priors and then scaling (a
> less ad hoc version of what Gelman and Hill recommend in
> their regression book."
>
> I read and re-read the Stan documentation more regularly than I should admit...I followed a lot of the best practices, like LKJ priors.
>
> "And yes, correlations near -1 or 1 are going to be problematic
> no matter what sampler you use.  This is largely a fact of the
> way floating point arithmetic works.  You can represent numbers
> like 1e-300 --- in other words, get very close to zero, but the
> closest you can get to 1 or -1 in floating point is around 1 - 1e-15.
> If there's nothing stopping you from wanting to get closer, you're
> going to get divergences because you just can't even represent a number
> that's closer to 1 or -1 without rounding error to 1 or -1, which in
> turns makes the covariance matrix singular."
>
> I've been fitting the model with OLS and no pooling and comparing it to the results to Stan's output. So for instance, I can plot the distribution of intercepts vs. slopes in OLS and compare that to what the mean intercepts and slopes are from Stan. The correlation of the intercepts to the slopes from the OLS output is probably closer to -0.6. So it's modest, but it's not that extreme. I think the issue more is that Stan will move towards that +1 or -1 and then get stuck there. Also, the Stan plots looks much more like a multivariate normal than the OLS plots do. I suspect this is because of the divergences.
>
> "But this is just what Andrew calls the "folk theorem".  If your
> inferences want a correlation near 1 or -1, you have two linearly
> redundant parameters in your regression and you probably just want
> to get rid of one.  Otherwise, they're only going to be identified
> by the prior (see the manual section on problematic priors for a simple
> example using two intercepts, which is just an extreme case of
> the same problem)."
>
> I've made that mistake of effectively putting in two intercepts before...One thing that would make life a little easier is if divergences can be printed at the end of each chain or perhaps an option to exit early if there is a divergence (for instance, equivalent to a field that indicates success or failure in an optimization). Beyond that, I don't know if it would be possible for someone to write a program that parses a Stan model and it warns you if there are problems, at least for simple things like identification.
>
> Anyway, this part of your post caused me to go back and run a few more models. After double-checking, the divergences problem was showing up with explicitly multivariate normal intercepts/slopes, regardless of whether I used a constant standard deviation or varying standard deviations by group. However, I also realized that under some conditions, I would also get divergences when I did the model with varying intercepts, slopes, and standard deviations (which I don't think I had realized before double-checking). I could avoid these with some simple changes, like having 2 of 3 vary or changing the priors (for my data, varying standard deviations was more important than varying intercepts).
>
> There are two separate points I want to address with respect to the model being wrong:
>
> 1) The multivariate case. The idea that the model is wrong makes some sense since the empirical distribution of the OLS parameters I discussed above aren't REALLY multivariate normal. So there may be computational problems because I'm forcing a distribution to be multivariate normal, when it is really more complicated than that. In my case, I had wanted the intercepts and slopes to vary by individual. I knew from looking at the OLS results that individuals with high slopes tended to have low intercepts, so I assumed it was important to explicitly model the correlation with a multivariate normal. But I almost always had worse results when I did that. That's what I find intuitive. The model isn't wrong with separate univariate normal priors, but it becomes wrong with a multivariate normal one.
>
> 2) Varying intercepts/slopes/standard deviations. Stan can fit a univariate model with an intercept, slope, and standard deviation. And it can fit a no pooling version of that with many separate individuals each having their own intercepts, slopes, and standard deviations. But give all those parameters hierarchical priors and you get divergences. I don't find this intuitive. Why has the model become wrong?
>
>
>
> On Tue, Mar 21, 2017 at 4:25 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> > It's not so much a Stan problem as a general problem.
> > There's no way to tweak multivariate proposals in Gibbs unless
> > you block them, and they tend not to work in Metropolis unless
> > you know the curvature (second derivative matrix) explicitly and
> > it doesn't vary around the posterior.  What you may be finding
> > is just that Stan's much better at exploring out the boundaries of
> > parameter space and reporting when it gets into trouble.
> >
> > To see this for yourself, we recommend simulating data from a model
> > that looks like what you want and trying to fit in various systems
> > and look at the boundaries on 80% or 90% intervals you're getting
> > (95% or higher will be too noisy without a high effective sample size).
> > But you need to use Stan's posterior summary tools, which are also
> > more conservative than Coda or other tools often applied to BUGS
> > or JAGS models.
> >
> > It's not the correlation that causes so much of a problem as
> > when the curvature (second derivative matrix aka Hessian) varies
> > around the posterior, as in the funnel example.
> >
> > For arithmetic stability, we recommend using Cholesky factors
> > of correlation matrices with LKJ priors and then scaling (a
> > less ad hoc version of what Gelman and Hill recommend in
> > their regression book.
> >
> > And yes, correlations near -1 or 1 are going to be problematic
> > no matter what sampler you use.  This is largely a fact of the
> > way floating point arithmetic works.  You can represent numbers
> > like 1e-300 --- in other words, get very close to zero, but the
> > closest you can get to 1 or -1 in floating point is around 1 - 1e-15.

> >
> > But this is just what Andrew calls the "folk theorem".  If your
> > inferences want a correlation near 1 or -1, you have two linearly
> > redundant parameters in your regression and you probably just want
> > to get rid of one.  Otherwise, they're only going to be identified
> > by the prior (see the manual section on problematic priors for a simple
> > example using two intercepts, which is just an extreme case of
> > the same problem).
> >
> > - Bob
> >
> >
> > > On Mar 21, 2017, at 3:58 PM, John Hall <john.mic...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > There are already a few threads on the subject, but I'm not interested in a particular model. Rather, I'm just observing that models with explicitly correlated parameters are a bit quirky in Stan. I'm curious if people out there have a lot of success with explicitly correlated parameters versus the implicit case. I'm also curious about best practices on when to use them and when to not use. My thoughts are below.
> > >
> > > By explicitly correlated parameters, I mean a model that contains something like what is in Section 26.6 of the documentation under Multivariate Reparameterizations, rather than the previous section that handles the univariate case.
> > >
> > > With Gibbs sampling and Metropolis-Hastings, you have to include a multivariate distribution or the posterior distribution would be almost forced to have uncorrelated parameters. I believe the situation was similar with BUGS/JAGS. I suspect the focus in those techniques is why there is a decent amount of focus in the Stan documentation on models with correlated parameters.
> > >
> > > In Stan, my experience with correlated parameters in Stan has been rather frustrating. I almost always get worse results (in terms of having divergences, low N_eff, time to estimate, etc.) compared to univariate models. With a univariate prior on sets of parameters, the resulting posterior distribution on parameters might have some correlation when you look at them together, or maybe they won't. The only downside is that if you have some new observation, then you might need to make some assumptions in order to make predictions about it.
> > >
> > > I suspect that this is driven by the restrictions imposed by the multivariate normal prior. For instance, one model I'm estimating is a linear regression on some panel data, each regressed on one common time series variable with parameters varying cross-sectionally on the intercepts, slopes, and std. deviations (hierarchical priors on each of these three). If you leave the priors on the varying parameters univariate, it fits pretty well, pretty quickly, all things considered. By contrast, if you explicitly impose any kind of correlated parameters (centered or non-centered on the slopes and intercepts), then you get divergences or low N_eff and it takes forever way longer.
> > >
> > > To understand why this is, I focused on the posterior distribution of the parameters in the univariate case. Upon inspection, the slope looks a more log-normal than normal and the relationship of the intercept and the slope (or the slope and the standard deviations) looks non-linear. Thus, I suspect that imposing the linear correlation in the multivariate normal prevents the Stan sampler from finding the non-linear result.
> > >
> > > Another potential explanation is sort of brought up in the wiki section on priors
> > > https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Prior-Choice-Recommendations
> > > under "Boundary-avoiding priors for modal estimation". I'm not sure it entirely applies, but it discusses the varying slope and intercept model and discusses the potential for a correlation of 1. Well, my example above often had a correlation near -1 between the intercepts and slopes. But, I'm not sure if this is a product of the divergences though.

I tried the code below yesterday. My data was 120X565 originally, so to get it to work with stan_glmer it becomes like 70,000X3. At least when I write it myself in Stan I have some idea what's going on and I can exploit some knowledge of the data set to speed things up.

fit_mkt_rstanarm <- stan_glmer(y ~ (1 + x | stock), data = rstanarm_data_mkt,
                               family = gaussian(link = "identity"),
                               prior=hs(df=7),
                               prior_intercept=normal(0, 1),

messages.body_plain:
You want the data to inform you about the corrs, but if the predictors are roughly zero-centered, then maybe you don't expect corrs to be fully degenerate.  In a model with one correlation, you can put a Beta(2,2) prior on (rho + 1)/2.  In a model with multiple correlations, you can use a Wishart (not inverse-Wishart) priors, as discussed here:
http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/chung_cov_matrices.pdf
A

messages.body_plain:
Glad it finally fit for you, but there are problems with this
from a Stan perspective.  First, you could use some indentation and
spacing around operators so that it's more readable.

These two:

  real<lower=0> phi; //variance
...
  phi~uniform(0,100000);

are not compatible.  You really should be declaring

  real<lower=0, upper=1000000> phi;

because Stan requires every variable meeting the constraints
to have a finite log density (2000000 meets your constraint
but has 0 log density because of the bounds on the uniform).

But then you'll get initializations around 500,000 because
you've said the values are equally likely to be anywhere
between 0 and 1M.  Is that what you intended?  If not,
we recommend actually using priors that do express what
you know ahead of time about phi.

You can also just get rid of the uniform(...) and use
an improper prior.  Then you initialize around 1 because
that's the center of the exp() transform to get values
to be positive.

For efficiency, don't duplicate calculations:

    sk[1]=(Y[2*i-1]-yhat[1])^2;
    sk[2]=(Y[2*i]-yhat[2])^2;
    Fk[1]=Y[2*i-1]-yhat[1];
    Fk[2]=Y[2*i]-yhat[2];

Instead, you can vectorize the definition of sk as

 Fk[1] = Y[2*i-1] - yhat[1];
 Fk[2] = Y[2*i] - yhat[2];
 sk[1] = square(Fk[1])
 sk[2] = square(Fk[2]);

or

 Fk[1:2] = Y[(2 * i - 1):(2 * i)] - yhat[1:2];
 sk[1:2] = square(Fk[1:2]);

Also later,

  V[4, 4] = V[3, 3];

You never want to compute inverses, so instead of

    u= D'*inverse(V)*Fk;

it's much more stable to write

  D' / V * Fk;

where  D' / V  =def=  D' * inverse(V).   Same with later calc.

We have a quad form, but you're inverting, so you can't use that.
We should probably have an inverse quad form, and also a more
general multiply_self_transpose---as is, we don't have the inverse
quad form and only have multiply_self_transpose for triangular
matrices.

- Bob

> On Mar 23, 2017, at 5:17 PM, Jaron <arbe...@umn.edu> wrote:
>
> For those not familiar with bayesian generalized method of moments (GMM), the basic idea is really simple:
> 1) construct estimating equations u for parameters of interest theta
> we are interested in solving u=0 to obtain estimates of theta
> 2)  then the sample mean U = 1/N * sum(u_1,....,u_N) will be asymptotically normal with mean 0 and covariance which is consistently estimated by Sigma_hat (formula is given in Yin's paper).
> 3) Apply a normal likelihood function to U (with mean 0 and covariance Sigma_hat) and flat priors for theta, then use MCMC to estimate the posterior distribution for all parameters of interest
>
> Yin's 2009 paper proposed the Bayesian GMM which I am trying to fit in STAN.  Essentially the model I'm trying to fit is a Bayesian anlog to the frequentist GEE model using an indepdence working correlation structure.  I simulated some simple data which consists of N 2-person families, thus we do not have independent subjects since the response (Y) will be correlated within each family.  However, GMM can be used to conduct valid inference on the mean parameters despite the fact that our working independent correlation structure is wrong.
>
> I attached some simple simulated data and my current .stan file.  Lastly, here is my R code to fit the model in Rstan:
> library(rstan)
> load("GEE1data1.RData")
> data=list(Y=simdata$Y,X1=simdata$X1,N=length(table(simdata$famID)),N2=100.0)
> fit = stan(file = "stan_GEE1_ind.stan",data = data, cores = 1, chains = 1, iter = 10)
>
> However the model fails to fit.  Specifically, it appears the main problem is with the final line in my .stan file where i attempt to define the multivariate normal likelihood from step (3):
> target += -0.5*U'*inverse(Sigma)*U;

You really don't want to implement this this way.
You can do U' / Sigma * U, and it should be more stable.

>
>  Any help getting this model to fit would be greatly appreciated!! I will note that I was unable to get this model to fit in JAGS, and I'm now trying to decide if it's possible to fit bayesian GMM models in STAN.
>
> Thanks
>

messages.body_plain:
> On Mar 23, 2017, at 5:58 PM, John Yao <yuanyao...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Thank you very much Bob for the advise about prior selection!
>
> Your direction solves the problem! But I still have few concerns:
>
> But first of all, I am not sure why you say my priors are improper. According to Stan-reference 2.14.0, page 124, section "Proper Uniform Priors: Interval Constraints", I have both upper and lower limits specified on the parameters, which, I guess, should gives me proper uniform priors. Of course, you are the one who knows what is really going on there. I only want to present you my confusion.

You're right.  Sorry about that.  If you have upper and lower bounds
on parameters, it's just uniform over the bounds (all our parameters
are implicitly uniform over the values that satisfy their constraints).

> Secondly, the problem I was reporting is that I can not use gamma_cdf() or gamma_p() as a regular math function. If I replace the gamma_p with gamma_cdf, with parameters changed accordingly, the same problem remains. But if I replace it with normal_cdf, things work fine.

We're working on some of the CDFs to try to make them more
stable, but we're not there yet.

>
> Anyway, following your suggestions, I removed the boundaries on parameter k and theta, and replaced them with specified gamma priors. Then the calculation returns to its normal speed, and sampling no longer gets stuck. My problem solved!
> parameters {
>   real k;
>   real theta;
> }
> transformed parameters {
>   real<lower=0,upper=1> prob[N];
>   for (j in 1:N) prob[j] = gamma_cdf(D[j], k, 1/theta);
> }
> model {
>   k ~ gamma(2, 0.1);
>   theta ~ gamma(2, 0.1);
>   ntcp ~ bernoulli(prob);
> }
>
> But I get exceptions below from running the model. How could I get negative parameters, given my priors are gamma distributions with positive support?
>
> Exception thrown at line 13: gamma_cdf: Scale parameter is -0.100042, but must be > 0!                   1
> Exception thrown at line 13: gamma_cdf: Scale parameter is -0.107527, but must be > 0!                   1
>
> So, I have to put back half of the constraint on parameters k and theta like below, then no exception any more.
>    real<lower=0> k;
>    real<lower=0> theta;
>

messages.subject: Re: Fitting coupled ODE a'la Kuramoto model
messages.subject_clean: Fitting coupled ODE a'la Kuramoto model
messages.body_plain:
Oha... if you mean you want to put S=100 ODE equations into Stan, then this is the largest I have ever seen. Note that Stan must calculate the sensitivities of the ODEs. That means it calculates for all S states the derivatives wrt to all parameters. You end up with having to solve S * (1 + P) ODE equations if P is the total number of parameters and here I assume that your initial condition is known.

If this works then this would be so cool, but it will be hard and as a start you maybe should not start with full Bayes but rather optimization or ADVI.

Your problem would indeed benefit from putting it onto a GPU which is doable. Assuming you can live with the non-stiff solver which uses odeint, then it should be doable with reasonable effort to put this on a GPU. Boosts odeint has bindings to various GPU frameworks which should make it doable.

Sebastian

PS: I do not know these problems, but a FFT is in the works and maybe this helps you to reformulate the problem?

On Friday, March 24, 2017 at 10:02:25 AM UTC-4, Ru Wang wrote:
> I am a very new beginner for rstan, I referred to help(stan) today, and am confused about algorithm = c("NUTS", "HMC", "Fixed_param"). I know that stan uses Hamiltonian Monte Carlo sampling, so the basic algorithm in rstan should also be HMC. Then what does algorithm = c("NUTS", "HMC", "Fixed_param") mean? And I rstan, the default is NUTS, does this mean that if i want to use HMC to sampling, I need to add algorithm = c("HMC") in my stan() code? Thank you a lot.

You don't want to use (static) HMC; you want to use NUTS (which is the default) because the number of leapfrog steps it takes on each iteration is not fixed. By leapfrogging until it reaches the u-turn point, you get better exploration and less dependence between draws.

Ben

Notationally, "NUTS" refers to the No-U-Turn sampler which is an extremely efficient implementation of Hamiltonian Monte Carlo and the best option for almost every application, hence it being a default.

The "HMC" algorithm in RStan refers to static HMC, sometimes called vanilla HMC, which is the original but less efficient implementation of the Hamiltonian Monte Carlo method.  Sorry for the confusing notation -- we'll be sure to change it when we evolve the interfaces.

Hi Bob,

Thanks for the STAN coding advice.  Here are my comments:
I simply want a flat non-informative prior for phi and I know STAN applies flat priors by default so I will remove the "uniform(0,100000);" prior specification since it is unnecessary and incorrect as you mentioned
I will try to vectorize my code more.  As you probably noticed, I am filling in the elements of a vector or matrix one element at a time which is tedious... I look forward to the future STAN 2.15 update you mentioned (in my other thread) that will allow me to easily fill in the elements of matrices and vectors.
Not sure what you mean by "Also later,  V[4, 4] = V[3, 3];".... I think you may be confused about V and Sigma.  V is a 4x4 matrix used in the construction of the estimating equation u , and u is a 3x1 vector.  Sigma is the 3x3 estimated covariance matrix of u.
Instead of using the inverse() function to calculate the inverse of a matrix, I will use the division operator "/" instead as you mentioned

Thanks again

On Thursday, March 23, 2017 at 8:22:20 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Glad it finally fit for you, but there are problems with this
> from a Stan perspective.  First, you could use some indentation and
> spacing around operators so that it's more readable.
>
> These two:
>
>   real<lower=0> phi; //variance
> ...
>   phi~uniform(0,100000);
>
> are not compatible.  You really should be declaring
>
>   real<lower=0, upper=1000000> phi;
>
> because Stan requires every variable meeting the constraints
> to have a finite log density (2000000 meets your constraint
> but has 0 log density because of the bounds on the uniform).
>
> But then you'll get initializations around 500,000 because
> you've said the values are equally likely to be anywhere
> between 0 and 1M.  Is that what you intended?  If not,
> we recommend actually using priors that do express what
> you know ahead of time about phi.
>
> You can also just get rid of the uniform(...) and use
> an improper prior.  Then you initialize around 1 because
> that's the center of the exp() transform to get values
> to be positive.
>
> For efficiency, don't duplicate calculations:
>
>     sk[1]=(Y[2*i-1]-yhat[1])^2;
>     sk[2]=(Y[2*i]-yhat[2])^2;
>     Fk[1]=Y[2*i-1]-yhat[1];
>     Fk[2]=Y[2*i]-yhat[2];
>
> Instead, you can vectorize the definition of sk as
>
>  Fk[1] = Y[2*i-1] - yhat[1];
>  Fk[2] = Y[2*i] - yhat[2];
>  sk[1] = square(Fk[1])
>  sk[2] = square(Fk[2]);
>
> or
>
>  Fk[1:2] = Y[(2 * i - 1):(2 * i)] - yhat[1:2];
>  sk[1:2] = square(Fk[1:2]);
>
> Also later,
>
>   V[4, 4] = V[3, 3];
>
> You never want to compute inverses, so instead of
>
>     u= D'*inverse(V)*Fk;
>
> it's much more stable to write
>
>   D' / V * Fk;
>
> where  D' / V  =def=  D' * inverse(V).   Same with later calc.
>
> We have a quad form, but you're inverting, so you can't use that.
> We should probably have an inverse quad form, and also a more
> general multiply_self_transpose---as is, we don't have the inverse
> quad form and only have multiply_self_transpose for triangular
> matrices.
>
> - Bob
>

> > 1) construct estimating equations u for parameters of interest theta
> > we are interested in solving u=0 to obtain estimates of theta
> > 2)  then the sample mean U = 1/N * sum(u_1,....,u_N) will be asymptotically normal with mean 0 and covariance which is consistently estimated by Sigma_hat (formula is given in Yin's paper).
> > 3) Apply a normal likelihood function to U (with mean 0 and covariance Sigma_hat) and flat priors for theta, then use MCMC to estimate the posterior distribution for all parameters of interest
> >
> > Yin's 2009 paper proposed the Bayesian GMM which I am trying to fit in STAN.  Essentially the model I'm trying to fit is a Bayesian anlog to the frequentist GEE model using an indepdence working correlation structure.  I simulated some simple data which consists of N 2-person families, thus we do not have independent subjects since the response (Y) will be correlated within each family.  However, GMM can be used to conduct valid inference on the mean parameters despite the fact that our working independent correlation structure is wrong.

messages.subject: Shutting stan up?
messages.subject_clean: Shutting stan up?
messages.body_plain:
Hey all,

I'm currently running a simulation study comparing different modeling techniques for a certain kind of data. The stan model in question is run 10,000 times for 240 different data conditions (varying in N, skewness, variance difference between groups, and imbalance of N between groups, so, basically, lots of simulations).

To save time, I'm using stan's optimizer and the hessians for some approximations, and I promise it makes sense in this case.

However, I've noticed that the optimizer will occasionally hang, so it's using 100% CPU but not progressing or providing output. I can stop the process, restart the condition, and get the 10,000 simulations for that condition within a few seconds.

I can't figure out why this is, but I /suspect/ it may be due to a gigantic number of messages that stan is sending (e.g., warnings about initial values not being evaluated, occasional problems evaluating the density on an optimizing stage).

Is there any way I can test this by truly shutting up stan? No messages, no warnings, no nothing; just the final converged output (and it always converges, so it doesn't appear to be a convergence issue)?

It's /really/ obnoxious having to hover over the rstudio output waiting for the optimizer to hang, killing the processes, restarting the sim after the last complete condition, etc.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Explicitly Correlated Parameters
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Explicitly Correlated Parameters
messages.body_plain:
This simpler model has one correlation, so I tried the Beta(2,2) prior that you discuss. I had the same issue.

One thing I noticed is that the standard deviation on the hierarchical intercept tends to get driven to zero, so I was curious if standardizing the data made any difference. But it didn't seem to make much of an improvement in one set of models. I'm currently running a Stan model with standardized variables* and correlation as you describe. Given how slow it's going, I'm expecting divergences.

I suspect it's some kind of identification issue, but I don't understand why if there's no identification problem with a univariate model, then there becomes one with a hierarchical one.

*With hierarchical models, it's correct to standardize with the overall mean and standard deviation, not the individual, correct?

On Thu, Mar 23, 2017 at 6:39 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
> You want the data to inform you about the corrs, but if the predictors are roughly zero-centered, then maybe you don't expect corrs to be fully degenerate.  In a model with one correlation, you can put a Beta(2,2) prior on (rho + 1)/2.  In a model with multiple correlations, you can use a Wishart (not inverse-Wishart) priors, as discussed here:
> http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/chung_cov_matrices.pdf
> A
>
> > On Mar 23, 2017, at 6:37 PM, John Hall <john.mic...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > "Let me just add to this discussion that there's nothing wrong at all about identifying parameters with the prior!  Suppose you have a regression with two collinear predictors and you have some prior information on the coefficients.  Then include the prior information!  No need to throw predictors out of the model just because of some scruple that prior info is cheating."
> >
> > I try to use reasonable priors on means and standard deviations, not overly tight but not too wide.
> >
> > The correlations are more tricky. Academic theory in my case has historically been that there's no correlation between the intercepts and slopes. However, recent studies have disputed the theory. Do I base the prior on the theory or the recent studies?
> >
> > On Thu, Mar 23, 2017 at 6:30 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
> > > Let me just add to this discussion that there's nothing wrong at all about identifying parameters with the prior!  Suppose you have a regression with two collinear predictors and you have some prior information on the coefficients.  Then include the prior information!  No need to throw predictors out of the model just because of some scruple that prior info is cheating.
> > > A
> > >
> > > > On Mar 23, 2017, at 6:27 PM, John Hall <john.mic...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > >
> > > > Some good points. I wanted to take some time to digest. A few comments:
> > > >
> > > > "To see this for yourself, we recommend simulating data from a model
> > > > that looks like what you want"
> > > >
> > > > The simulations I have used in the past often simulate the parameters as effectively multivariate normal. There are relatively fewer problems with the model in these cases because the model assumes multivariate normal and that's how the parameters are distributed when simulated. I get more problems when I switch to the actual data set and the parameters are no longer multivariate normal.
> > > >
> > > > "For arithmetic stability, we recommend using Cholesky factors
> > > > of correlation matrices with LKJ priors and then scaling (a
> > > > less ad hoc version of what Gelman and Hill recommend in
> > > > their regression book."
> > > >
> > > > I read and re-read the Stan documentation more regularly than I should admit...I followed a lot of the best practices, like LKJ priors.
> > > >
> > > > "And yes, correlations near -1 or 1 are going to be problematic
> > > > no matter what sampler you use.  This is largely a fact of the
> > > > way floating point arithmetic works.  You can represent numbers
> > > > like 1e-300 --- in other words, get very close to zero, but the
> > > > closest you can get to 1 or -1 in floating point is around 1 - 1e-15.
> > > > If there's nothing stopping you from wanting to get closer, you're
> > > > going to get divergences because you just can't even represent a number
> > > > that's closer to 1 or -1 without rounding error to 1 or -1, which in
> > > > turns makes the covariance matrix singular."
> > > >
> > > > I've been fitting the model with OLS and no pooling and comparing it to the results to Stan's output. So for instance, I can plot the distribution of intercepts vs. slopes in OLS and compare that to what the mean intercepts and slopes are from Stan. The correlation of the intercepts to the slopes from the OLS output is probably closer to -0.6. So it's modest, but it's not that extreme. I think the issue more is that Stan will move towards that +1 or -1 and then get stuck there. Also, the Stan plots looks much more like a multivariate normal than the OLS plots do. I suspect this is because of the divergences.
> > > >
> > > > "But this is just what Andrew calls the "folk theorem".  If your
> > > > inferences want a correlation near 1 or -1, you have two linearly
> > > > redundant parameters in your regression and you probably just want
> > > > to get rid of one.  Otherwise, they're only going to be identified
> > > > by the prior (see the manual section on problematic priors for a simple
> > > > example using two intercepts, which is just an extreme case of
> > > > the same problem)."
> > > >
> > > > I've made that mistake of effectively putting in two intercepts before...One thing that would make life a little easier is if divergences can be printed at the end of each chain or perhaps an option to exit early if there is a divergence (for instance, equivalent to a field that indicates success or failure in an optimization). Beyond that, I don't know if it would be possible for someone to write a program that parses a Stan model and it warns you if there are problems, at least for simple things like identification.
> > > >
> > > > Anyway, this part of your post caused me to go back and run a few more models. After double-checking, the divergences problem was showing up with explicitly multivariate normal intercepts/slopes, regardless of whether I used a constant standard deviation or varying standard deviations by group. However, I also realized that under some conditions, I would also get divergences when I did the model with varying intercepts, slopes, and standard deviations (which I don't think I had realized before double-checking). I could avoid these with some simple changes, like having 2 of 3 vary or changing the priors (for my data, varying standard deviations was more important than varying intercepts).
> > > >
> > > > There are two separate points I want to address with respect to the model being wrong:
> > > >
> > > > 1) The multivariate case. The idea that the model is wrong makes some sense since the empirical distribution of the OLS parameters I discussed above aren't REALLY multivariate normal. So there may be computational problems because I'm forcing a distribution to be multivariate normal, when it is really more complicated than that. In my case, I had wanted the intercepts and slopes to vary by individual. I knew from looking at the OLS results that individuals with high slopes tended to have low intercepts, so I assumed it was important to explicitly model the correlation with a multivariate normal. But I almost always had worse results when I did that. That's what I find intuitive. The model isn't wrong with separate univariate normal priors, but it becomes wrong with a multivariate normal one.
> > > >
> > > > 2) Varying intercepts/slopes/standard deviations. Stan can fit a univariate model with an intercept, slope, and standard deviation. And it can fit a no pooling version of that with many separate individuals each having their own intercepts, slopes, and standard deviations. But give all those parameters hierarchical priors and you get divergences. I don't find this intuitive. Why has the model become wrong?
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > On Tue, Mar 21, 2017 at 4:25 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> > > > > It's not so much a Stan problem as a general problem.
> > > > > There's no way to tweak multivariate proposals in Gibbs unless
> > > > > you block them, and they tend not to work in Metropolis unless
> > > > > you know the curvature (second derivative matrix) explicitly and
> > > > > it doesn't vary around the posterior.  What you may be finding
> > > > > is just that Stan's much better at exploring out the boundaries of
> > > > > parameter space and reporting when it gets into trouble.
> > > > >
> > > > > To see this for yourself, we recommend simulating data from a model
> > > > > that looks like what you want and trying to fit in various systems
> > > > > and look at the boundaries on 80% or 90% intervals you're getting
> > > > > (95% or higher will be too noisy without a high effective sample size).
> > > > > But you need to use Stan's posterior summary tools, which are also
> > > > > more conservative than Coda or other tools often applied to BUGS
> > > > > or JAGS models.
> > > > >
> > > > > It's not the correlation that causes so much of a problem as
> > > > > when the curvature (second derivative matrix aka Hessian) varies
> > > > > around the posterior, as in the funnel example.
> > > > >
> > > > > For arithmetic stability, we recommend using Cholesky factors
> > > > > of correlation matrices with LKJ priors and then scaling (a
> > > > > less ad hoc version of what Gelman and Hill recommend in
> > > > > their regression book.
> > > > >
> > > > > And yes, correlations near -1 or 1 are going to be problematic
> > > > > no matter what sampler you use.  This is largely a fact of the
> > > > > way floating point arithmetic works.  You can represent numbers
> > > > > like 1e-300 --- in other words, get very close to zero, but the
> > > > > closest you can get to 1 or -1 in floating point is around 1 - 1e-15.
> > > > > If there's nothing stopping you from wanting to get closer, you're
> > > > > going to get divergences because you just can't even represent a number
> > > > > that's closer to 1 or -1 without rounding error to 1 or -1, which in
> > > > > turns makes the covariance matrix singular.
> > > > >
> > > > > But this is just what Andrew calls the "folk theorem".  If your
> > > > > inferences want a correlation near 1 or -1, you have two linearly
> > > > > redundant parameters in your regression and you probably just want
> > > > > to get rid of one.  Otherwise, they're only going to be identified
> > > > > by the prior (see the manual section on problematic priors for a simple
> > > > > example using two intercepts, which is just an extreme case of
> > > > > the same problem).
> > > > >
> > > > > - Bob

> > > > > > There are already a few threads on the subject, but I'm not interested in a particular model. Rather, I'm just observing that models with explicitly correlated parameters are a bit quirky in Stan. I'm curious if people out there have a lot of success with explicitly correlated parameters versus the implicit case. I'm also curious about best practices on when to use them and when to not use. My thoughts are below.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > By explicitly correlated parameters, I mean a model that contains something like what is in Section 26.6 of the documentation under Multivariate Reparameterizations, rather than the previous section that handles the univariate case.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > With Gibbs sampling and Metropolis-Hastings, you have to include a multivariate distribution or the posterior distribution would be almost forced to have uncorrelated parameters. I believe the situation was similar with BUGS/JAGS. I suspect the focus in those techniques is why there is a decent amount of focus in the Stan documentation on models with correlated parameters.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > In Stan, my experience with correlated parameters in Stan has been rather frustrating. I almost always get worse results (in terms of having divergences, low N_eff, time to estimate, etc.) compared to univariate models. With a univariate prior on sets of parameters, the resulting posterior distribution on parameters might have some correlation when you look at them together, or maybe they won't. The only downside is that if you have some new observation, then you might need to make some assumptions in order to make predictions about it.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > I suspect that this is driven by the restrictions imposed by the multivariate normal prior. For instance, one model I'm estimating is a linear regression on some panel data, each regressed on one common time series variable with parameters varying cross-sectionally on the intercepts, slopes, and std. deviations (hierarchical priors on each of these three). By contrast, if you explicitly impose any kind of correlated parameters (centered or non-centered on the slopes and intercepts), then you get divergences or low N_eff and it takes forever way longer.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > To understand why this is, I focused on the posterior distribution of the parameters in the univariate case. Upon inspection, the slope looks a more log-normal than normal and the relationship of the intercept and the slope (or the slope and the standard deviations) looks non-linear. Thus, I suspect that imposing the linear correlation in the multivariate normal prevents the Stan sampler from finding the non-linear result.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Another potential explanation is sort of brought up in the wiki section on priors
> > > > > > https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Prior-Choice-Recommendations
> > > > > > under "Boundary-avoiding priors for modal estimation". I'm not sure it entirely applies, but it discusses the varying slope and intercept model and discusses the potential for a correlation of 1. Well, my example above often had a correlation near -1 between the intercepts and slopes. But, I'm not sure if this is a product of the divergences though.

messages.subject: Re: Shutting stan up?
messages.subject_clean: Shutting stan up?
messages.body_plain:
False alarm! It's failing due to occasional infinite loops caused by bad random inits. I used init=0 and the issues seem to have gone away.

That said, it /would/ be nice to shut stan up sometimes; it can flood the output window and nearly crashes my browser when using my rstudio server from my [crappy] laptop.
I've tried everything; sink('/dev/null'), the R functions for suppressing messages/warnings/output/etc, stan still finds a way to say something on my output window which can be an issue when you're running 10,000 models * 240 conditions.

On Friday, March 24, 2017 at 2:19:48 PM UTC-5, Stephen Martin wrote:
> Hey all,
>
> I'm currently running a simulation study comparing different modeling techniques for a certain kind of data. The stan model in question is run 10,000 times for 240 different data conditions (varying in N, skewness, variance difference between groups, and imbalance of N between groups, so, basically, lots of simulations).
>
> To save time, I'm using stan's optimizer and the hessians for some approximations, and I promise it makes sense in this case.
>
> However, I've noticed that the optimizer will occasionally hang, so it's using 100% CPU but not progressing or providing output. I can stop the process, restart the condition, and get the 10,000 simulations for that condition within a few seconds.
>
> I can't figure out why this is, but I /suspect/ it may be due to a gigantic number of messages that stan is sending (e.g., warnings about initial values not being evaluated, occasional problems evaluating the density on an optimizing stage).
>
> Is there any way I can test this by truly shutting up stan? No messages, no warnings, no nothing; just the final converged output (and it always converges, so it doesn't appear to be a convergence issue)?
>
> It's /really/ obnoxious having to hover over the rstudio output waiting for the optimizer to hang, killing the processes, restarting the sim after the last complete condition, etc.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] about paramter contrain
messages.body_plain:
If you want kappa in (0, 1) declare it as:

  real<lower=0, upper=1> kappa;

You can also define

  real kappa_raw;

  real<lower=0, upper=1> kappa = inv_logit(kappa_raw);

But if you do the latter, then you have to put the prior on kappa_raw
or adjust for the Jacobian of the transform yourself.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Explicitly Correlated Parameters
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Explicitly Correlated Parameters
messages.body_plain:
The hierarchical model can often collapse because
normal_lpdf(y | mu, sigma) is unbounded as sigma -> 0 and y -> mu.
That's why you can't do ordinary optimization or MLE with them.

You can get identifiability problems if you add in intercepts
and intercepts for the priors, because you essentially get two
intercepts.  This is the kind of thing that often gets identified
with priors.

If you're finding the real data a lot harder to fit than simulated
data, you might want to try to diagnose where the actual data's
violating the modeling assumptions.

- Bob

Given how slow it's going, I'm expecting divergences.
>

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

My goal is to evaluate rstan::log_prob() on a fitted Stan object (i.e., of class 'stanfit') in parallel using a cluster created with parallel::makeCluster().

The problem is that calling log_prob() on the model on the nodes (after exporting the stanfit object) produces the following error:
the model object is not created or not valid

I have tried a variety of things (trying to compile the object again on the nodes by calling rstan::sampling or rstan::stan_model), but nothing has worked so far. Any help would be very much appreciated. Below follows some example code exemplifying the problem.

Cheers,
Henrik

library(rstan)
# model
stancode <- 'data {
  int<lower=1> N; // number of observations
  vector[N] y; // observations
}
parameters {
  real<lower=0> sigma2;
}
model {
  target += cauchy_lpdf(sigma2 | 1, 1) - cauchy_lccdf(0 | 1, 1);
  target += normal_lpdf(y | 0, sqrt(sigma2));
}
'
stanmodel <- stan_model(model_code = stancode, model_name="stanmodel")

# generate data
set.seed(1)
N <- 5
sigma2_gen <- 1
y <- rnorm(N, sd = sqrt(sigma2_gen))

# fit model
stanobject <- sampling(stanmodel, data = list(y = y, N = N))
pars <- extract(object = stanobject, par = c("sigma2", "lp__"))
sigma2_t <- log(pars$sigma2)  # unconstrained pars

log_prob(stanobject, sigma2_t[1])
# [1] -7.545463

require(parallel)
cl <- makeCluster(2, useXDR = FALSE)

clusterEvalQ(cl, require(rstan))
clusterExport(cl = cl, varlist = c("stanobject", "sigma2_t"))
clusterEvalQ(cl, log_prob(stanobject, sigma2_t[1]))
# Error in checkForRemoteErrors(lapply(cl, recvResult)) :
#   2 nodes produced errors; first error: the model object is not created or not valid

stopCluster(cl)

messages.body_plain:
I'd just code it up and then see how well it scales with
multiple ODEs.  We've run large numbers of ODEs as parts of
likelihood calculations, but not ones with huge numbers of
parameters because internally we wind up needing Jacobians for
stiff systems and even for non-stiff systems we need the
derivatives of all state solutions w.r.t. parameters.  This
lets us solve the ODEs with control on the sensitivity (derivative)
errors.

In Bayesian models, we don't think in terms of things like least
squares algorithms.  Instead, we'd build a forward model of the
scientific process that depends on some unknown parameters about
which we'd like to learn (this may be deterministic and have unexplained
errors), and couple that with a model of the measurement process (such
as taking a stopwatch and ruler to measure a pendulum).  Then we
just run standard Bayesian inference to calculate probabilities over
the parameters conditioned on the data (so-called Bayesian inversion).

You could run Stan's maximum likelihood inference, which just
chooses optimal parameters.   If the noise is Gaussian, this
reduces to least squares.

- Bob

> On Mar 24, 2017, at 12:02 PM, Jaron <arbe...@umn.edu> wrote:
>

> ...
> 	• Not sure what you mean by "Also later,  V[4, 4] = V[3, 3];".... I think you may be confused about V and Sigma.  V is a 4x4 matrix used in the construction of the estimating equation u , and u is a 3x1 vector.  Sigma is the 3x3 estimated covariance matrix of u.

I just meant your program contained these two statements:

 V[3,3]=2*phi^2;
 V[4,4]=2*phi^2;

and the second should be replaced with:

 V[4, 4] = V[3, 3];

It saves a multiply and square going forward and an equivalent
amount of work in propagating derivatives (though it's worse because
it's like interpreted code) going backwards.  In general, you want
to reuse values rather than recompute them.  When they're recomputed,
they take up more space on the expression graph.

Maybe Sean will get around to finding them in code and optimizing
our graphs so it'll do this automatically under the hood.  But that's
not going into 2.15!

- Bob

What gets created by stan_model()?  Is that just a fit object
with no MCMC draws or data?

Would it be hard to have an object specifically for a model
instantiated with data?  That's what we want to use for the log
density and gradient calcs.  And maybe we'll eventually make the
data mutable to support more flexible algorithm development.

The pipeline that the C++ interface to Stan forces on interfaces is
basically:

1. stan program -> c++ class -> instantiated object code

2. data + c++ class -> c++ class instance

3. data + inits + seeds + other config -> MCMC draws object

Step (3) can be replaced with optimization, diagnostis, ADVI, etc.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Cannot evaluate rstan::log_prob on stanfit object passed to parallel nodes
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Cannot evaluate rstan::log_prob on stanfit object passed to parallel nodes
messages.body_plain:
Our current usecase is the following (an extension of what is available here https://cran.r-project.org/package=bridgesampling):

1. Users program their model and obtain samples from the posterior.
2. They pass the fitted model with the samples to our functions. We extract the posteriors samples on the unconstrained scale from the object.
3. We evaluate log_prob with old (i.e., posterior draws) and new samples on the unconstrained scale.

Right now one problem is that when the model is fitted (i.e., step 1) on a different PC, we cannot use the model object for evaluating log_prob. We can only use it to extract the samples on the constrained scale. For obtaining the unconstrained samples and running log_prob() we need a newly created stanfit object (without samples), However, we cannot recreate it from the model once it is loaded.

For an implementation of this see: https://github.com/quentingronau/bridgesampling/tree/stan_interface
Function: stan_bridge_sampler()

So we can get it to work with the current version, but it is not super convenient.

Cheers,
Henrik (and Quentin)

>
> What gets created by stan_model()?  Is that just a fit object

> instantiated with data?  That's what we want to use for the log

> basically:
>

>
> 3. data + inits + seeds + other config -> MCMC draws object
>
> Step (3) can be replaced with optimization, diagnostis, ADVI, etc.
>
> - Bob

You need a model class instantiated with data for log
density and constraining/unconstraining transforms.  That
involves platform-specific object code, so no way to port
cross platform without recompiling.  Right now, you have

generated to do all the transforms at once.  But we need to do that
anyway to make the C++ code for models more useful.

messages.subject: A meta analysis incorporating individual study uncertainty without raw data
messages.subject_clean: A meta analysis incorporating individual study uncertainty without raw data
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am currently working on a meta analysis of an aspect of the epidemiology of malaria. For those that are interested I am looking at the duration of the extrinsic incubation period (EIP; the time after a mosquito becomes infected with the parasite before it can transmit the parasite to a human).

The individual studies tend not to have the data that was used to form their estimates of EIP, but sometimes have an uncertainty associated with the quantity. For example they may quote EIP = 10 days +- 1 day.

As I said this is sometimes the case, although not always. As common is to just quote the point estimate of EIP = 10 days.

My question is, does anyone have any bright ideas as to how I could bring together this heterogeneous data in a meta analysis? I'm assuming that I'll use a hierarchical model, where the individual EIPs, and their uncertainties, are drawn from a population-level distribution. However I am not really clear what form the model should take, and how it can be sufficiently flexible to encompass both types of aforementioned data -- that with uncertainty and that without.

One idea is to assume the individual study data -- both the point estimate and the uncertainty parameterise the mean and sd of a normal distribution. However I can't really see how this helps.

Any references to relevant literature would also be most welcome! Having trouble finding comparable studies.

Best,

Ben

You have to integrate out the states. I believe there is an example in the manual.

> It would also be nice to keep kk[T] as a parameter but int params are not allowed.

The parameters block does not allow you to declare an int because NUTS requires the posterior log-kernel to be differentiable with respect to the unknowns. messages.body_plain:
Hi all,
I've been struggling for a while with a quite complex model involving numerical integration - a simple model with the integrator worked well, while more complex designs always gave divergent transitions. I was trying to built the model incrementally, but even adding the smallest complexities introduced divergent transitions. Now I am asking for help, because it seems that just using a vector with 1 element instead of a scalar in what is otherwise exactly the same model with exactly the same data causes problems. Honestly, I have ran out of ideas how to solve this.

More details on the model:
This is a model of gene expression where the synthesis of new mRNA is governed by the current level of a regulatory protein. In one model ('training-simplified.stan'), only one regulator is allowed. In the other model ('training.stan') multiple regulators are possible. Nevertheless, I modified the models to accept the exact same data format and only call 'training.stan' with num_regulators = 1, so the models should be exactly equal. I've removed all other differences - if you diff the files, you can see that they only differ in added for loops which go in 1:num_regulators (and num_regulators is 1).

Still one model produces divergent transitions and the other does not. Also there are noticeably different posterior distributions for some parameters.

Both models, data and code to reproduce are attached (the main code is in 'problem.R')

Note that the data I work with is simulated using the exact model I am trying to fit.

My specs:
Stan 2.14.0
Latest RStan built from source (to avoid bug https://github.com/stan-dev/rstan/issues/399)
R 3.3.2
gcc (i686-posix-dwarf, Built by MinGW-W64 project) 4.9.3
Windows 10

Thanks a lot for any hints

Martin

MCMC. The Stan language has almost no logic capabilities and cannot infer when there is an analytical solution.

> May I be less worried about the convergence of these models?

No, but convergence is rarely a problem for Stan. Mixing can be a problem but if the model is simple enough to have an analytical solution, then NUTS will probably mix really quickly.
