messages.subject: Joint model for Missing data in stan
messages.subject_clean: Joint model for Missing data in stan
messages.body_plain:
Hey Stan Community
Am attempting to build a joint model that takes care of missing data in a model with multiple predictors as recommended by Bob here <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/stan-users/missing$20data$20%7Csort:date/stan-users/0hqV_RDx9MU/NK5A74atBQAJ> and also in the manual. Using one of the R datasets mtcars, i have created a temporal missing values in three variables (disp, cyl,gear). The model runs fine and converges but the resultant coefficients are quite different when compared with data without missing values. Am i missing something in my model specification?. I have attached data and stan model below. Thanks in advance for your response.
Smockin.

Stan Code

data {
  int<lower=0>  N;     // total cases
  int<lower=0>  p;        //predictors
  int<lower=0> N_obs;   //observed cases both dependent & independent variables
  int<lower=0> N_miss;  //missed data in the independent variables but has data on dependent variable
  real y_obs[N_obs];      //dependent var with complete cases
  real y_miss[N_miss];    //dependent var with incomplete cases
  matrix[N_obs,p] x_obs;   //the model matrix of complete cases
}
parameters {
  real<lower=0> sigma;   //population standard dev
   vector[p] beta;     //the regression parameters & intercept
  real x_mu;                  // mean of dist of x values
  real<lower=0> x_sigma;      // sd of dist of x values
  matrix[N_miss,p] x_miss;   //imputed matrix
}

model {
    beta~ cauchy( 0 , 2.5 );
  sigma ~ uniform( 0 , 100 );
  x_mu ~ cauchy( 0 , 2.5 );
  x_sigma ~ uniform( 0 , 100 );

  //observed
  for (n in 1:N_obs) {
    for (k in 1:p)  {
      x_obs[n,k] ~ normal( x_mu , x_sigma );
      y_obs[n] ~ normal(beta[k]*x_obs[n,k], sigma);
      }
  }

  //missing; impute
  for (n in 1:N_miss) {
    for (k in 1:p)  {
      x_miss[n,k] ~ normal( x_mu , x_sigma );
      y_miss[n] ~ normal(beta[k]*x_miss[n,k], sigma);
    }
  }
}

Data

data("mtcars")
testData= mtcars

#Factors
testData$cyl<- factor(testData$cyl)
testData$gear<- factor(testData$gear)

#Dependent variable
y=testData$mpg

#True coefficients
trueCoef=coef(lm(mpg~cyl+disp+gear, data=testData))

# indices with mssing values
set.seed(1)
cyl.miss=sample(1:nrow(testData), 7,replace = F)
set.seed(2)
disp.miss=sample(1:nrow(testData), 7,replace = F)
set.seed(3)
gear.miss=sample(1:nrow(testData), 7,replace = F)

#Create missing values in data
testData$cyl[cyl.miss]<- NA_integer_
testData$disp[disp.miss]<- NA_real_

messages.subject: Re: A meta analysis incorporating individual study uncertainty without raw data
messages.subject_clean: A meta analysis incorporating individual study uncertainty without raw data
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ben,

With Stan there is little complication in fitting a model without the raw data (see the '8 schools' example), so if you believe the uncertainty estimates given, then you are good to go. If the studies just give you summary statistics (e.g "+- 1 day." --> is that a confidence interval?), you would need to assume a probability model to apply it (e.g the Normal example you describe)

Where uncertainty estimates are not given, it seems to me you could treat this as a missing data problem. On this list you should find examples of how people have dealt with missing data. If all studies report sample size, it might be reasonable to assume the underlying sd of data from different studies is the same, and then the missing uncertainty estimates can be predicted from the 'complete data' studies as a function of sqrt(sample size). However, is it reasonable to assume that the missing uncertainty estimates are missing-at-random?  If there is some signal in the fact that uncertainty is not reported (ie studies without uncertainty estimates mix some valid results with some rubbish), then it might be better to leave these results out.

Anyway, as they say about free advice, it may be worth exactly what you paid for it...

On Sunday, 26 March 2017 18:36:49 UTC-4, Ben Lambert wrote:
> Hi,
>
> I am currently working on a meta analysis of an aspect of the epidemiology of malaria. For those that are interested I am looking at the duration of the extrinsic incubation period (EIP; the time after a mosquito becomes infected with the parasite before it can transmit the parasite to a human).
>
> The individual studies tend not to have the data that was used to form their estimates of EIP, but sometimes have an uncertainty associated with the quantity. For example they may quote EIP = 10 days +- 1 day.
>
> As I said this is sometimes the case, although not always. As common is to just quote the point estimate of EIP = 10 days.
>
> My question is, does anyone have any bright ideas as to how I could bring together this heterogeneous data in a meta analysis? I'm assuming that I'll use a hierarchical model, where the individual EIPs, and their uncertainties, are drawn from a population-level distribution. However I am not really clear what form the model should take, and how it can be sufficiently flexible to encompass both types of aforementioned data -- that with uncertainty and that without.
>
> One idea is to assume the individual study data -- both the point estimate and the uncertainty parameterise the mean and sd of a normal distribution. However I can't really see how this helps.
>
> Any references to relevant literature would also be most welcome! Having trouble finding comparable studies.
>
> Best,
>
> Ben

>
> I suspect the problem is in how I construct the covariance matrix. I want to build
> the covariance using matrices S and FA and then use quad_form_sym(S, FA) (see line 71).
> However, if I build Sigma like this then I'm not sure how to use the built-in
> cov_matrix type to get the appropriate parameter transformations.

What transformation do you want?  It sounds like you're just
building your own covariance matrix.  If so, you just need to make
sure it's symmetric and positive definite.

> Without the automatic parameter transformations, I am not sure which prior
> to put on the X & dX covariance parameter XdX.
>
> Is there a better way to set up this model?

Not sure what you're trying to do.  You'd want to put a prior on
the components you use to construct the covariance matrix, so you
don't need to declare anything a covariance matrix.

I'd recommend recoding that loop to only solve each covariance
matrix once and to simplify the index logic, which is too
error prone.  Something like the following for J subjects:

  FA[embedD + 3] = L3;
  for (j in 1:J) {
    FA[embedD + 1] = 1 + eta[j] * L3;
    FA[embedD + 2] = L2 + zeta[j] * L3;
    Sigma = quad_form_sym(S, FA);
    X[start[j] : end[j]] ~ multi_normal(mu, Sigma);
  }

You add start[1:J] and end[1:J] for positions each
subject starts and ends in the X array.  This will be much
faster because you only have to solve Sigma once.

I didn't trace through all the logic building a covariance matrix.

Direct scaling by hand might be faster than our quad form given that
you have a roughly diagonal matrix.  All those multiplies by zero are
costly because they build out the expression graph.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hello Stan Community,

I am relatively new to Stan and I am struggling with one problem. I am creating a model with N+2 parameters:

parameters {
  real alpha;
  real beta;
  vector<lower=0>[N] lambda;
}

I would like to initialize alpha and beta to the value 3 and let Stan handle the vector lambda. In RStan I can simply write:

fit <- stan(file="pois_g1.stan",data=stan_data,chains=1,init=list(list(alpha=3,beta=3)))

I tried to do the same in cmdStan by creating an init.R file with the following

alpha <- 3
beta <- 3

But I always get the error:

Initialization from source failed.
variable lambda missing

It runs fine without the init.R file so I know it is a problem of initialization. How do I create an init.R file for cmdStan that allows for fixed alpha and beta while allowing Stan to handle the vector lambda of size N?

Thanks.

messages.subject: Hierarchical binomial with group-level predictors: Optimizing and predicting for new groups
messages.subject_clean: Hierarchical binomial with group-level predictors: Optimizing and predicting for new groups
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am attempting to fit a hierarchical multilevel binomial model with group-level predictors*, then use the resulting model to simulate predicted values for new groups.

My first issue is that the sampling is terribly slow, averaging about 8 samples/chain/minute while running 3 chains in parallel on 3 cores (2015 MacBook pro, 16gb ram, 2.9 GHz Intel Core i5). My dataset is fairly large (6300 rows) and I have 3 individual-level predictors and 2 group-level predictors with all interactions included within each level. I think I've implemented Matt's trick correctly, but is there some other way to speed up the sampling? I am also getting rather low n_eff, usually around 3000-5000 for 22,500 total post-warmup draws.

My second issue is that ultimately I would like to simulate predicted values for new groups with new data matrices of group- and individual level-predictors. I couldn't find any examples online of this type of predictions so I would love some validation that I wrote that section correctly in the "generated quantities" block.

Thank you very much,

Sam

*Background: The data come from a series of replicated experiments on the survival of crab larvae exposed to ultraviolet radiation. Experiments were conducted on different days (hence varying intercept for experiment) and on a total of 11 species of crabs. Larvae were grouped 4/chamber and the survival in individual chambers (replicates) was tracked over 3 days. Group (species)-level predictors are degree of pigmentation (proportion cover) and size of larvae of each species. Individual-level predictors are days of exposure, UV treatment (coded as 0, 1, or 2 for no UV, UVA, or UVA+UVB respectively), and cumulative light exposure (quantitative index of sun exposure).

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Models with an analytic solution
messages.body_plain:
No, Stan doesn't exploit any conjugacy---it just does HMC
on the log density.

If you have analytic posteriors, you don't need to use Stan!

Or if you can't do pure Monte Carlo on the analytic posterior,
just code up the posterior in Stan directly---the log density only
has to be equal to the posterior up to a constant---it doesn't have to
be the log joint.  There's a section in the optimization chapter
of the manual on how to do this for (partial) analytic posteriors.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Bug in log_mix?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Bug in log_mix?
messages.body_plain:
To answer your direct question, you can see if log_mix is doing the
right thing by comparing

  target += log_mix(p, lp1, lp2);

with

  target += log_sum_exp(log(p) + lp1, log1m(p) + lp2);

They should produce the same result.

But you're going to have a problem because you restrict y to (-1, 1)
but don't constraint the normal_lpdf.  This is usually OK under
two conditions:  (1) no Stan parameters are involved as parameters (violated
by your model), and (2) you don't use them in mixtures (also violated
by your model).  The solution's the same here --- you need to do the
explicit truncation with normal_lpdf(), using instead:

  normal_lpdf(y | 0, sigma) - (log(normal_cdf(1, 0, sigma) - normal_cdf(-1, 0, sigma))

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Using external software inside Stan
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Using external software inside Stan
messages.body_plain:
This should all be OK if you're writing a function for
your own use and can deal with the LAPACK linkage.  Our
existing functions tend to be much more C++ oriented, with
constant reference arguments and return values;  under the hood
we sometimes work with raw pointers when we need to control our
own memory.

Basically, you need to be able to construct the vari objects
that correspond to your results with chain() methods that do
the reverse mode autodiff (multiply the function's result's
adjoints by the partials and add to the corresponding operand's
adjoints). This is all explained in our arXiv paper.

If you just want an example of multivariate functions, all
of the matrix functions are like this, but their code's pretty
involved.

For constants (double arguments, presumably), you don't need
to do anything.  You won't be able to run Stan programs
that deal with them as parameters, but you shouldn't need to.
We don't have built-in functions like that.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Joint model for Missing data in stan
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Joint model for Missing data in stan
messages.body_plain:
Usually only some values are missing and you want to impute
them using some kind of joint model that depends on other variables.
And then put them back together with the observed components before
doing the regression.

Here it looks like you're just doing a global imputation marginally on
each x value.  And if one covariate is missing, they're all missing?

You shouldn't combine

  real<lower=0> x_sigma;      // sd of dist of x values

and

  x_sigma ~ uniform( 0 , 100 );

Stan requires positive density for all variables meeting constraints,
and x_sigma = 101 meets the constraints on x_sigma but has zero
density.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Initialization in cmdStan with fixed and randomized parameters
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Initialization in cmdStan with fixed and randomized parameters
messages.body_plain:
You shouldn't need to initialize anything in simple models.
Does the model not fit with fully Stan-generated random inits?

The place where random inits go bad is if you have upper and lower
bounds, because Stan tries to initialize around the middle of the range.

With the develop version of CmdStan I don't have a problem with
partial inits.  Are you sure you're using 2.14?  I don't think the inits
have been changed in develop since then.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Hierarchical binomial with group-level predictors: Optimizing and predicting for new groups
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Hierarchical binomial with group-level predictors: Optimizing and predicting for new groups
messages.body_plain:
It's hard to follow long programs, though much easier than trying
to tease apart fragments.

You can run into slow sampling if you run out of memory and have
to start swapping.  You might test relative speed of running one
chain at a time (3 is probably too many for an i5 as I think they
only have 2 cores---again, it's an empirical question that depends on
your CPU and memory speed).

How fast is it without the generated quantities?  You want to pull
repeated arithmetic out of loops:

  for (j in 1:S_N_Species)
    S_bet[j,] = multi_normal_cholesky_rng((S_U[j,] * gam)', diag_pre_multiply(tau, omegaL))';

So do that multiplication of tau and omegaL outside of the loop.
And try to avoid all the transpositions by rearraning the ata where possible.
And you can probably just do S_U * gam and store it in a local variable
rather than trying to slice it apart by row (inefficient because Eigen stores
matrices column-major).

And there are more efficient ways to generate multinormals than
multi_normal_cholesky---I think the GP sections of the manual explain
some alternatives, but I can't recall --- the idea is to generate
a standard normal and then transform (rotate and scale) by covariance.

There are other things you could do to reduce some
redundant calcs, such as storing

bet[Species[n]]' + B

for all the species then indexing in the 1:N loop, but unless N is much
greater than the number of species, that won't help much.

- Bob

P.S.  We're going to deprecate # as a comment really soon when we
add includes --- please switch to using // for line comments.

2.9 GHz Intel Core i5). My dataset is fairly large (6300 rows) and I have 3 individual-level predictors and 2 group-level predictors with all interactions included within each level. I am also getting rather low n_eff, usually around 3000-5000 for 22,500 total post-warmup draws.

My second issue is that ultimately I would like to simulate predicted values for new groups with new data matrices of group- and individual level-predictors. I couldn't find any examples online of this type of predictions so I would love some validation that I wrote that section correctly in the "generated quantities" block.

Thank you very much,

Sam

*Background: The data come from a series of replicated experiments on the survival of crab larvae exposed to ultraviolet radiation. You probably want to try non-centered parameterizations
down at the lower level, such as here:

> for(i in 1:2) ex_mean[i] ~ normal(ex_mean_mean, ex_mean_sd);

That's probably important for those gammas, too, but I don't know
how to do that off the top of my head (someone else probably does).

You can also try including some priors to keep those sd
parameters away from zero.

More generally, try turning adapt_delta up near 1 and see if
that helps with the numerical issues.

messages.body_plain:
Hi to everyone,

I am completely new in Stan, reason why I write to ask for advice, opinions and suggestions.

I am working with a system of 8 coupled ordinary differential equations to model a biological fermentation process. It is a quite classic model from the point of view of theoretical biology, which as most problems in this field, counts with a considerable number of parameters (24 in total) that need to be estimated. So far, I have been working under a deterministic framework (solving the system by means of linearization which its objective is to minimize a sum of squares difference between real and simulated data). However, this approach gives me a vast uncertainty of my parameter solution space since it seems to have multiple solutions and very likely, local optimal regions.

For this reason, I was wondering if you might give me advice from your experience if such problem could be tackled with bayesian optimization using Stan. If so, what interface would you suggest me? (Rstan, PyStan?), where can I find examples of something alike (papers, websites, etc)

Any help is more than appreciated,

Waiting to hear from you soon,

Kind regards,

Mauricio

Hey folks

After running pystan successfully for several months, last night I ran pystan in an interactive python session (for debugging) on an interactive node on a linux cluster and I got this error:

/tmp/tmpsQ7Mbx/stanfit4anon_model_e2c1f38939a832118f4bc52b1339b844_5550264428218593261.cpp: At global scope:

My question is whether there's a way to redirect these temporary files & folders to a different directory of my choosing?  I don't want to have to bother the sysadmin each time the folder fills up (other people leave very large files sometimes).   They're supposed to be deleted automatically but for some reason they weren't this time...  Also, if I submit a few hundred jobs on a few hundred machines and some of them fail this way then I'll have to bother the sysadmin to track down the errors for me.

If someone can let me know if there's a way to redirect these files it might help for the future.

David

messages.body_plain:
Hi!

Is it possible to disable *all* data manipulations from RStanArm?

I learned that I need to use autoscale=FALSE to avoid any scaling, but then I am left with automatic centering. At least this is what the prior_summary function tells me (or I understand it as such).

So how can I avoid that RStanArm does any scaling or centering for me such that the priors have their actual meaning as specified?

I know that scaling and centering are really important, but I much prefer to do that myself. Using means and standard deviations from the data is only a quick and dirty solution to me, I prefer to center and scale using meaningful references which are problem specific.

Many thanks!

Best,
Sebastian

messages.subject: Hierarchical multi-group Poisson model: low n_eff on pooled scale priors
messages.subject_clean: Hierarchical multi-group Poisson model: low n_eff on pooled scale priors
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am doing an epidemiological study, where I am trying to see if some exposure (Ex) increases a subsequent event (Ev) for a given population. For every person that has the exposure, I've randomly sampled 5 controls that did not have the exposure, matched by sex and age-group. There are 10 different age groups. There are also some other covariates used for matching, but I have left them out to keep the model as simple as possible.

I want to estimate the relative risk between the Ex and Ev. To do this I have implemented a Poisson model,

Y ~ Poisson(b0 + bSex + bAge + bEx + bEv + bEx:Ev + offset)

The offset is the total number of people within a stratification group (i.e., a given combination of sex and age). To keep the number of model parameters low, I have taken the mean of an age group and used as a continous variable, instead of adding nine different variables for the age groups. The age has been scaled to mean=0 and unit variance.

The idea is that the exponentiated interaction between the Ex and Ev is the relative risk ratio (~relative risk). To complete the model, I've specified that the coefficients of the linear model has normal priors, and the scale of the normal distribution is determined by a truncated t-distribution with 7 df. I have put a pretty constrained prior on the scale for the sex and age coefficients, since I expect these to be very, very close to zero due to the case-control structure. Some experiments with scale=1 on the coefficients indicate that the magnitude of the sex and age coefficients is between 10^-4 to 10^-6.  The coefficients for Ex, Ev and Ex:Ev are set to weakly informative, as this coefficient typically be between -1.5 and 1.5

Simulating the priors in R, I get the following (may vary due to tails of the t-distribution):

sigma <- rt(1000, df=7); sigma[sigma < 0] <- 0; beta <- rnorm(1000, 0, sigma); quantile(beta, c(2.5/100, 97.5/100))
     2.5%     97.5%
-1.579362  1.410655

sigma <- rt(1000, df=7); sigma[sigma < 0] <- 0; beta <- rnorm(1000, 0, sigma*0.001); quantile(beta, c(2.5/100, 97.5/100))
        2.5%        97.5%
-0.001614221  0.001864774

Additionally, I have multiple different Ex->Ev risks I want to estimate, so I have grouped them into a hierarchical model with a pooled prior on the scale. In total I have J=52 groups. The Stan model can be seen at https://gist.github.com/demodw/df5c9b042d1de50a9694dd098385bc44. The scales for the age and sex coefficient seem to be in the order of 10^-4 to 10^-3, where the scale for the Ex, Ev and interaction is on the unit scale.

My problem is that the n_eff for the scale priors on sex and age is incredibly low and, I guess, consequently R-hat is ~1.1. with warmup=2000 and samples=2000, I get about an n_eff < 40 and n_eff/s ~ 10^-3 to 10^-4. All other parameters look acceptable. The output from stansummary can be seen at https://gist.github.com/demodw/23c31ca5304d3304f15ad2b17e35dfef.
 The n_eff for the regression coefficients are all well above 200. Posterior predictions are actually looking OK, but I am wondering if they could be better if I found a way to increase the n_eff for the scales.

What I have tried so far:

1. The Matt trick. I re-parameterized all parameters using the Matt-trick. No effect. The tree depth started maxing past warm-up, and the n_eff for the _raw parameters were as low as the transformed parameters.
2. A partial Matt trick. I re-parameterized only the troublesome scale priors using the Matt trick. Same as above.
3. Changing priors. I've tried normal and gamma distributions. No effect.
4. Varying the scale-prior. Constraining it even more gives Stan trouble exploring the posterior.
5. Standardizing sex, even though it's a binary variable, to have mean=0 and sd=1. No effect.
6. Switching to a negative binomial model. This actually worsens the posterior prediction, except for when Ex=0 and Ev=0.

Any advice on how to proceed?

Cheers, and sorry for the wall of text! I tried to describe the exact problem in detail.

messages.body_plain:
Not clear on what you commented out here.

I think the problem is that the imputation model you're
using for the predictors is bad.  You're modeling each
predictor marginally, where what you want to do is model
them jointly.

I'm guessing that if you simulate data from the model (where
each predictor is independent in each instance), you'd get
much better fits.

- Bob

> them using some kind of joint model that depends on other variables.
> And then put them back together with the observed components before
> doing the regression.
>
> Here it looks like you're just doing a global imputation marginally on
> each x value.  And if one covariate is missing, they're all missing?
>
> You shouldn't combine
>
>   real<lower=0> x_sigma;      // sd of dist of x values
>
> and

> Stan requires positive density for all variables meeting constraints,

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] disabling *all* data transformations?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] disabling *all* data transformations?
messages.body_plain:
Are you worried that standardizing data leads to
data-specific priors?  I think you wind up getting very
similar results as to not transforming, but I'd like
to see that better formalized and I'd like to know roughly
how much data you need before the empirical standardization
on a specific sample converges within whatever tolerance
you have to not standardizing.

So in a simple case,

  Y ~ normal(alpha + X * beta, sigma);

where x and y are realization of the random variables
X and Y, then the sample standardization

  z = (x - mean(x)) / sd(x)

should converge as the size of x grows (assuming x is well behaved)
to (X - E[X]) / sd[X].

I just don't know how fast that's going to happen.

If you have weakly informative priors on alpha and beta,
then it probably won't make much of a difference because the
prior sensitivity will be similarly weak if the data is
consistent with the prior.

So I think Ben's just saying that you can transform your
priors based based on the expected standardization of X and Y,
and you should be OK.  To do that, of course, you need
to know E[X], sd[X], E[Y], and sd[Y].

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] disabling *all* data transformations?
messages.body_plain:
I simply don't want to give away control. There can be good reasons to not standardize using the data at hand, but to some other rationale. Whatever other rationale used should be close to the usual data standardization, yes, but there can be situations when this differs.

rstanarm was probably built for the "weak" prior regime and works-out-of-the-box using defaults. However, to me one of the biggest advantages from using Bayesian inference is whenever data is sparse or I can use informative prios. Hence, I *want* that my prior shows up in the analysis. In that case things matter.

I am just used by now to try to understand what is my model saying, i.e. what is my reference and what is my scale telling me. Its already hard enough for me to figure that out; and now I also need to take rstanarm arms magic into account... but maybe that's a personal preference and I belong to those 5% of users quoted earlier...

Anyway, as I understand Ben, I can always figure out my priors by shifting the prior by the data mean to get what I want. I would really prefer an option in rstanarm which allows me to disable all internal magic. How about an extra argument to the priors? In addition to autoscale an autocenter option?

Best,
Sebastian

messages.subject: Contradiction or misunderstanding
messages.subject_clean: Contradiction or misunderstanding
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

In page 325 of the Manual (latest version 2.14.0) I see something that sound contradictory.

A hierarchical model such as the above will suffer from the same kind of inefficiencies as Neal’s funnel, because the values of beta, mu_beta and sigma_beta are highly correlated in the posterior. The extremity of the correlation depends on the
amount of data, with Neal’s funnel being the extreme with no data. In these cases, the non-centered parameterization, discussed in the next section, is preferable; when there is a lot of data, the centered parameterization is more efficient. See Betancourt and Girolami (2013) for more information on the effects of centering in hierarchical
models fit with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo.

Non-Centered Parameterization

When there is a lot of data, such a hierarchical model can be made much more efficient
by shifting the data’s correlation with the parameters to the hyperparameters. Similar
to the funnel example, this will be much more efficient in terms of effective sample
size when there is not much data

Thus if I understand correctly then in both cases (no data or a lot of data) non-centered parameterization is preferable. Therefore the first statement is contradictory with the second one.

Or do I misunderstand something?

Kind regards,
Tran.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] disabling *all* data transformations?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] disabling *all* data transformations?
messages.body_plain:
I have the same preferences, but that exact level of
control isn't (and I'd argue shouldn't be) the goal
of RStanArm---we have RStan for that.

I also think features should be added with great care
so as not to complicate a product.  Each addition makes
the doc bigger and makes the whole harder to understand.
Horses for courses, as the bettors say.

I don't have an opinion on this particular feature for
RStanArm.  Sometimes the added complexity (and *any*
option is added complexity) is worth it.

I think if you actually have priors (that is prior to
the data), then you'll need to see the data and convert
to the equivalent prior after seeing the data.

- Bob

> On Mar 31, 2017, at 3:58 AM, Sebastian Weber <sdw....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> I simply don't want to give away control. There can be good reasons to not standardize using the data at hand, but to some other rationale. Whatever other rationale used should be close to the usual data standardization, yes, but there can be situations when this differs.
>
> rstanarm was probably built for the "weak" prior regime and works-out-of-the-box using defaults. However, to me one of the biggest advantages from using Bayesian inference is whenever data is sparse or I can use informative prios. Hence, I *want* that my prior shows up in the analysis. In that case things matter.
>
> I am just used by now to try to understand what is my model saying, i.e. what is my reference and what is my scale telling me. Its already hard enough for me to figure that out; and now I also need to take rstanarm arms magic into account... but maybe that's a personal preference and I belong to those 5% of users quoted earlier...
>
> Anyway, as I understand Ben, I can always figure out my priors by shifting the prior by the data mean to get what I want. I would really prefer an option in rstanarm which allows me to disable all internal magic. How about an extra argument to the priors? In addition to autoscale an autocenter option?
>
> Best,
> Sebastian
>
> On Thursday, March 30, 2017 at 4:11:50 PM UTC+2, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Are you worried that standardizing data leads to
> data-specific priors?  I think you wind up getting very
> similar results as to not transforming, but I'd like
> to see that better formalized and I'd like to know roughly
> how much data you need before the empirical standardization
> on a specific sample converges within whatever tolerance
> you have to not standardizing.
>
> So in a simple case,
>
>   Y ~ normal(alpha + X * beta, sigma);
>
> where x and y are realization of the random variables
> X and Y, then the sample standardization
>
>   z = (x - mean(x)) / sd(x)
>
> should converge as the size of x grows (assuming x is well behaved)
> to (X - E[X]) / sd[X].
>
> I just don't know how fast that's going to happen.
>
> If you have weakly informative priors on alpha and beta,
> then it probably won't make much of a difference because the
> prior sensitivity will be similarly weak if the data is
> consistent with the prior.
>
> So I think Ben's just saying that you can transform your
> priors based based on the expected standardization of X and Y,
> and you should be OK.  To do that, of course, you need
> to know E[X], sd[X], E[Y], and sd[Y].
>
> - Bob
>
>
>
>
>
>
>
>
>
>
>
>
>
>
> > On Mar 30, 2017, at 8:28 AM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > On Thursday, March 30, 2017 at 6:07:31 AM UTC-4, Sebastian Weber wrote:
> > I know that scaling and centering are really important, but I much prefer to do that myself. Using means and standard deviations from the data is only a quick and dirty solution to me, I prefer to center and scale using meaningful references which are problem specific.
> >
> > I think the only way to avoid centering is to specify sparse = TRUE, which will probably make it slower. But if you have strong prior beliefs about the intercept with the original predictors, it should be straightforward to figure out what your prior beliefs are when the predictors are centered.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Explicitly Correlated Parameters
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Explicitly Correlated Parameters
messages.body_plain:
> On Mar 29, 2017, at 2:59 PM, John Hall <john.mic...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Comments in line.
>
> On Fri, Mar 24, 2017 at 6:20 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> The hierarchical model can often collapse because
> normal_lpdf(y | mu, sigma) is unbounded as sigma -> 0 and y -> mu.
> That's why you can't do ordinary optimization or MLE with them.
>
> You can get identifiability problems if you add in intercepts
> and intercepts for the priors, because you essentially get two
> intercepts.  This is the kind of thing that often gets identified
> with priors.
>
> Just to confirm: you're saying that if you have intercepts, then you can't have intercepts in the priors. But, you can have intercepts in the priors if there is no intercept in the problem?

What I'm saying is that if you have multiple intercepts (say one
global one and then group-level intercepts), then you only get
identification through the prior because you can add to the global
intercept and subtract from the group intercepts and get the same
value.  Usually this is mitigated with using n-1 intercepts if
there are n groups and pinning one to zero.

>
> I'm prefacing the following with the reminder that the model I am discussing is a panel with each individual regressed one time series, and different intercepts, slopes, and standard deviations for each.
>
> With explicitly correlated parameters, I had originally been doing something like
>         B_mu ~ normal(B_prior_mu, B_prior_sd);
>         for (i in 1:N_Y)
>             B_n[i] ~ multi_normal_prec(B_mu , inv_sigma);
>
> B_prior_mu would have been something like {0, 1}, since I had a fairly good idea that the average slope would be closer to 1.
>
> And now I'm doing something like
>         for (i in 1:N_Y)
>             B_n[i] ~ multi_normal_prec(B_prior_mu, inv_sigma);
>
> As a result the divergences seem to have disappeared. However, I'm not sure this is exactly what you are suggesting.

You're making a normal-normal model of B_n in the first case and a normal
model in the second case.  I don't think you want to do the former unless
you have some kind of explicit measurement-error model, and even then, it's
usually on the data side.

> What you're saying seems closer to something like
>
>         B_mu ~ normal(0, B_prior_sd);
>         for (i in 1:N_Y)
>             B_n[i] ~ multi_normal_prec(B_prior_mu, inv_sigma);

I think B_mu and B_prior_mu were meant to be the same variable here,
so I'll assume that should be B_mu in the third line.

> which is similar to what is in the Stan manual in Section 8.13. However, the manual says that more information can be incorporated into u_{k} (might be a typo, since there is no u_{k}, only u_{j}). If it only makes sense to adjust the standard deviation of the prior, then it might be made more clear in the manual.

It's OK if the prior for B_mu here is any kind of constant --- it
doesn't have to be zero.  If it's a variable, then you just wind
up with a compound distribution for B_mu (sort of like beta-binomial
or gamma-Poisson [aka negative binomial]).

>
> Similarly, if I were doing this without explicit correlation, I should do something like (excluding the other stuff for brevity)
>
>     beta ~ normal(0, B_prior_sd[2]);
>     beta_n_sd ~ normal(0, B_n_prior_sd[2]);
>     beta_n ~ normal(beta, beta_n_sd);
>
> instead of
>
>     beta ~ normal(1, B_prior_sd[2]);
>     beta_n_sd ~ normal(0, B_n_prior_sd[2]);
>     beta_n ~ normal(beta, beta_n_sd);
>
> even if I have a good idea that beta should have a mean closer to 1?

No, if you think the mean's closer to 1, by all means use that second
case.  Zero isn't the relevant thing here, it's whether it's a parameter
or not.

> If you're finding the real data a lot harder to fit than simulated
> data, you might want to try to diagnose where the actual data's
> violating the modeling assumptions.
>
> This was a good suggestion, but it has been a rather time-consuming project. It turned out to be harder than I thought to figure out exactly what part of the data was violating the assumptions. I kept making it more and more realistic without finding where it was going wrong. Eventually I realized that the problem was that I had been filling a matrix with normal random variables and that I needed to center them before proceeding. Not centering meant that there was some extra variation in the intercept (i.e. I had made an inadvertent additional change in the assumptions). So I'm starting the search over now.

Yup, challenging, but usually worth the effort in model understanding and
peace of mind that your code works.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] biglm and rstanarm optimization
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] biglm and rstanarm optimization
messages.body_plain:
How big is big?  Doing this with anything other than
stochastic gradient for really big problems is madness.
And by really big, I mean ones that won't fit into memory.

Then if you have sparse predictors, you really really need
sparse arithmetic.

Something like Vowpal Wabbit can scale pretty well for
these kinds of problems, though it's not exact given the way
it encodes features.

Just writing the linear model in Stan and optimizing will
be faster than lm() and more scalable probably.  Don't know
how RStan impacts this equation, but in CmdStan you can
run medium-sized data sets (not what I'd call big and nothing
that won't fit in memory).

- Bob

> On Mar 29, 2017, at 1:48 PM, Andrew Gelman <Gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>
> Hi all.  Phil was telling me how he's running simple regressions with big datasets and using the R package biglm which feeds the data into lm() piece by piece so R's memory won't choke.  I was thinking maybe we should build something that would do the same thing for rstanarm.  When stan_lm() or stan_glm() is in optimization mode, it's super-fast, so this would seem to make a lot of sense, no?
> A
>
>

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Hierarchical multi-group Poisson model: low n_eff on pooled scale priors
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Hierarchical multi-group Poisson model: low n_eff on pooled scale priors
messages.body_plain:
It's often challenging to get high n_eff for the hierarchical parameters,
and often nailing them down precisely doesn't do anythnig to the posterior
predictions you care about.

You want to check consistency of your priors and posteriors---mismatches
are problematic as are any other kind of model misspecification.

Otherwise, you want to look at things like posterior pairs to see if
some of the parameter pairs produce bad geometries like bananas or
funnels.  If so, that can give you a clue as to where to look.

The other thing to do is run longer warmups to make sure adaptation
have converged, then run longer chains.  If the n_eff/time stays the
same and n_eff grows with iteration, you should eventually get to convergence.

- Bob

> On Mar 30, 2017, at 8:30 AM, David Westergaard <da...@harsk.dk> wrote:
>
> Hi,
>
> I am doing an epidemiological study, where I am trying to see if some exposure (Ex) increases a subsequent event (Ev) for a given population. For every person that has the exposure, I've randomly sampled 5 controls that did not have the exposure, matched by sex and age-group. There are 10 different age groups. There are also some other covariates used for matching, but I have left them out to keep the model as simple as possible.
>
> I want to estimate the relative risk between the Ex and Ev. To do this I have implemented a Poisson model,
>
> Y ~ Poisson(b0 + bSex + bAge + bEx + bEv + bEx:Ev + offset)
>
> The offset is the total number of people within a stratification group (i.e., a given combination of sex and age). To keep the number of model parameters low, I have taken the mean of an age group and used as a continous variable, instead of adding nine different variables for the age groups. The age has been scaled to mean=0 and unit variance.
>
> The idea is that the exponentiated interaction between the Ex and Ev is the relative risk ratio (~relative risk). To complete the model, I've specified that the coefficients of the linear model has normal priors, and the scale of the normal distribution is determined by a truncated t-distribution with 7 df. I have put a pretty constrained prior on the scale for the sex and age coefficients, since I expect these to be very, very close to zero due to the case-control structure. Some experiments with scale=1 on the coefficients indicate that the magnitude of the sex and age coefficients is between 10^-4 to 10^-6.  The coefficients for Ex, Ev and Ex:Ev are set to weakly informative, as this coefficient typically be between -1.5 and 1.5
>
> Simulating the priors in R, I get the following (may vary due to tails of the t-distribution):
>
> sigma <- rt(1000, df=7); sigma[sigma < 0] <- 0; beta <- rnorm(1000, 0, sigma); quantile(beta, c(2.5/100, 97.5/100))
>      2.5%     97.5%
> -1.579362  1.410655
>
> sigma <- rt(1000, df=7); sigma[sigma < 0] <- 0; beta <- rnorm(1000, 0, sigma*0.001); quantile(beta, c(2.5/100, 97.5/100))
>         2.5%        97.5%
> -0.001614221  0.001864774
>
>
> Additionally, I have multiple different Ex->Ev risks I want to estimate, so I have grouped them into a hierarchical model with a pooled prior on the scale. In total I have J=52 groups. The Stan model can be seen at https://gist.github.com/demodw/df5c9b042d1de50a9694dd098385bc44. The scales for the age and sex coefficient seem to be in the order of 10^-4 to 10^-3, where the scale for the Ex, Ev and interaction is on the unit scale.
>
> My problem is that the n_eff for the scale priors on sex and age is incredibly low and, I guess, consequently R-hat is ~1.1. with warmup=2000 and samples=2000, I get about an n_eff < 40 and n_eff/s ~ 10^-3 to 10^-4. All other parameters look acceptable. The output from stansummary can be seen at https://gist.github.com/demodw/23c31ca5304d3304f15ad2b17e35dfef.
>  The n_eff for the regression coefficients are all well above 200. Posterior predictions are actually looking OK, but I am wondering if they could be better if I found a way to increase the n_eff for the scales.
>
> What I have tried so far:
>
> 1. The Matt trick. I re-parameterized all parameters using the Matt-trick. No effect. The tree depth started maxing past warm-up, and the n_eff for the _raw parameters were as low as the transformed parameters.
> 2. A partial Matt trick. I re-parameterized only the troublesome scale priors using the Matt trick. Same as above.
> 3. Changing priors. I've tried normal and gamma distributions. No effect.
> 4. Varying the scale-prior. Constraining it even more gives Stan trouble exploring the posterior.
> 5. Standardizing sex, even though it's a binary variable, to have mean=0 and sd=1. No effect.
> 6. Switching to a negative binomial model. This actually worsens the posterior prediction, except for when Ex=0 and Ev=0.
>
>
> Any advice on how to proceed?
>
> Cheers, and sorry for the wall of text! I tried to describe the exact problem in detail.
>

Pretty much unlimited in the number of observations. The stan_{big}lm() function uses OLS estimates as sufficient statistics to evaluate the likelihood and the biglm() function produces OLS estimates by incrementally updating the QR decomposition as each batch of data is read off the disk. Both the biglm part and the Stan part of stan_biglm() are quadratic in the number of predictors.

messages.body_plain:
On Friday, March 31, 2017 at 3:48:49 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Neat.    I had no idea there were functions like that in
> RStanArm.  Is there a feature list somewhere?

There is a list of the stan_foo fitting functions in the overview page of the doc, but we don't re-document what foo() does.

> They're quadratic rather than cubic?  I thought you needed
> to solve N x N matrices where there are N predictors?

The biglm() function is documented to be quadratic in the number of predictors for memory. It does a bunch of Jacobi rotations, which is presumably of cubic complexity, but that only has to be done once. After it gets to Stan, the log-likelihood is pretty much just a dot_self() on the difference between the OLS coefficients and the proposed coefficients (in orthogonalized coordinates, so it is Euclidean distance rather than Mahalanobis).

> I guess that's all feasible with the simple structure of LMs.
> For GLMs, I've always seen stochastic gradient used.  Would there
> be a way to do something similar under the link function for
> logistic regression?

No.

Ben
